articles.title: From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military
articles.summary: Kazakhstan has asked Moscow to help bring home citizens who say they were pressured into signing military contracts to fight in Ukraine. The request puts a fresh spotlight on the vulnerability of Central Asian migrants to Russia’s military enlistment efforts.

articles.title: Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence
articles.summary: The Lenin District Court in Bishkek found activist and politician Mavlyan Askarbekov guilty and sentenced to two years in prison on offenses related to a law on incitement of racial, ethnic, national, religious, or interregional hatred, a verdict he called "absurd."

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan To Become Spacefaring Nation With Mini Satellite
articles.summary: Kyrgyzstan is set to send a domestically produced satellite into orbit on October 1, marking the Central Asian state's first feat of spacefaring. Uzbekistan has announced its own plans for a domestic satellite.

articles.title: 'Million Dollar' Mutton: Kyrgyzstan's New Monster Sheep Breed
articles.summary: A new Kyrgyz sheep breed is charging to fame in Central Asia for the size of its males and the massive prices being reported for prime specimens of the variety.

articles.title: Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen
articles.summary: The hijab has long been a hot topic in Muslim-majority Central Asia, where many authoritarian governments have suppressed Islamic political and religious groups and any outward signs of religiosity. The debate has been rekindled as the new academic year started this month.

articles.title: In US-China AI Race, Kazakhstan Faces Pressure To Pick A Side
articles.summary: Kazakhstan is the only country to have joined both a US-led artificial intelligence initiative and a China-led rival. Now Washington is signaling that it may not be possible to sit on both sides of the emerging AI divide.

articles.summary: Families of dozens of Kyrgyz women imprisoned in Iraq are calling on the government to bring them home. The women -- mostly wives and relatives of Islamic State fighters -- traveled to Iraq and Syria more than a decade ago as the extremist group seized swaths of territory.

articles.summary: Tajikistan has begun receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran in a move to diversify supplies long dominated by Russia. articles.title: Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Russia's war against Ukraine is at a stalemate but could escalate into a broader regional conflict if the deadlock pushes either side toward increasingly dangerous actions.

articles.title: Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine
articles.summary: As Ukraine prepares for its fifth winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, a document obtained by RFE/RL sets out a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water.

articles.title: More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine
articles.summary: Moldova saw more Russian drones crash on its territory in August than it did over all of 2025. Moldovan authorities are increasingly rattled—but there’s little a cash-strapped government can do beyond complaining diplomatically.

articles.title: Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk
articles.summary: Dozens of people were killed in a Russian strike on the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on October 8, according to local authorities, a day after another deadly barrage killed at least 25 people across Ukraine.

articles.title: US Reports 81 US Aircraft Lost Or Damaged In Iran War
articles.summary: As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis.

articles.title: 'Psychological War': Exiled Russian Activist Describes How Kremlin Targets Critics Abroad
articles.summary: Mikhail Klimaryov fled Russia to escape political persecution and now lives in Germany, but says he is still not safe. The constant pressure from Kremlin agents has, he says, driven him to "a kind of paranoia" about his security.

articles.title: No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies
articles.summary: Authoritarian states such as Russia and Iran are increasingly pursuing their opponents even after they find shelter in apparently safe Western countries. RFE/RL talks to some of those affected.

articles.title: Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk
articles.summary: Belarus’s Minsk Automobile Plant is under Western sanctions, limiting who can buy the vehicles produced there. That may be the reason trucks branded with the previously unknown “HAL” badge have been spotted amid strengthening trade relations between Belarus and Indonesia.

articles.title: EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations
articles.summary: The European Union has expressed “deep concern” over Kosovo’s adoption of legislation that seeks to narrow the jurisdiction of a Hague-based war crimes court, saying the changes violate the country’s international obligations toward the bloc.

articles.title: Testing Times For Mecca Alliance Partners As Iran-Aligned Houthis Mount Attacks
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia’s allies Pakistan and Turkey are facing a major test just two months after signing a joint defense agreement as the rise of Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen test the deal that says “any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.”

articles.title: Rubio In Athens Warns Iran It Will Never Have A Nuclear Weapon
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran will never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon, declaring that preventing Tehran from doing so is a red line for President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Massive Russian Attack Kills At Least 22, Devastates Pryluky Apartment Block
articles.summary: Russia launched a massive overnight missile and drone attack across Ukraine, killing at least 22 people. Strikes severely damaged a 5-story apartment building in the northeastern city of Pryluky and caused extensive damage to homes and infrastructure in Kremenchuk in the central Poltava region.

articles.title: Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder
articles.summary: Two decades after the murder of Anna Politkovskaya, a tenacious investigative reporter who exposed the brutality of Russia's war in Chechnya and documented how President Vladimir Putin curtailed democracy in Russia, her daughter Vera says little has changed in the country's political climate.

articles.title: Oil Tanker Hit By Naval Drones Near Sochi, Sparking Massive Fire On Black Sea
articles.summary: A Liberian-flagged oil tanker caught fire off the Russian resort city of Sochi after an apparent drone attack, Russian authorities said on October 6. The 23 crew members, all Indian, were rescued. A Ukrainian monitoring site said the vessel as part of Russia’s so-called shadow fleet.

articles.title: Russia Missile Blasts Ukraine Apartment Block, Killing At Least 22
articles.summary: Rescuers frantically picked through rubble and debris of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine as they search for survivors of a Russian missile attack that killed at least 22 people.

articles.title: Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has signaled a renewed American push to strengthen security in the Arctic, warning that US adversaries and competitors are already acting in a region of growing strategic importance.

articles.title: 20 Years Since The Death Of Russian Journalist Anna Politkovskaya
articles.summary: October 7 marks the 20th anniversary of the murder of prominent Kremlin critic Anna Politkovskaya, a tenacious investigative reporter who exposed the brutality of Russia's war in Chechnya and documented how President Vladimir Putin curtailed democracy in Russia.

articles.title: Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs
articles.summary: Iran’s worsening medicine shortages are driving patients to a booming black market, where essential drugs can cost several times official prices. Cancer and chronic disease patients face soaring costs, while authorities struggle with imports, currency shortages, and supply disruptions.

articles.title: Death At Russian Plague Lab: How Much Should We Worry?
articles.summary: A suspected case of pneumonic plague killing a laboratory technician in Russia has sparked global alarm about the possibility of wider transmission. RFE/RL spoke to Brendan Wren, a professor of microbial pathogenesis, about the situation and Russia's moves to deal with it.

articles.title: Wider Europe Briefing: The New EU Enlargement Strategy
articles.summary: In this week's Wider Europe, Rikard Jozwiak drills down on two issues: the EU's new enlargement strategy and the EU's game plan to keep Russia (and Belarus) out of sports.

https://adcmemorial.org/en/news/witnesse.body: Facebook Twitter Вконтакте Elie Wiesel , a survivor of Auschwitz and Buchenwald and the author of the well-known autobiographical novel Night, wrote that “only those who experienced Auschwitz know what it was; the rest will never know.” As Wiesel saw it, “the witness knew then, as he knows now,” that his experience could not be conveyed or fully comprehended by those who had not been in a concentration camp and had not endured torture and humiliation. The author of the testimony asks: “Others will not know, but will they be able to understand?” And yet, despite his doubts, Wiesel “simply could not remain silent.” Reflecting on the destruction of European Jewry by the German Nazis, Wiesel concludes that over the years not only the actions but also the aims of the antisemites changed: if at the beginning of their rule the Nazis set themselves the task of “building a society without Jews,” towards the end they wanted “to leave behind a world in which Jews seemed never to have existed at all.” Violence against people — Jewish men, women and children — was accompanied by the destruction of the very memory of this people, their culture, language and religion. For many witnesses, the struggle against the destruction of memory became the purpose of their lives, an act of resistance. Contemporary antifascists often repeat that “to remember means to resist,” holding events in memory of comrades killed by neo-Nazis. “Memory Is Resistance” is the slogan on the website of members of Memorial who study the history of political repression in the USSR and preserve testimonies of the horrors of the Soviet past. Memory matters to everyone: both to those who refuse to let themselves or others forget the crimes of the past and the suffering of the victims, and to those who take pride in that past. It is not simply a matter of knowing something — Wiesel was right about that — achieving understanding is much more difficult. We can see how declared aims and ideological attitudes continue to change in our own time. From “Holocaust denial” — until quite recently, apologists for German nationalism claimed that Jews had not been exterminated and had themselves invented both the camps and the crematoria in order to slander innocent Germans (there were even claims that Jews themselves had organised the mass murder of Jews to spite the Aryans) — to contemporary proposals by Alternative for Germany not to teach about Hitlerism in schools and instead devote more attention to Bismarck. Germany’s far-right politicians are now closer to the cynical attitude: “Here’s your beer, here’s your ham, and what happened yesterday is in the past” (the ever-relevant words of a song by Yuliy Kim). No one is saying that it did not happen: it did. The only question is how to regard it, how to understand it. The militarist and nationalist Bismarck is, for the AfD, something good, something to take pride in, while schoolchildren need not be told about certain costs of twentieth-century history: enough already, so much has been said about it. The lavish funeral held in Belgrade with military honours for Ratko Mladić, convicted by the Hague Tribunal of crimes against humanity, is a striking manifestation of the contemporary conflict over memory: for some, the victims and witnesses of crimes matter; for others, what matters is the glorification of war criminals. Everyone wants to remember — but they remember different things and understand the past differently. Those who are erecting ever more monuments to Stalin in the Russian Federation obviously want to remind people of him, often making no attempt to conceal the fact that Stalinism was terror. They simply like terror and want to put it back on a pedestal. And they are prepared to remember the Gulag as well — not to deny its existence, but to explain it in their own way, interpreting it within the framework of the “inadmissibility of distorting the history of the USSR.” Thus, for example, one can hold an academic conference in a former Soviet camp, highlighting “examples of the extraordinary courage and patriotism of our compatriots, whose military and labour achievements have more than once become a central theme of academic conferences organised for ten years by the Perm-36 Museum-Reserve.” But telling the history of the Stalinist era as it was seen by those who survived despite the terror, those who neither forgot nor forgave, is treated as extremism. This is why Memorial was banned and the Gulag History Museum in Moscow was closed. It is not memory that is forbidden — it is understanding that is forbidden, precisely what Elie Wiesel and many others sought to achieve through their testimonies. The struggle to foster an understanding that terror and war crimes are unacceptable does not end even when a verdict has been handed down by the Hague (or Nuremberg) Tribunal. Constant efforts are required not only to prevent people from forgetting, but also to show history — including the most recent history — through the eyes of victims of violence, those who suffered, and surviving witnesses. To show their truth rather than the perpetrator’s version: the perpetrator who does not even conceal what he is doing — who may even take pride in it — but who always has an explanation of his own, most often that he was forced to “strike first,” to assert his right to dominance, and so on. The perpetrators themselves are also eager to preserve the memory of violence — in military monuments, bas-reliefs and installations. The voices of those who suffered can be heard in their memories, accounts and testimonies, which must be collected and published, as is being done today by the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group’s “Voices of War” project and in human rights reports , which bring together the tragic experiences of Ukrainian women and men who have suffered as a result of Russia’s military aggression. Stephania KULAEVA First published on the Radio Svoboda blog Facebook Twitter Вконтакте

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2026/.body: Updated June 12, 2026, 12:30 PM EDT A Bangkok court on Thursday sentenced two Uyghur men to death for triggering a bomb explosion which killed twenty and injured over a hundred others over a decade ago. “The deaths and injuries caused by the attack were a terrible tragedy, and the victims and their families deserve justice,” Rebiya Kadeer of the International Uyghur Human Rights and Democracy Foundation (IUHRDF) told RFA. “However, justice cannot be achieved through proceedings that leave significant questions unanswered regarding due process, the treatment of defendants , and the reliability of key evidence,” Kadeer added. uyghuyr-bomb-suspect-thailand-trial_0 Forensic officials and rescue foundation volunteers clean up the Erawan Shrine in Bangkok, a day after the bomb explosion killed 20 people, Aug. 18, 2015. (RFA) No group claimed responsibility for the Erawan Shrine bombing in central Bangkok on Aug. 17, 2015, but speculation called it an act of retaliation against the forced deportation of more than 109 Uyghurs from Thailand a month earlier. Shortly after the bombing, Thai police named 17 suspects. Arrested were two Uyghurs, Adem Karadag (alias Bilal Mohammed) and Yusufu Mieraili, who went on trial in 2016 for planting explosives. Both have denied all charges brought against them Upon hearing the verdict delivered by a four-judge panel on Thursday, Mieraili shouted “Injustice!” in the courtroom in both English and Thai. “RIP Thailand’s justice system. I don’t accept any of this,” Mieraili added. “I didn’t do anything wrong.” uyghur-bangkok-erawan-shrine-bombing-verdict Adem Karadag (alias Bilal Mohammed), left, and Yusufu Mieraili during a Feb.16, 2016, appearance at a Thai military court. (Nicolas Asfouri/AFP) During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mieraili and Karadag had been near the shrine around the time of the explosion, that they had communicated with each other by telephone, and that a taxi driver had transported them away from the area after the incident. The judges stated that although the defendants had denied committing the crime, they had failed to refute the evidence presented against them. The court granted both men 30 days to file an appeal. Defense lawyer Choochat Kanpai told reporters they “will appeal the ruling because there are many aspects of the case that the court has not fully considered, including the treatment of the defendants during the proceedings.” The decade-long trial was beset by delays due to the coronavirus pandemic and problems securing translators. uyghur-bangkok-erawan-shrine-bombing-verdict Defense lawyers speak to reporters at Bangkok South Criminal Court, June 11, 2026, after the verdict for the Erawan Shrine bombing. (Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP) Seven Chinese tourists were among the fatalities when explosives—apparently left in a backpack—detonated. Beijing welcomed the death sentences. “The attackers were totally inhumane and extremely heinous,” foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters. “China supports Thailand in conducting the trial in accordance with the law and severely punishing the murderers.” Bahtiyar Bora of the Australian Uyghur Association who provided assistance and translation for Karadag and Mieraili during court proceedings in Thailand, spoke to RFA about China’s response to the verdict. “These two Uyghurs fled Chinese oppression and came to Thailand. China is, of course, pleased with their severe punishment and can continue to accuse Uyghurs of terrorism internationally,” Bora said. Thailand deported 40 Uyghurs to China in February 2025 despite warnings from human rights groups that they would face persecution on their return, drawing swift condemnation from the United Nations. uyghur-bangkok-erawan-shrine-bombing-verdict Rebiya Kadeer at the fourth General Assembly of the World Uyghur Congress in Tokyo May 14, 2012. (Yuriko Nakao/Reuters) “These actions have reinforced concerns that decisions involving Uyghurs in Thailand may be influenced by political and economic considerations linked to Beijing rather than by international human rights obligations,” Rebiya Kadeer told RFA. “Against this background, it is difficult for many in the Uyghur community to have confidence that this verdict was reached entirely free from political influence,” Kadeer said. Adds quote from Bahtiyar Bora of the Australian Uyghur Association. Pimuk Rakkanam reported from Bangkok, Tahir Hamut Izgil reported from Washington. With reporting from AFP and Reuters. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

https://hrf.org/latest/imprisoned-karaka.body: @HRF View post Dauletmurat Tazhimuratov, a prisoner of conscience in Uzbekistan, has shared a letter from prison detailing the abuse and severe mistreatment he is suffering while incarcerated. Tazhimuratov is a Karakalpak lawyer, journalist, and human rights defender who has been detained in Uzbekistan since July 2022, when the Uzbek government cracked down on protesters who opposed constitutional amendments that would have stripped Karakalpakstan of its status as a sovereign republic. Writing from detention, Tazhimuratov describes brutal beatings he has received at the hands of prison officials, who force him to recite the Uzbek national anthem or deny his Karakalpak identity by declaring that he is Uzbek. He is also denied access to bathing facilities, medical care, writing materials, and religious items. HRF calls on Uzbekistan to treat Dauletmurat Tazhimuratov with dignity and recognize his fundamental rights by providing him with access to basic necessities and investigating all incidents of violence against him. Most of all, the Uzbek government must enforce the opinion of the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention and release him from prison immediately. View post

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2025/.body: A new report says major Chinese producers of critical minerals are using state-imposed forced labor programs in the Uyghur region to meet rising global demand, putting international brands they export to at risk of complicity in human rights violations. According to the report by Hague-based rights group Global Rights Compliance , 77 companies and downstream manufacturers of critical minerals-based products operate in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR), placing them at risk of participation in the labor transfer programs in the lithium, titanium, beryllium, and magnesium industries. The findings are likely to add to the due diligence concerns of foreign and multinational companies that source those products. Forced labor is on a long list of serious human rights problems that have been documented in Xinjiang, where the U.S. government determined in 2021 that China was committing genocide against the Uyghurs. The Uyghur region is a major source of four critical minerals. It is the top source of beryllium, crucial for nuclear applications and advanced electronics, and one of the five province-level jurisdictions that produces raw magnesium. The region is also seeing a surge in lithium exploration, mining, and battery production to feed the electric vehicle industry, and accounts for 11.6% of the world’s titanium sponge, a key input in titanium metal that is used in aerospace and defense. Over the past decade, Beijing has expanded exploration, mining, processing and manufacturing of critical minerals in the XUAR, transforming the region into a major “extractive hub,” Global Rights Compliance said in its report titled “Risk at the Source: Critical Mineral Supply Chains and State-Imposed Forced Labor in the Uyghur Region.” China dominates global mineral production. The country leads production of 30 out of the 44 minerals that the U.S. government has designated as critical. uyghur-rare-earths The June 2025 Global Rights Compliance report on mineral supply chains and forced labor in the Uyghur region. (Global Rights Compliance) “The emergence of the region as an extractive hub relies, in part, on state-imposed forced labor transfer programs, targeting Uyghurs and other Turkic ethnic groups,” the rights group said. The report highlights the “substantial influence” that these critical minerals – found abundantly in XUAR – have on global supply chains and multinational brands, including leading paint companies, aerospace applications, thermos producers, and defense and nuclear tools and components. It uncovers 15 companies with documented sourcing directly from Uyghur region-based companies in the last two years and 68 downstream customers of Chinese producers who source inputs from the Uyghur region, highlighting the risk of companies’ direct and indirect participation in the forced labor programs. “The XUAR’s systemic forced labor practices are not only a means to subsidize operating costs but also facilitate the government’s persecution of the Uyghur population through familial separation, land expropriation, and forced re-education,” Global Rights Alliance said. The report highlights that China’s practices in the Uyghur region create unfair competitive advantages and trade and environmental violations that extend beyond human rights concerns. Lax environmental standards and heavy dependence on coal have also made the region the epicenter of the energy-intensive mineral mining and processing industry and have enabled goods to enter global markets at artificially low prices, it said. “Minerals mined and/or refined in the region routinely enter global supply chains through unregulated or opaque mineral distribution channels. As a result, significant portions of the world’s economy are potentially exposed to products tainted by forced labor and high carbon footprints,” the rights group added. The report’s findings were based on analyses of state media, shipping records, and marketing and corporate annual reports. Edited by Mat Pennington.

WASHINGTON — The House passed the Uyghur Policy Act on Tuesday, a bill that advances a strategy for the United States to support Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities enduring persecution at the hands of China’s government. It’s the latest try for the measure, which was passed by the House in the past two congressional terms without advancing further. Sponsored by a bipartisan group led by Rep. Young Kim, a California Republican, and Rep. Ami Bera, a California Democrat, the measure calls on the State Department to oversee Uyghur human rights-related policies and programs that preserve Uyghurs’ ethnic, religious, cultural and linguistic identities. The Uyghur people have been imprisoned, tortured, & brainwashed at the hands of the Chinese Communist Party. I spoke on the House floor in favor of my Uyghur Policy Act — so we can show through words & actions that we stand against the CCP's heinous crimes. pic.twitter.com/QU3JhwutIc — Young Kim (@RepYoungKim) September 2, 2025 The bill aims to increase accountability for human rights organizations and sets a strategy to close detention facilities and political reeducation camps in China. It also creates reporting mechanisms for Uyghur victims. “For too long, the Chinese Communist Party has orchestrated the forced sterilization, enslavement, and systematic murder of the Uyghur people,” Kim said in a statement. “The United States cannot sit idly by as innocent families are torn apart, identities are erased, and generations silenced by these atrocious acts of genocide.” Rushan Abbas , executive director of the Campaign for Uyghurs and chair of the executive committee of the World Uyghur Congress, said the measure was a “vital step to ensure America stands firmly with the Uyghur people amid China’s ongoing genocide.” “By making Uyghur human rights a clear priority in U.S. foreign policy, this bill strengthens accountability for the Chinese government’s crimes and delivers a powerful message of solidarity to millions of Uyghur families suffering under repression,” she said.

A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers this week announced a bill that would broaden existing sanctions to combat what one senator called “a deliberate and systematic campaign to destroy the Uyghur people” — one of a set of bills targeting China over its treatment of minority groups, dissidents and Taiwan as bilateral trade negotiations continue. The measure would expand the sanctions under a previous law to include actions like forced family separations and organ harvesting . It would also deny entry to the U.S. for people found to have participated in forced abortions or sterilizations . In interviews with RFA Uyghur , Uyghur women have detailed birth control procedures they say were forced on them by authorities in northwest China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. The bill would bar the U.S. military from buying Chinese seafood out of concern that Uyghur and North Korean forced labor is used in its production. It would direct the State Department to create a plan for countering Chinese propaganda that denies “the genocide, crimes against humanity, and other egregious human rights abusese experienced by Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethic groups” in Xinjiang. It would also appropriate $2 million for the Smithsonian to create research and programs that would preserve Uyghur language and culture threatened by the Chinese government . “The evidence is clear. The Chinese Communist Party has waged a deliberate and systematic campaign to destroy the Uyghur people through forced sterilization, mass internment, and forced labor,” Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), the chairman of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China and one of the bill’s co-sponsors, said in a statement. “This legislation ensures the United States holds accountable not only the perpetrators of these horrific crimes but also those who support or profit from them.” Joining Sullivan in co-sponsoring the bill are Rep. Chris Smith (R-N.J.), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.), and Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.). Rushan Abbas, executive director of the Campaign for Uyghurs, a U.S.-based nonprofit advocacy group, and the chairwoman of the Executive Committee of the World Uyghur Congress, an international organization promoting Uyghur rights, said the measure’s introduction is “a critical step toward dismantling the systems of control and repression that have enabled genocide and devastated Uyghur families and communities.” “For Uyghurs who have endured years of silence and separation, this bill represents a meaningful step toward exposing the truth, advancing justice, and creating pathways to family reunification,” Abbas told RFA. U.S. lawmakers this week also planned to release a bill that would aim to help Taiwan and support countries that maintain official diplomatic relations with its government, as well as a measure to combat efforts by any foreign government to reach beyond its borders to intimidate, harass or harm activists, dissidents or journalists. In response to the bills, China’s foreign ministry on Tuesday rejected U.S. accusations on Xinjiang and Taiwan. “The related accusations are entirely fabricated and are malicious slander,” the ministry said. The measures come as an Aug. 12 deadline looms for a durable trade deal between the U.S. and China. A U.S. official told reporters that progress is being made toward a deal, Reuters reported Friday. Includes reporting by Reuters.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2026/.body: Human rights and Taiwan are “red lines” for China that cannot be crossed, the country’s ambassador to the U.S. warned on Wednesday, ahead of President Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington for a three-day summit. Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng, writing in the ruling Communist Party’s official People’s Daily, said managing differences hinges on good faith, and the U.S. should stop “fabricating pretexts” such as national security, economic imbalances and forced labor to try to constrain China. “China’s sovereignty, security, and development interests cannot be violated, and four red lines — the Taiwan question, democracy and human rights, development paths and systems, and development rights — cannot be challenged,” Xie said. RFA Uyghur’s Shohret Hoshur interviewed Rebiya Kadeer of the Washington-based International Uyghur Human Rights and Democracy Foundation (IUHRDF) for her reaction to China’s “red lines” statement ahead of Xi’s meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump . The interview has been edited for length and clarity. RFA: Why do you think Beijing issued this warning at this particular moment? Rebiya Kadeer: The Uyghur genocide and human rights issue is China’s greatest vulnerability. It is also a crime that China has spent enormous financial resources attempting to conceal from the international community. At this important moment, when the world is paying close attention, China does not want this vulnerability to be exposed. RFA: Do you interpret the warning as a sign that Beijing fears President Trump may raise what his administration has called the Uyghur genocide and individual Uyghur political-prisoner cases during his meeting with Xi Jinping? If so, what does it reveal about Beijing’s concerns? Rebiya Kadeer: Ahead of Xi Jinping’s visit, several members of Congress called on President Trump to raise the cases of political prisoners—including Gulshan Abbas, Ilham Tohti, Rahile Dawut and Ekpar Asat—and demand their release. China knows that, in a democratic country such as the United States, the views of members of Congress carry weight and receive serious attention. Therefore, through this statement, China is attempting to pressure President Trump. RFA: Does this warning demonstrate confidence—or fear that China’s human-rights abuses could become part of the summit negotiations? Rebiya Kadeer: This is certainly not the kind of statement made by a strong country. China’s economic development is not healthy development; it has been built upon unfair competition and coercion. The stability China has established within the country, particularly in East Turkistan (Xinjiang in Chinese), is not natural stability—it is artificially imposed stability. Therefore, although the Chinese government may appear strong, it is fundamentally weak. A government that fears its own people and is unable to embrace democratic elections is a fearful government. It is especially afraid of criticism. RFA: How should President Trump respond to Beijing’s effort to place human rights outside the summit discussions? Rebiya Kadeer: China’s statement itself demonstrates why President Trump must raise the Uyghur genocide and human rights. I believe that raising these issues would give President Trump the upper hand at the negotiating table and help him achieve his objectives on other matters. If he does not raise them, he will not only be acting against the will of the American people, but he will also lose ground on the other issues under negotiation. I call upon—and hope—President Trump will follow a course befitting the strong president of a powerful country. With reporting by Reuters. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2025/0.body: A human rights group is urging Kazakhstan not to deport to China a 23-year-old ethnic Kazakh man who fled from Xinjiang several weeks ago, warning he could face persecution and internment there. Atajurt, a volunteer group that campaigns for Kazakh victims of oppression in Xinjiang, said Friday it had confirmed that the man, Yerzhanat Abai, has been detained by Kazakh police. Serikzhan Bilash, who heads the group, said Yerzhanat Abai, a Chinese national, is being held in the Panfilov City Detention Center in Zharkent county, Almaty province, which is about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from the border with China. “He could be secretly escorted to China by Xinjiang’s national security or Kazakhstan’s National Security Bureau at any time, and no one knows his specific situation. Only if this matter is made public to the world will the Kazakh government be unable to repatriate him,” said Serikzhan. Serikzhan, who lives in exile in the United States, has been a vocal campaigner for the release of fellow ethnic Kazakhs from Chinese camps, where the ruling Chinese Communist Party held an estimated 1.8 million ethnic minority Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and other Muslims in mass incarceration centers after 2017. Beijing denies the allegations. “Many young people in Xinjiang are often summoned by the police, or sent to learning centers under various pretexts, saying they are providing employment opportunities. In fact, they are arranged to work in factories in the mainland, most of which are chemical factories that are harmful to health, and the wages are even lower than in Xinjiang,” Serikzhan said. According to Atajurt, Yerzhanat Abai entered Kazakhstan on March 27 and sought help from the group in the Kazakh city of Almaty four days later. He said he was from Gongliu county, Yili prefecture in Xinjiang, China. The circumstances of his leaving China and why he was detained in Kazakhstan weren’t immediately clear. RFA sought comment without success from the Kazakhstan Interior Ministry and the Chinese Consulate General in Almaty. Edited by Mat Pennington.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2025/.body: BANGKOK – A Thai court slashed the number of prosecution witnesses for the long-stalled trial of two Uyghur men incarcerated for a decade following the retaliatory bombing of a Bangkok shrine popular with Chinese visitors. Adem Karadag and Yusufu Mieraili, both handcuffed and shackled, appeared Thursday at a Bangkok criminal court for a fresh arraignment aimed at speeding up proceedings in the politically sensitive case. “I still have hope for freedom,” Karadag told Radio Free Asia through a courtroom interpreter. “I want to go anywhere but not to be sent back to China like others.” Both men smiled and hugged their Thai lawyer and Uyghur interpreter. “I exercised. I can eat well,” Mieraili said in Thai. Both men deny they triggered the Erawan Shrine bomb in the Aug. 17, 2015 attack that was apparent retaliation for Thailand’s repatriation of dozens of Uyghur migrants to China, where they face high risk of persecution. Twenty people died in the bombing of the Hindu shrine in downtown Bangkok and more than 120 more injured. The trial has languished due to jurisdiction changing between civilian and military courts amid regime changes in Thailand. Lack of qualified courtroom interpreters also has caused delays. The criminal court on Thursday cut the number of prosecution witnesses to 20 from 55 to shorten the trial. It has set 11 court dates from September to December. The pair are charged with first-degree murder and could face execution if found guilty. Police arrested Karadag and Mieraili shortly after the bombing based on CCTV footage, but failed to find dozens of other alleged perpetrators. The trial is expected to finish next year, said Chuchart Gunpai, a lawyer for the defendants. Uyghur exodus through Southeast Asia Uyghurs are Turkic-speaking Muslims who mostly live in the Xinjiang region of China but are also spread across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkey. They have been fleeing China in large numbers to escape what they describe as persecution and repression by Chinese authorities – allegations that Beijing denies. Before the bombing, nearly 400 Uyghurs who fled China were arrested in Thailand in 2014, according to the Thai foreign ministry. The fleeing Uyghurs were hoping for resettlement in Turkey via Malaysia, right advocates and other lawyers said. Others likely slipped through the Thai-Malaysian border without detection by authorities. In June 2015, Thailand allowed 172 Uyghur women and children to leave for Turkey, but two weeks later appeared to bow to pressure from Beijing and put 109 Uyghur men, blindfolded, on a plane back to China, provoking international condemnation. The Thai foreign ministry said at that time the men “have been verified as Chinese and evidence of their involvement in criminal activities has been sent by the Government of China.” The decision drew condemnation from the World Uyghur Congress, an exiled Uyghur group, which claimed 25 Uyghurs were killed resisting the forced deportation. Thailand denied any deaths. “Had Thailand followed the principle of not sending people into harm’s way, these mishaps could have been avoided,” Chalida Tarjaroensuk, the director of the People’s Empowerment Foundation, who assisted the Uyghurs, told RFA. Related Stories Previous Lack of Interpreter Stalls Uyghur Suspects’ Trial in 2015 Bangkok Bombing 2 Uyghur suspects in Bangkok bombing return to court after 9-month delay US condemns Thailand’s deportation of 40 Uyghurs to China Next Poor conditions Following the deportations and the arrests of Karadag and Mieraili in 2015, more than 50 Uyghurs remained in Thai immigration prison until earlier this year. Some said they were denied proper lawyer visits and kept in cramped unhygienic cells without adequate medical care. Thai officials said three detainees died during their imprisonment. Some 40 of the imprisoned Uyghurs were deported to China in the dead of night on Feb. 27. Reporters who traveled with Thai officials to China to check on conditions for the deported men said they were subjected to Chinese surveillance. Another three Uyghur men, who held Kyrgyzstan passports, were resettled in Canada. Five Uyghurs are continuing to serve sentences for jailbreaking, according to Chalida, who fears they will also face deportation to China after their release in the next year or two. Edited by Stephen Wright and Taejun Kang.

https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2026/0.body: Taiwan’s plan to open a second trade office in the Philippines is an example of Manila and Taipei accelerating cooperation in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, analysts told Radio Free Asia. During a radio interview on Sept. 15, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said that Taipei’s plan to open a second representative office in Cebu, the Philippines’ second largest city, was going smoothly. Taipei’s trade offices serve as de facto embassies and consulates in countries that officially recognize China, but maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be a rogue province. Foreign Minister Lin said that the additional trade office would serve travelers and businesses in the central Philippines, and would be an integral part of a proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor. Days later, Taiwan confirmed that it had donated a decommissioned patrol vessel to the Philippines for use in its coast guard. These developments are directly related to Beijing’s hostile tactics in the South China Sea, Ray Powell, executive director of Stanford University’s SeaLight maritime transparency project, told RFA. Beijing claims the entirety of the sea as its territory, including the area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which Manila calls the West Philippine Sea. china and philippines claims The overlapping claims of China and the Philippines in the South China Sea. (AFP) “Of course China’s aggression in the West Philippine Sea is a central part of this story,” said Powell. “It has made Manila less willing to grant Beijing the kind of deference that other countries like Malaysia or Papua New Guinea have recently been so eager to show on Taiwan policy.” Papua New Guinea announced in July that it would close the Taiwan trade office in Port Moresby, and Malaysia’s Prime Minister Ibrahim Anwar in August controversially stated in an interview with Al Jazeera that he sees “Taiwan as part of China, period.” The trend of smaller countries showing deference to China “has conditioned Beijing to expect that its coercive methods will always produce compliance eventually,” Powell said. “For now at least it has not produced that kind of result in the Philippines.” Defining “one China” As a condition of entering into official relations with China, countries must affirm that there is one China and recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China. China’s official stance, the one-China principle, states that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Many countries maintain their own one-China policies that stop short of the principle to allow unofficial ties with Taipei. When Taiwan announced the plan to open a new trade office in Cebu, Beijing protested, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urging the Philippines to uphold the one-China Principle through “concrete actions” and refrain from taking steps that could damage relations with China. “No matter how the DPP authorities collude with external forces or in what form they seek so-called ‘diplomatic breakthroughs,’ their efforts to serve the goal of ‘Taiwan independence’ are doomed to be futile,” Guo said, referring to Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party. The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs responded that Manila’s one-China policy remained unchanged but did not prevent economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan. Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. was more direct, telling local media: “We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them.” The exchange highlights a widening difference between Manila and Beijing over what the Philippines’ one-China policy allows. The Taiwan trade office in Cebu should not be interpreted as a change in Manila’s formal position, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA. “Rather, I think it reflects the ongoing expansion and institutionalization of the Philippines’ unofficial and functional relationship with Taiwan,” he said. “This distinction is important: Manila continues to recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China under its one-China Policy, yet it does not view this policy as precluding economic, cultural, or other practical forms of engagement with Taiwan.” That relationship had already begun expanding before the latest dispute. In April 2025, Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration relaxed decades-old restrictions on engagement with Taiwan. Most Philippine officials may now travel there for economic, trade and investment purposes if they use ordinary passports and do not use their official titles. The restrictions continue to apply to the president, vice president, foreign secretary and defense secretary, illustrating the line Manila is trying to maintain between functional engagement and steps that might resemble formal diplomatic recognition. “Currently, Manila appears intent on maintaining a distinction between expanding functional ties and taking actions that could be construed as formal diplomatic recognition,” Kristanto said. “The 2025 guidelines are particularly illustrative: they facilitate interactions with Taiwan for economic and investment purposes while retaining restrictions on contacts involving the Philippines’ most senior officials.” Economic interdependence Practical interests are also driving the relationship. More than 200,000 Filipinos work in Taiwan, and the two sides offer visa-free entry to each other’s citizens. Taipei has also placed greater emphasis on trade, investment, tourism and supply-chain cooperation with the Philippines. Foreign Minister Lin said the proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor would connect with the U.S.-Japan-Philippines-backed Luzon Economic Corridor, an initiative aimed at strengthening infrastructure and supply chains. Kristanto cautioned against explaining the closer relationship entirely through the South China Sea dispute. “The deterioration in Manila-Beijing relations has certainly made Taiwan more strategically relevant to the Philippines, and we have seen indications of expanding practical cooperation in areas such as maritime security,” he said. “But many drivers of closer Philippines-Taiwan relations – economic links, labor, geographical proximity, and supply-chain cooperation – exist independently of the South China Sea dispute. I therefore see pressure from China more as an accelerant to an existing trend than as its sole cause.” Powell said the Philippines increasingly viewed China’s treatment of Taiwan as part of a wider effort to pressure smaller countries that resisted Beijing’s preferred regional order. “There’s an active attempt by China, very obvious now, to make a more Sinocentric world and to put down others who do not agree with them – particularly when these others are smaller countries,” Powell said, quoting from a recent SeaLight podcast interview with Teodoro. Kristanto said the significance of the Cebu office lay less in the facility itself than in Manila’s growing confidence in defining its relationship with Taipei on its own terms. “Manila appears increasingly willing to insist that maintaining a one-China policy does not give Beijing a veto over its unofficial relationship with Taiwan,” Kristanto said. “So, in my view, the significance of the Cebu office lies less in the office itself than in what it tells us about how much more comfortable Manila has become in expanding ties with Taiwan while arguing that its formal diplomatic position remains unchanged.” Edited by Eugene Whong.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2026/.body: Read RFA coverage of this story in Uyghur Chinese authorities in Xinjiang’s regional capital Urumqi on July 4 arrested two Uyghur sisters and their mother for sending goods to their eldest sister in Turkey, and a third sister was arrested a week later, the eldest told Radio Free Asia. Guzelnur Kamil said her family had been shipping ordinary household goods, including clothing, footwear, hats, daily necessities, seasonings, and packaged food items to support her business in Turkey. “They were simply miscellaneous everyday items,” she told RFA. “My mother said, ‘Even if we cannot send you cash, let us send you goods so you can do business, my child, and provide for your children,’” she said. Guzelnur, who moved to Turkey in 2016, said the shipments were assembled by her sister, Guljennet Kamil, who from 2018-2020 was detained in an internment camp . Guljennet also suffers from partial paralysis following an accident and was helped by her sister with a share of the profits from her business. However, according to Guzelnur, the police used this communication as a pretext to target the family. Investigation Guzelnur said the police interrogation of her family began on July 1, and explained that her mother, Bahargul Tohti, along with her sisters Guljennet and Gulzeper Hekim, were interrogated several times. Police used Guljennet’s shipping of goods to Turkey as a pretext, alleging suspicion of “supporting terrorists,” she said, adding that her mother and sisters were ordered to lead police to the exact shops where they purchased the goods and the logistics companies they used to ship them. “On the 4th, they spoke very politely, asking my mother to come to the police station at 9:00 AM,” she said. “After taking her in, they also brought in my sisters. They took their blood samples and photographed them from the front, back, and sides. After that, they just took them away without saying a word.” Turkey is one of 26 countries that China considers “sensitive,” along with primarily Muslim-majority nations such as Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Kazakhstan according to Human Rights Watch . Under China’s “ Strike Hard Campaign ,” those who have been to these countries, have families, or otherwise communicate with people there, have been questioned, detained, and even imprisoned. Guzelnur said her family in Urumqi has not sent her any goods for more than a year. Instead, she has been importing merchandise from Central Asian countries. The shipments from her family had already ceased long before her family was arrested by police. “We have documentation for everything—from where it was shipped, and even who received the goods,” Guzelnur said. “We provided those files, and my mother and sisters provided everything to the police. Yet the police still told them, ‘We will investigate you; there are also things going on over there in Turkey.’ What things could be going on here? We have nothing going on here. We can even present clean records from here.” According to Guzelnur, her mother and sisters were taken to the Nanjiao Police Station in Urumqi. “One is an orphan girl, one is my mother, and one is my disabled sister... What am I supposed to do now?!” she told RFA, referring to her adopted sister Gulzeper. RFA confirmed that Guljennet was moved from the police station and is currently being held at the Tianshan District Detention Center. Ethnic unity law The arrests came just days after China’s new ethnic unity law went into effect. On July 10, Norway-based Uyghur activist Abduweli Ayup posted on X , “Three Uyghurs detained in Urumqi. The National Security police didn’t tell the reasons, they put them in detention on July 4th. They are the first target we learned after China enacted the ethnic unity promotion law.” Critics of China’s ethnic unity law warn that the law brings accelerated forced assimilation and cultural erasure of Uyghurs and Tibetans . It also raises fears of Beijing’s increasing transnational repression and its ability to stifle dissident voices overseas. Guzelnur told RFA that her third sister, Gulmire Kamil, who remained at home after her mother and two sisters were arrested on July 4, was arrested by police a week later. Gulmire previously served 10 years in prison for her connection with the July 5, 2009 unrest in Urumqi. Translated by Tahir Izgil. Edited by Charlie Dharapak and Eugene Whong.

https://www.rferl.org/a/kyrgyz-activist-.body: News Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence By RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service and Zamira Eshanova October 01, 2026 18:08 CET Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Kyrgyz activist Mavlyan Askarbekov was detained in June after criticizing the growing presence of Chinese citizens in Kyrgyzstan, including their involvement in small and midsize businesses. (file photo) The Lenin District Court in Bishkek found activist and politician Mavlyan Askarbekov guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison on offenses related to a law on incitement of racial, ethnic, national, religious, or interregional hatred, a verdict he called "absurd." Askarbekov was detained in June after criticizing the growing presence of Chinese citizens in Kyrgyzstan, including their involvement in small and midsize businesses. Prosecutors said Askarbekov's Facebook posts contained explicit calls to incite interethnic discord. "When does incitement to hatred occur? When someone writes something against a particular ethnic group and calls for some kind of action against them. Expressing criticism alone does not constitute incitement to hatred," lawyer and human rights defender Klara Sooronkulova told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: China's Growing Footprint In Kyrgyzstan Fuels Concerns Over Resources, Sovereignty "No one in those posts called for action against the Chinese. People everywhere are saying, ‘'There are too many Chinese.' Are they going to imprison everyone for that?" she added. China's expanding role in Kyrgyzstan has become increasingly hard to ignore. During the first half of 2026, Kyrgyzstan issued some 61,000 work visas, according to the Foreign Ministry's Consular Department, with about 60 percent going to Chinese citizens. That influx of Chinese workers is part of a wider economic expansion and also hard to miss on city streets. In a country of just more than 7 million people -- where hundreds of thousands leave to work abroad, mainly in Russia, and remittances sustain many households -- the arrival of so many Chinese workers has been difficult to accept for many Kyrgyz. Kyrgyz officials have defended Chinese involvement as necessary for development and have tried to keep a lid on the government for failing to provide clear information about Chinese migration and employment. In battling online criticism, the state has turned to what it calls "forensic linguistic examination" to determine whether social media posts break the law. Joomart Karabaev, a former researcher at the Kyrgyz National Academy of Sciences, said the practice has been entirely weaponized. He knows that firsthand. Karabaev was arrested and given a three-year probationary sentence after publicly exposing how state security forces dictate expert findings. "They have started playing the role of a court, effectively becoming an institution that rubber-stamps the guilt established by the investigation and prosecution," he said. "It has become common to dig up someone's old and new opinions when their political position is disliked, find an article under which they can be charged, and then imprison them based on the conclusions of a linguistic examination," Karabaev added. In Askarbekov's case, he criticized the growing number of Chinese citizens involved in Kyrgyzstan's small and medium-sized businesses, arguing they were displacing local entrepreneurs. SEE ALSO: As Trump Courts Xi, Pressure Mounts To Confront China Over Support For Iran He publicly called on the prime minister to discuss the issue in a live debate. Instead of public dialogue, the initiative ended in Askarbekov's prosecution and imprisonment. The case comes as China's economic clout in Central Asia continues to grow. As of June, Kyrgyzstan owed about $1.4 billion to China, according to the Kyrgyz Finance Ministry. China remained the country's largest external creditor, accounting for 28.1 percent of total external debt at the end of 2025, according to the International Monetary Fund. This deep economic reliance has made public criticism of Chinese influence a highly sensitive political issue across the region. In 2019, Kyrgyz activist Guljamila Saparalieva was arrested and charged with inciting ethnic hatred after participating in a protest against Beijing's treatment of Muslims in Xinjiang and the influx of Chinese migrants. SEE ALSO: In US-China AI Race, Kazakhstan Faces Pressure To Pick A Side In neighboring Uzbekistan, farmers in several regions accused local authorities of pressuring them to surrender farmland that was subsequently leased or earmarked for Chinese investors between late 2024 and early 2026. Beijing is reported to closely monitor such developments and has shown a willingness to deploy diplomatic pressure when public demonstrations affect its strategic interests. In November 2025, members of the Nagyz Atajurt movement in Kazakhstan protested near the border with China, demonstrating against Beijing's treatment of ethnic Kazakhs in Xinjiang and demanding the release of a Kazakh citizen detained there. The activists also raised broader alarms about China's growing leverage over Astana. The demonstration prompted China's Consulate General in Almaty to issue a sharp diplomatic note to Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry. The note, obtained and reviewed by RFE/RL's Kazakh Service, called the protest "an open provocation against the dignity of the People's Republic of China" and an insult to the Chinese Communist Party and its leadership, urging Kazakh authorities to "seriously investigate" the incident. Kazakh court documents reveal that investigators placed the diplomatic note directly into the case file. The prosecution cited China's formal objections as evidence that the protest damaged bilateral relations. The activists were subsequently convicted of inciting ethnic discord and each received a five-year prison sentence. https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2025/0.body: Online censorship in China by some regional governments is even more aggressive than enforcement of the national-level ‘Great Firewall’ by the central government, according to a recent study and local sources. The Great Firewall Report (GFW Report) highlights how the central Chinese province of Henan has adopted its own provincial firewall which is less sophisticated and robust than the central government’s but more volatile and aggressive, blocking significantly more websites than the national-level censorship system. Local sources told Radio Free Asia that the heightened restrictions at the provincial government level may reflect uncertainty about instructions from higher authorities, leading to “excessive blocking” to avoid blame for failing to carry out their duties. GFW Report is a censorship monitoring platform, primarily focused on China. During one experiment its researchers ran between Dec. 26, 2023 and March 31, 2025, they found that the Henan Firewall blocked 4.2 million domains, about six times that of the 741,542 at the national level. Since 2023, netizens in Henan had reported a rise in the number of websites that were inaccessible in the region but accessible elsewhere in China, the study found. “This localized censorship suggests a departure from China’s centralized censorship apparatus, enabling local authorities to exert a greater degree of control within their respective regions,” researchers Mingshi Wu at GFW, Ali Zohaib and Amir Houmansadr at University of Massachusetts Amherst, Zakir Durumeric at Stanford University, and Eric Wustrow at the University of Colorado Boulder wrote in the GFW Report published in May, “A Wall Behind A Wall: Emerging Regional Censorship in China.” But the phenomenon extends beyond Henan, sources inside China told RFA. Local governments in neighboring Hebei, another central Chinese province, as well as those in Tibet and Xinjiang have been operating similar censorship systems as the one reported in Henan for at least four years, Zhao Yuan, a network engineer based in Hebei, said. “In the past, we could access overseas websites that were not blocked by the national firewall,” Zhao said. “Now, even virtual private networks (VPNs) in Henan and Hubei don’t work.” While the national-level firewall, known as the Great Firewall, targets more news and media sites, in line with China’s long-standing policy of censoring politically sensitive information, the provincial-level firewall systems, like the one in Henan, blocks domains focusing on topics like the economy, technology, and business, GFW Report researchers found. The Chinese Communist Party has, in recent years, emphasized a multi-pronged approach to censorship , including the management of all types of propaganda at the domestic and international level through a framework known as “territorial management” and implementation of “digital stability maintenance” measures, such as policing of sensitive content online on dates deemed politically sensitive by the government. “Local governments have taken the initiative to establish local blocking systems, indicating that the top leaders are increasingly vigilant about the flow of information,” Wei Sicong, a Beijing-based political observer, said. china-regional-censorship-firewall-local-province Commuters wearing face masks to help curb the spread of the coronavirus browse their smartphones inside a subway train in Beijing Wednesday, Feb. 10, 2021. China's internet watchdog cracked down on online speech and issued a new requirement that bloggers and influencers have a license before they can publish on certain topics. (Andy Wong/AP) ‘Turning off the whole world’ Researchers at GFW found that the Henan firewall monitors and blocks traffic leaving and entering the province, as opposed to the national-level censorship system that is focused on traffic entering and exiting the country. Other sources in the region told RFA that the heightened restrictions at the provincial government level suggest lack of clear legal know-how about how to enforce instructions from higher-ups. “Officials would rather block more and more than take responsibility. So the result you see is ‘turning off the whole world’,” network engineer Zhang Jianan said. GFW Report researchers said their analysis showed no regional censorship in other areas they studied, such as Beijing, Guangdong, Shanghai, and Jiangsu. In Henan and Hebei, however, local residents told RFA that even the websites of some foreign universities are inaccessible, as a result of which they turn to VPNs and other circumvention tools to bypass government censorship and surveillance. “Some classmates can connect in Beijing and Shanghai, but we can’t in Zhengzhou and can only rely on circumvention software,” Zhang, a student at Henan’s Zhengzhou University, said. Hebei-based network engineer Zhao said, “The censorship is getting stricter and stricter. We can’t even connect to some foreign university websites.” RFA found that as early as December 2023, a university in Henan province sought to purchase a “public opinion monitoring system,” specifically aimed at international students, students and dissidents, and had conducted an open bidding process. Henan University of Science and Technology had laid out a 2024-2025 budget of 120,000 yuan (or US$16,657) for the public opinion monitoring service system to provide 24/7 real-time monitoring, early warning analysis and crisis response of public opinion information on the entire network, covering news websites and social media platforms such as Weibo and Douyin, the university’s website showed. When RFA contacted the university, a teacher confirmed they are using an old monitoring system and that they have now started a bidding process for a new one. Edited by Mat Pennington.

https://www.rferl.org/a/politkovskaya-ru.body: Russia Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder By RFE/RL October 07, 2026 12:45 CET Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Activists attend a rally in honor of slain journalist Anna Politkovskaya in Moscow. (file photo) Two decades after the murder of Anna Politkovskaya, a tenacious investigative reporter who exposed the brutality of Russia's war in Chechnya and documented how President Vladimir Putin curtailed democracy in Russia, her daughter, Vera, says little has changed in the country's political climate. People told her, “You’re exaggerating. You see everything through a dark lens,” she told RFE/RL's Russian Service in an interview ahead of the 20th anniversary of Politkovskaya's brutal killing on October 7, 2006. "And now it’s the same thing, except that the divide has deepened so much. Everything has become so stark, even compared with what she predicted more than 20 years ago". Politkovskaya, who worked for the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was gunned down in her Moscow apartment. The shooting occurred on President Vladimir Putin's birthday, prompting speculation that it was meant as a "gift" to the president. Embed share 20 Years Since The Death Of Russian Journalist Anna Politkovskaya by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:29 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.6MB 360p | 6.2MB 480p | 8.9MB 720p | 14.7MB 1080p | 25.1MB Former Russian police officer Sergei Khadzhikurbanov -- who denied the charges -- was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in organizing the assassination but received a pardon from Putin in 2023 after taking part in Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Two natives of Russia's North Caucasus region of Chechnya, Rustam Makhmudov and Lom-Ali Gaitukayev, were subsequently handed life sentences after a jury found Makhmudov guilty of shooting Politkovskaya, while Gaitukayev was convicted of organizing the assassination. Gaitukayev later died in prison. Another defendant in the case, former Moscow police officer Denis Pavlyuchenkov, was sentenced to 11 years in prison after he confessed to organizing the surveillance of Politkovskaya before she was murdered. Six Novaya Gazeta journalists and contributors -- Igor Domnikov (2000), Yury Shchekochikhin (2003), Politkovskaya (2006), Anastasia Baburova (2009), Stanislav Markelov (2009), and Natalya Estimirova (2009) -- have been killed in attacks that the newspaper and human rights activists say were retribution for their work. SEE ALSO: Daughter Blames 'System' Built By Putin, Kadyrov For Rights Activist Estemirova’s Death Since Politkovskaya's death, Russian authorities have gradually expanded the legal toolbox used to punish dissent, censor independent media, shutter civil society groups, and silence opposition lawmakers. This includes measures such as the "foreign agent" law, which punishes individuals and groups that receive foreign funding, and the "undesirables" law, which bans foreign organizations deemed a threat to national security and criminalizes people who work for, associate with, or donate money to such organizations. Such moves are exactly what her mother's reporting was aimed at exposing, said Vera Politkovskaya, who now lives abroad at an undisclosed location. "Essentially, the main theme of my mother's work was telling the stories of ordinary people," she said. "And how that everyday person was run over by the political and military system...That's what my mom witnessed and talked about back then. She saw, so to speak, further ahead than many other people did. And people didn't believe her." SEE ALSO: The List Is Long: Russians Who Have Died After Running Afoul Of The Kremlin Anna Politkovskaya was born in New York in 1958, the daughter of a Soviet diplomat from Ukraine. She was won numerous Russian and international awards, including an Amnesty International Global Award for Human Rights Journalism in 2001, a PEN Freedom to Write award in 2002, and an Olaf Palme Prize in 2004. In 2007, she became the first person ever to receive a posthumous UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize. https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-mobilizat.body: Russia Invades Ukraine From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military By RFE/RL's Kazakh Service and RFE/RL's Russian Service October 05, 2026 21:29 CET From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Miras Tasharghanov, pictured here with his mother, Gulzhan Tasharghanova, thought he was going to be working in a Russian meat-processing plant. Instead he ended up in Ukraine with the Russian Army. Listen to this article 5 min This audio is automated Learn more Miras Taszharghanov traveled to the Russian city of Kursk on August 20 to work at a meat-processing plant, expecting to earn 90,000 rubles (about $1,000) a month. Instead, his family says, the 25-year-old Kazakh national was taken from his workplace directly to a military recruitment center, where he was forced to sign a contract with the Russian Army. “He told me, ‘They throw a contract at you, put a gun to your head, and tell you to sign, and that’s it. They didn’t even ask us whether we wanted to or not,’” said Tashzharghanov’s mother, Gulzhan Taszharghanova, describing a harrowing phone call with her son. Following a brief two-week military training period, Tashzharghanov was transferred to the Voronezh region, which borders Ukraine. Fearing her son would be deployed to the front lines as an assault trooper, Taszharghanova pleaded with authorities in Astana to intervene. In response to his case and others like it, Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry announced that its embassy in Moscow sent a diplomatic note to the Russian Foreign Ministry on September 18, formally asking for the return of citizens who said they had been coerced into military service. But by early October, geolocation information Taszharghanov had sent to relatives indicated that he was near Bilolutsk in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine, RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service reported . His plight illustrates the risks facing some Central Asian migrants. Millions travel to Russia in search of livelihoods -- working in construction, agriculture, retail, and manufacturing. Uzbek migrant workers plant tomato seedlings in Astrakhan, Russia. (file photo) Rights advocates and migrants interviewed by RFE/RL have described cases in which foreign workers have faced pressure to join the Russian military. They say recruitment has taken place during police raids, workplace sweeps, at migration offices and in detention centers and prisons. Other migrants have been recruited with promises of large cash bonuses and fast-tracked Russian citizenship. Some sign up voluntarily, including for financial reasons, while others have alleged deception, threats, or physical coercion. SEE ALSO: Thousands Of Central Asians Enlisted To Fight Russia's War In Ukraine Through 'Coercion, Enticements' In September, a 44-year-old Uzbek migrant from Samarkand recounted being detained during a police raid in Rostov-on-Don over an expired work permit. He claimed that officers beat and pressured him until he signed a contract. After being deployed to the front line and wounded in the occupied Luhansk region, he spoke to RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service from a military hospital in St. Petersburg, begging the Uzbek government to help him return to his four children. For others, the realization comes too late. In Tajikistan’s northern Sughd region, a family recently buried their 58-year-old father whose body was returned from Ukraine in August, just months after he voluntarily signed a six-month contract. “He had financial issues, and going to Ukraine seemed to be a quick fix,” a source close to the family told RFE/RL on condition of anonymity. Pressure Takes Different Forms According to Russian migration-rights expert Valentina Chupik, recruitment tactics vary wildly: In some cases, she says, contracts are intentionally slipped into piles of routine paperwork that migrants sign at migration offices. In other cases, she alleges, coercion is explicitly violent. “There were mass raids, real torture with electric shocks and beatings,” Chupik told RFE/RL’s Russian Service, describing the measures allegedly used to force compliance. The reports of recruitment pressure come amid a broader, state-driven tightening of migration laws. Russian authorities have expanded workplace bans, stepped up deportations, and enforced stricter entry restrictions even as domestic industries face critical labor shortages. “Russia is not currently a safe country for Central Asian workers, and, naturally, where possible it is better to avoid traveling there,” warned Denis Jivaga, director of the Kazakhstan Bureau for Human Rights. SEE ALSO: Russia’s War Dead In Ukraine Believed To Include Hundreds Of Central Asians The true scale of foreign recruitment remains difficult to establish independently, as Moscow does not disclose comprehensive figures regarding foreign nationals serving in its armed forces. Ukraine's state-run I Want to Live project, which helps Russian soldiers surrender and tracks foreign nationals serving in Moscow’s military, said that as of May 2026, it had identified 12,919 citizens from Central Asian countries who had signed contracts with Russia's Defense Ministry. These figures have not been independently verified by RFE/RL. (Written and reported by Farangis Najibullah, with additional reporting by RFE/RL’s Azattyq Asia and RFE/RL’s Russian Service) From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print RFE/RL's Kazakh Service RFE/RL's Kazakh Service offers informed and accurate reporting in the Kazakh and Russian languages about issues that matter in Kazakhstan, while providing a dynamic platform for audience engagement and the free exchange of news and ideas.
