Tajikistan’s Humo Bank has warned its Russian clients that their cards will be blocked on October 1 unless they visit one of its offices in Tajikistan by September 30 to undergo biometric identification. “If you can’t come to Tajikistan in person and complete the identification, unfortunately, your card will be closed,” the bank told Russian news site Lenta.ru, advising clients to move their remaining balances to ruble cards before the deadline. The bank cited the need to protect clients from fraud. A Russian client, however, told the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti that the bank’s support staff explained it had decided to restrict services for “certain categories of non-resident individuals” whose cards were opened online. She said a transfer of about 300 euros had been stuck for a week and that the bank had stopped responding to her complaints. Humo offered her a new card if she traveled to Tajikistan, valid only for the duration of her legal stay and for no longer than a year. With Visa and Mastercard gone from Russia since 2022, Russians have relied on cards issued in “friendly” countries to make payments abroad. When Kazakhstan limited non-resident cards to 12 months and required in-person issuance in January 2025, intermediaries moved their business to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Humo and the International Bank of Tajikistan began offering remotely issued five-year cards in U.S. dollars and euros, sold through intermediaries for roughly 15,000 to 70,000 rubles. Humo is a newcomer to banking. Owned by the Japanese investment holding Gojo & Company , the former microcredit deposit organization received a full banking license from the National Bank of Tajikistan in July 2025. It was also among the few Tajik financial institutions with access to Visa Direct, a real-time payment service that became a conduit for Russian money headed to Europe. An investigation by The Bell found last year that Sberbank clients could send money to Revolut and N26 accounts through Central Asian intermediaries, with the funds appearing to originate from Dushanbe or Tashkent. The Humo ultimatum follows a year of Western pressure on Tajik banks. In October 2025, the European Union included Dushanbe City Bank, Spitamen, and Commercebank of Tajikistan in its 19th sanctions package, targeting banks closely linked to Russia’s financial system or processing cross-border payments that support the Russian economy. The three banks held roughly a fifth of all deposits in Tajikistan, and other Tajik banks responded by restricting transfers to Russia. In December, Revolut stopped accepting top-ups from cards issued in Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan for EU residents, citing payment systems’ classification of those countries as high-risk. The EU removed the three Tajik banks from its sanctions list in April 2026, with the National Bank crediting improved compliance and anti-money laundering standards. For Dushanbe, the stakes go well beyond fees collected from Russian cardholders. Remittances, mostly from Tajik migrants in Russia, reached $5.8 billion in 2024, or the equivalent of 45.3 percent of Tajikistan’s GDP, the highest share in the world. Протест связан с публикацией журнала Der Spiegel по поводу расследования в отношении бывшего главы германской Федеральной разведывательной службы (BND) Августа Ханнинга. По данным Der Spiegel, Ханнингу инкриминируется шпионаж в пользу Азербайджана. Якобы он подготовил аналитический материал для азербайджанской разведки, использовав для этого секретные документы. Между тем с осуждением публикации открыто выступил Совет по медиа и вещанию Азербайджана. В его заявлении выражается обеспокоенность тем, что «необоснованные утверждения, связывающие Азербайджан с упомянутым расследованием, первоначально распространенные немецким изданием Der Spiegel», преподносятся «широкой аудитории как факты». 80-летний Ханнинг был задержан 6 октября в Баварии. Также задержали его бывшего помощника, Манфреда Д., возглавлявшего аппарат нескольких руководителей БНД в период с марта 2012-го по март 2026 года. Их обоих подозревают в работе на иностранную разведку. Ханнинг возглавлял БНД в 1998–2005 годах. Пресс-служба Федеральной прокуратуры Германии, сообщившая 7 октября об аресте Ханнинга, не уточнила, шпионаж в пользу какой страны ему инкриминируется. Известно только, что, по версии следствия, Манфред Д. по меньшей мере с 2010 года передавал за деньги секретную информацию своему бывшему шефу. Предположительно, Ханнинг получил, таким образом, в общей сложности 2 тыс. документов. Многие из них были секретными. По информации Интерфакса

What was Pakistan bombing? Suspected camps of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan – the TTP for short – and the Islamic State of Khorasan Province. The Taliban regime in Afghanistan retaliated by hitting Pakistani border posts. Pakistan then upped the ante. Its military launched Operation Ghazab Lil-Haq — which means Righteous Fury — against Afghanistan. “Our patience has now run out. Now it is open war between us,” Pakistan’s defense minister said on February 27. Pakistan and Afghanistan have engaged in numerous strikes and counter-strikes in the months since. While these have declined in frequency and magnitude, thanks to mediation efforts by China, the military strikes were still happening into September 2026. TTP attacks in Pakistan have also continued. Few would have expected Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to turn on each other. They had been close allies for over 30 years – through the Taliban’s entire existence. When the Taliban captured power in Kabul in August 2021, Pakistan celebrated. So why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé? Is there more to Pakistan’s military strikes on Afghanistan than taking out TTP camps? And can the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship be salvaged? Already have an account? Log in . https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/investig.body: Credit: olympic.uz Subscribe for ads-free reading In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate. Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik . Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk. As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.” Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov. Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States. Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman. According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP. It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased. While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly. OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork. A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “ Golden Visa ” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case. Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik , we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities. Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship. Already have an account? Log in . https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/uzbekist.body: Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis Credit: Uzbekistan Presidency Subscribe for ads-free reading For the second time in the span of a year a brutal child abuse case has sparked heated public discussion in Uzbekistan. Reportedly, a five-year-old girl was repeatedly raped in a public kindergarten by a facilities manager who worked at the school in the Uchkurgan district of Namangan. According to the mother of the survivor, the alleged perpetrator is their neighbor and she became suspicious after she saw him smiling at her five-year-old daughter. She gently asked the girl questions only to find out that the facilities manager would buy sweets for the girl, tell her he loved her, and promised to buy more presents and sweets if she didn’t expose him. The mother suspects the man had threatened her daughter. Last year a similar case, which also occurred in Namangan, where a previously imprisoned convict raped a seven-year-old girl, caused a wave of demands by the public to restore the death penalty for serious crimes such as the sexual assault of minors. Public discussions over the death penalty typically emerge in Uzbekistan after news of an especially brutal crime against children breaks. An earlier wave of loud discussions took place in 2024 after a three-year-old was stabbed 12 times. What’s new this time is that high-ranking political figures are getting involved. Saida Mirziyoyeva, the head of the presidential administration and a deputy chair of the Security Council (and also the president’s daughter) chimed in. “In my opinion, the death penalty should be used for such heinous crimes. Unfortunately, the current legislation does not provide for the death penalty,” she wrote on her Telegram channel on September 27. “We are preparing a proposal to amend the legislation to maximize liability for this type of crime,” she added. Echoing Mirziyoyeva’s words, Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish (National Revival) Democratic Party and deputy speaker of the Uzbek parliament, called death penalty a “necessity.” Qodirov is famous for making nationalist, sometimes controversial statements. “The continued existence of those who intentionally kill innocent people, especially child murderers and pedophiles, is a motivation for further crimes of this kind!” Qodirov wrote on his Telegram, reposting Mirziyoyeva’s earlier statement. This is not the first time Qodirov has voiced his position on the death penalty. Previously, in 2024, after news reports about a three-year-old girl being murdered, Qodirov suggested “cleansing” society. “It’s illogical to use our taxes to support a criminal who’s become an animal, keep him healthy, feed him, and then wait for someone else to die! Society needs to be cleansed of such people!” he wrote . Both Mirziyoyeva and Qodirov know that Uzbekistan abolished capital punishment in 2008 and acceded to the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aimed at abolition. Uzbekistan has no mechanism to reinstate the death penalty without a much larger legal overhaul, and no such overhaul is presently underway. In a rather unusual course of developments for Uzbekistan, the discussion over the death penalty divided the country’s political parties. As a new bill to increase liability for violence against children was introduced to the Legislative Chamber on September 29, Qodirov announced a neutral position on the proposed bill and doubled down on his stance regarding the need to resurrect the death penalty. Qodirov referred to Norwegian neo-Nazi and mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik , stating that he had complained “about the lack of facilities for writing a book, and those conditions were subsequently provided for him.” Qodirov’s interpretation isn’t quite accurate. While Breivik did complain about the “stab-resistant” pen he was made to write with and was reportedly provided with an electronic typewriter, Breivik’s communications continue to be censored by prison authorities and he has not published a book. Nevertheless, using Breivik as a point of reference, Qodirov questioned the compatibility of Uzbek values and international law. “Whose footsteps are we following!?” he asked. “We will also be forced to create conditions for our pedophile if he asks, because the international law we follow sees him as a human being, not as a dead person.” Bobur Bekmurodov, a member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis and leader of the Yuksalish movement, opposed Qodirov’s statements openly. His arguments are clear: the constitution prohibits the death penalty, bringing the death penalty back could put child victims in greater danger, break Uzbekistan’s international obligations and raise the possibility of errors in judicial practices. “If child rape is punishable by death, there is nothing to stop the perpetrator from destroying the only witness, the child himself,” wrote Bekmurodov. While the grief over the case is genuine, the debate over the death penalty is a populist, opportunistic response. In a country where no other important questions are debated by high (or low) profile politicians, children and women’s abuse is a risk-free topic. Not only does it attract empathy from millions of citizens, but it also gains praise from international organizations. Siding with an innocent child is always a winning move. As outrage grows, officials do their best to appease the public. The investigation over the case is now under the prosecutor general’s control . Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, another daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and the first deputy director of the National Agency for Social Protection, reported that her agency is also involved in the case and the survivor’s family will be moved to another city and provided with housing. The agency also suggested changing the girl’s surname to ensure her privacy as she rehabilitates. The Ministry of Preschool and School Education formed a working group to address the situation. Right now, all attention is being given to maximizing punishment for one perpetrator and not letting another incident happen. What is left out of these debates is the failure of the systems that should have protected this girl. The mother of the survivor told local media that the cameras in the kindergarten did not record anything that day. And more absurdly, she had been told that the perpetrator was responsible for the cameras. The perpetrator’s wife allegedly offered her a bribe to close the case, too. The staff of the kindergarten who are supposed to protect the children in their care, are hiding behind paperwork instead of showing compassion. The director of the kindergarten said she was on a holiday when the alleged incident occurred and she had already provided explanatory letters to the police. She also added that children are never left unsupervised. The girl’s teacher also swore the girl was never left alone – “Not an hour, not a minute, would [she] be left unattended.” Local media outlets and the authorities have not disclosed the perpetrator’s name or released a mugshot. Netizens, however, have found his photos and full name and doxed his identity on social media pages. Yesterday, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva noted that her agency, together with other relevant bodies, had been working on a draft law that would introduce life imprisonment for crimes involving child sexual abuse. “We also propose to strengthen the responsibility of parents for neglecting children and of educators for allowing violence and discrimination, and to provide legal assistance and protection to child victims at every stage of the investigation and trial,” the agency’s Telegram post stated . From 2022 to 2026 445 cases of rape involving minors under 14 years old were formally registered in Uzbekistan. Not all cases make headlines. Journalist and economist Bakhodir Abdullayev noted that the legislation on lifetime imprisonment for sexual abuse of minors was supposed to be passed by April 2026. https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/can-a-ne.body: Condos in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, often use scarce potable water to support non-native plants such as roses. Credit: Walt Ohnesorge Subscribe for ads-free reading Can gardens act as a network of miniature sponge cities to have a positive impact on climate change in Central Asia? A preponderance of aesthetic decisions and other barriers hold back the adaptation of Central Asia’s cities, but individuals and local authorities can make a difference. Kyrgyzstan, and Central Asia more broadly, are experiencing stress on available groundwater reserves. As Dr. Eric Rudenshiold noted in an article for the Caspian Policy Center last year, “Driven by regional temperature increases, the region’s glaciers are melting at a rate four times faster than the global average and far faster than anticipated.” Central Asia’s glaciers feed rivers and streams throughout the year. One can easily imagine a future in which rivers run dry and entire cities are required to use only water gathered from rain that falls in just a few short months of the year. In a future like this, having the ability to retain water in place could mean the difference between thriving and ceasing to exist. Stronger storms, floods, droughts, deadly heatwaves, and mass migration are putting pressure on policymakers to follow through with plans to update infrastructure. An empty canal in Bishkek. Water from rain and glacial melt is directed through and away from the city to evaporate downstream. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) What Can Central Asia Learn from Sponge Cities? During a public lecture in 2003, architect Kongjian Yu coined the term “sponge cities” while outlining a set of urban planning principles developed to manage water in flood-prone regions of China. Sponge cities have since been enshrined in Chinese public policy by the Chinese Communist Party as a regulatory framework for development in the country. Kyrgyzstan has been interested in China’s governance model as a way to alleviate poverty, but its development and domestic urban planning initiatives offer other lessons. Time is running out for risk-prone areas of the world to make lasting, meaningful changes in the face of climate change, and some adaptation ideas may have been overlooked in parts of Central Asia. This oversight is evidenced by the colossal loss of green space in Bishkek since the Soviet era. While Kyrgyzstan’s cities have lost greenery, China has mandated the construction of climate-resilient urban spaces. Adopting a strong approach to state funding and regulation of green spaces is likely to create jobs in the industry and holds potential, where green spaces are fruit-bearing, to reduce food insecurity. Both of these outcomes could reduce poverty in Kyrgyzstan, and Bishkek’s own Green Cities Action Plan acknowledges the need for climate resilience and adequate green spaces. However, in lieu of decisive regulatory action and funding, much of the work of adapting to new climate realities falls on individual gardeners and cooperatives. Climate change has a disproportionate impact, both geographically on specific regions of Kyrgyzstan, and particularly on marginalized communities. As members of the El-Too foundation point out, “at the municipality and political level, women are not included in the decision-making processes; all issues related to land are discussed with the participation of men mainly... The situation is especially difficult for women that are employed as invisible forces in agriculture and have no other source of income.” Miniaturizing Sponge Cities While researching this topic, we were struck by a lack of sources for community-lead gardening initiatives in Kyrgyzstan. We discovered that Bishkek has no immediately identifiable grass roots collectives piloting alternative or sustainable agriculture inside the city. Even a cursory glance at New York City yields several sources and projects, and the same is true for other global cities. It is far easier to identify the challenges, like existing attention to inefficient practices, than attempts at solutions. The scale of new development in Bishkek is profound, dwarfing initiatives to create a greener city, preserve green spaces, and retrofit existing spaces for greater efficiency. With that in mind, we considered what it might look like if individuals in Bishkek took it upon themselves to implement better water preservation systems. Homemade drip irrigation feeds an area near a condo in Bishkek, where residents improvise to utilize water efficiently during summer months. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) One dacha owner, Asel, shared that she has never thought of climate change when managing her garden. She planted species that her landscape designer recommended, who was guided by beauty rather than water management or other climate change concerns. The same could be said about the managed gardens of some condominium buildings. Bakyt, a groundskeeper at one such building, said, “We plant roses here and use drinking water to water them.” Another dacha owner, Zarina, said she’d never seen a list of plants recommended for the local climate, but expressed interest in such a list. This interest leads us to believe that, given a coordinated campaign to make information and tools available, individuals might be easily motivated to shift their habits toward more sustainable gardening practices. A small container garden near a condo in Bishkek reflects a local desire for more green spaces. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) As Walt Ohnesorge, an artist and designer (and one of the authors of this piece) observed of many condos in Bishkek, “they could attach a catchment system to the gutter and plant perennial, food bearing plants to save drinking water, supplement tenants’ groceries, and utilize rain water for a more efficient system.” Nuraiym Syrgak, Kyrgyzstani social researcher and ecologist, and former executive director of the El-Too Public Foundation and a board member of the Association of Legal Entities “Green Alliance of Kyrgyzstan,” shared her ideas and experience implementing ecological projects. There are things people can do, at all levels, to help the land adapt to a changing climate. She noted that specific patterns of water allocation in villages have consequences. “Water for irrigation is mainly given to large plots. Gardens and zones within the village receive little water,” Syrgak said. “Therefore, we wanted precisely these small areas to become the center of attention.” Syrgak added that women, in particular, are good agents of change. “Men tend to be skeptical of anything new, especially at first, whereas women try to apply every new thing. In this sense, women are fantastic change agents. That is why we started working with them and later brought the men on board. As a result, we ended up with a family-based approach to agriculture.” Beyond villages and gardens, parks can also be transformed into miniature sponges within urban landscapes. “We often see these trees in our parks, which are not adapted to our climate,” Syrgak noted “Of course, they are beautiful. But at the same time they do not give more function. They do not give shade. They require a lot of work. And permaculture is such a philosophy, so that a person works less. And cooperates with nature to minimize work.” Syrgak stressed that there was no clear list of priority species for cultivation to fight climate change, but the centering of local species is a good place to start. “If you look at our deserts or abandoned zones, there are always these elms, which is a local type of tree and does not require watering,” Syrgak pointed out. “Then there are a lot of species like local shrubs, which could be useful for changes. https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/chinas-y.body: Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading In the U.S. state of Hawai‘i, Iris lives far from the pressures of urban China. Growing up in Zhejiang, she spent much of her childhood on what her mother called “self-improvement”: Olympiad math, piano lessons, and daily swimming. After graduating from New York University (NYU), Iris chose a simple, quiet life in Hawai‘i, using geographic distance to protect her personal autonomy from the pressure facing Chinese women in their 20s to settle down, marry, and have children. Halfway across the world, Jessica is confronting the same expectations from within China. After studying in Shanghai and Europe and working at an international organization in New York, where a mentor once urged her to stop working late and “enjoy the New York night,” Jessica returned to China to finish her master’s thesis and enter the domestic job market. There, she met a second, more intimate pressure: the expectation that she should marry and have children. Rather than quietly accepting it, she confronted the idea directly, over dinner with her mother, asking: “Are you actually happy in your own marriage? What has it genuinely brought you?” Iris and Jessica belong to a highly educated cohort of young Chinese women whose lives are unfolding alongside a demographic problem the state is eager to solve. Facing an aging population, a shrinking workforce, and historically low fertility rates, Beijing introduced the Three-Child Policy in 2021 , allowing Chinese couples to have up to three children. China’s government has since increasingly emphasized marriage and childbearing as social priorities . Yet China’s demographic crisis gained steam during the same decades of modernization that gave women access to more education, higher incomes, and greater mobility. That means women like Iris and Jessica have more reasons, and more means, to delay or reconsider marriage and motherhood. Research on China’s education expansion by Jiwei Chen and Jiangying Guo of Nanjing Agricultural University found that increased female education can delay entry into marriage and childbirth and reduce fertility, in part by raising the opportunity costs of childrearing. The modernization that expanded women’s choices has made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable. Jessica confronts this tension directly, pressing her own mother on whether marriage delivered what it promised and treating parenthood as a choice to question rather than a milestone to check off. Iris resists more obliquely: rather than arguing with the assumption that a good daughter eventually settles down close to home, she puts enough distance (first New York, then Hawai‘i) between herself and the people who would enforce the traditional path, letting their expectations fade into background noise instead of demands she has to answer. Neither is rejecting family, marriage, or children outright. Both are refusing to treat any of these options as the default for a Chinese woman. Jessica: Deconstructing the Script Upon returning to China to finish her thesis, Jessica found the job hunt less a search for a career than a reckoning with what kind of life she was willing to accept. In Europe and New York, she’d grown used to a workplace culture defined by what she calls “松弛感”: ease, dignity, being treated first as a person. One night, working late in New York, her mentor stopped her: “You are in New York. You should go enjoy the night.” The line stuck with her. The anecdote formed a sharp contrast with Jessica’s internship at a major Chinese internet company, where a hyper-competitive, results-only culture left people passing their anxiety down the hierarchy. She posted a comparison of the two experiences on Xiaohongshu and it sparked a fight in the comments: some dismissed it as a naive “student mindset”; others agreed with a Chinese woman writing from Europe, who argued that Western employers need their workers enough to treat them decently, while Chinese managers can simply replace anyone who underperforms. For Jessica, the real question was how much room there was for personal choice to override social norms. That questioning carried over from professional pressures straight into marriage. Years abroad had sharpened her sense of independence, but her father still pictured a conventional future for her, and relatives kept the pressure alive by mentioning which of her peers had already married. Jessica pushed back on the premise itself, arguing that a mother-daughter bond can matter as much as a marital one. She half-jokingly tells relatives that if marriage is unavoidable, it’s better to get in and out of it quickly than drag out something broken. The same skepticism shapes how she thinks about children. She’s fond of them but treats parenthood as a serious undertaking that shouldn’t simply follow marriage on a fixed timeline. She has watched enough families to conclude that unhappy marriages, and kids who are under-supported despite material comfort, are more common than the success stories that get celebrated. Teenagers hit adolescence with mental health struggles, some withdrawing from school, often because parents were too consumed by work to be present. Jessica has also watched women of her mother’s generation absorb the burden of family life, reshaping careers around husbands and children. She has no intention of doing the same by default. That came to a head at a family dinner, when marriage came up again and Jessica turned the question back on her mother: was she actually happy in her marriage? What had it given her? It was an invitation to examine whether women’s sacrifices for family are as inevitable as they’re made to seem. “If my pain can never be carried by anyone else,” Jessica told The Diplomat, “then my happiness has to be mine to build, too.” She’s stopped ruling out partners by age, and increasingly by nationality; a good match is rare enough without narrowing the field further. Her mother has softened too, no longer pressing on timelines. None of this makes her anti-marriage or anti-motherhood. But Jessica insists on the right to decide what place they hold in her life, rather than letting either define her adulthood before she’s had the chance to define it herself. Iris: Exiting the Room Growing up in Zhejiang, Iris Liu’s school breaks were a rotation of enrichment classes: Olympiad math, swimming, roller skating, dance, painting, piano. As an only child, she absorbed her mother’s conviction that giving her every possible advantage was simply what good parenting looked like. Before Iris had even reached middle school, her mother was already telling her she needed to learn to swim: American Ivy League universities, she’d heard, liked students who could swim. The plan was always aimed outward, toward a future far from home. Years later, Iris would indeed leave China. She just wouldn’t use that mobility the way her mother had imagined. The first crack came early, almost by accident. A two-week middle-school trip to Los Angeles was supposed to preview the life her mother was preparing her for. Instead, Iris came home unimpressed: a suburban campus, cafeteria pizza, none of the excitement she’d expected. Her disappointment rippled into her mother’s plans: the pressure around swimming eased, and the push toward an international high-school track quietly faded. Still, the broader trajectory held. Iris went on to NYU, and after graduation had the kind of options her education was supposed to produce: interviews for corporate jobs with six-figure salaries. She did not end up in any of these. She chose instead a job in Hawai‘i. Her parents had a particular idea of success. When Iris told them about interviews with major firms with salaries over $100,000 a year, they barely reacted. https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/the-less.body: A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Credit: Agnieszka Pikulicka Subscribe for ads-free reading In the female section of an upscale restaurant in Kabul’s Shar-e Naw, a waiter brings me a menu and a form. Only two lines are filled in: one bears an Italian name, the other a local one. The waiter explains that guests are required to fill it in at the request of the Ministry of Interior. It is for the guests’ own safety, he emphasizes, slightly uneasy. It is hard to tell if he believes it. I look at the form. It asks for the guest’s name, date of birth, passport number, address in Kabul, as well as when they visited the restaurant. “It is for your security,” the waiter repeats. I give him the blank form back. “I feel secure without it,” I say. He doesn’t insist. He takes my order and disappears. Five years after the withdrawal of NATO troops from Afghanistan, and into the rule of the Taliban, the group’s control over the country is stable. While the Taliban might not have access to the newest surveillance technologies, their infiltration of local communities is high. They had learned their lesson from their first period of rule, the emirate that ended in 2001 with the U.S. invasion, a United Nations official tells me. “You can say that fundamentally, ideologically, they haven’t really changed. But in terms of control, consolidation, management, messaging, they are far more sophisticated now,” he says. “The first emirate was a brand new experiment. The second emirate is still an experiment, but they have learned a lot of lessons. They are smart.” Kabul still reminds me of its former self, as if time had stopped. The streets are bustling with life; street vendors cover the pavements, selling products ranging from food and cigarettes to clothes and electronics. The new regime is seen in the details: fewer women walk the streets, less rubbish lies scattered across the city center – a lasting feature of the corrupt rule back in the Republic days – and the streets seem less chaotic. But at first glance, the changes are small, sometimes imperceptible. A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka. Everyone I speak with says that the country has become safer. Twenty years of war and decades of fighting have taken their toll on people. The Taliban, while brutal and devoted to anti-modern ideas, has nevertheless brought peace. The paradox is that the Taliban were the main perpetrators of violence during the Republic days. It was due to their attacks on cars that traveling between provinces used to be dangerous and caution was advised. Since they took power, traveling between different regions of Afghanistan has suddenly become possible. Now, Taliban checkpoints cover the whole country. Some of them are stricter, with soldiers standing under the white flag bearing the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, and the Taliban symbol, checking travel permits meticulously. Other checkpoints are more relaxed, and it is enough to slow down and let the Taliban gaze into the car. There are few roads that the group does not control. To leave their place of residence, drivers need special permits, and so do tourists. A letter from “Afghan Tour,” a unit responsible for travelers, is required to travel and stay in another province. It is unclear what its purpose is, other than surveillance. In Kabul, the “Afghan Tour” official says that getting a travel letter requires paying for an expensive tour. But it is possible to get it in Bamyan, another province, for a small fee. Most other regions also issue such letters in exchange for booking an inexpensive “tour” with an official guide. It is unclear if its price is official or simply a bribe paid for obtaining the letter. It is also hard to call it a tour. As part of the “tour” I book to stay in Mazar-i-Sharif, the local guide shows me into the Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, first built in the 12th century before Genghis Khan leveled the original building to the ground. But the tour included little in terms of a history lesson. The guide complained about his low earnings, suggesting I pay extra for his time. Then he demanded that I share my local contacts with him. For my own safety, of course. Today the new Taliban administration is stable. Ministries work, and courts solve disputes without the need to pay bribes, I am told. 96 percent of the poppy fields have been eradicated and hundreds of addicts who formerly squatted on Kabul’s streets and under bridges have been forced into rehabs. This is the kind of “stability” I know all too well from Central Asia’s autocracies, Afghanistan’s neighbors: they are brutal and relentless, but the pavements are clean. According to a recent report from Human Rights Watch , censorship of local media outlets and restrictions on freedom of expression have intensified, while journalists, activists, academics and other regime critics have faced repression, torture, and arbitrary arrests. “The Taliban always accuse us of being spies, it’s hard to work these days,” one local photojournalist told me. The Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, in Mazar-i-Sharif. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka. Women have been denied basic rights, such as the right to education beyond sixth grade. A woman visiting her parental home who does not return to her husband can be deemed a criminal. That includes survivors of domestic violence. A woman accused of touching, shaking hands with, or hugging a man who is not her mahram, a close male relative with whom marriage is prohibited, can spend a year in prison. Two months if a girl or a boy is seen dancing. A new “Preachers’ law” defines Muslims as followers of the Hanafi school of Islam. Local Hazaras, or Ismaili minority groups, are now officially deemed heretics. “Many Ismailis now hide their faith,” one man from the community tells me. He lost his job in a school in Badakhshan due to his faith. All that in the name of the “peaceful and clear sky above us,” as Uzbekistan’s late President Islam Karimov used to say in justifying his own repressive rule. Except that this is not the reality for most Afghans. While the war might be over – except for skirmishes in Badakhshan province and regular attacks from Pakistan – Afghanistan is hardly facing a post-war recovery. The withdrawal of U.S. and NATO troops and the coming to power of the Taliban, a government recognized only by Russia, meant that the United Nations mandate became much more restricted in scope. Cooperation with the de facto Taliban authorities has focused mostly on securing people’s very basic needs. Most international non-governmental and governmental organizations, and media, have left, and with them hundreds of local jobs disappeared. The biggest difference is noticeable in large cities: Kabul, Herat, or Mazar-i-Sharif, where previously educated, English-speaking men and women could find employment and develop careers. As another local journalist told me, during the Republic days he could support his family working as a photographer and videographer. Now, work is scarce. He has not had any projects for several months. “The situation seems to get worse every day and every year. Unemployment has reached a very high level, especially for people like me who work in the arts and creative fields,” he says. “People of Afghanistan are facing many other serious problems, including unemployment, untreated illnesses, hunger, poverty, and lack of adequate shelter. I do not see a clear government plan to address unemployment at its roots.” According to the United Nations , more than 17 million people, or 40 per cent of Afghanistan’s population, are projected to face acute food insecurity. And the situation is worsening. While following the U.S. withdrawal, thousands of Afghans left the country in search of a better life, this trend is now reversing – though not voluntarily. https://novastan.org/fr/kazakhstan/au-ka.body: 2 octobre 2026 Rédigé par : Eléa Muresan Tags Armée Astana Bizutages Défense Jeunesse Service militaire Violences Un paramilitaire kazakh lors d'exercices militaire en 2000 (illustration). Crédit : Wikicommons Au Kazakhstan, l’automne marque le retour de la conscription. Si certains jeunes hommes considèrent le service militaire comme un devoir envers leur pays, d’autres cherchent par tous les moyens à y échapper. À Astana, les récits de recrutements forcés dans les lieux publics et de violences dans les casernes nourrissent une défiance persistante envers l’armée. Au Kazakhstan, le mois de septembre a marqué l’ouverture de la campagne automnale de recrutement de jeunes, dans le cadre de la conscription. Le gouvernement kazakh prévoit le recrutement de 23 000 hommes , âgés de 18 à 25 ans, d’ici fin décembre. Faites un don à Novastan Héritage de l’ère soviétique, le service militaire représente au Kazakhstan un fait de société important, car il concerne l’ensemble des jeunes hommes. En principe, tous sont soumis à l’obligation de servir l’armée pendant une année entière, à travers une formation physique et théorique permettant de se familiariser avec l’univers militaire et sa discipline. Mais dans la pratique, de nombreux jeunes cherchent à y échapper, mettant en place un volet de stratégies pour obtenir des dispenses. Associée à une réputation sulfureuse, l’armée peine à recruter, malgré le caractère obligatoire de la conscription. Des méthodes de recrutement plus offensives que la simple convocation se sont développées depuis quelques années, parmi lesquelles des formes d’enlèvement de jeunes orchestrés par la police dans des espaces publics. Violence et controverses dans l’armée Novastan est allé à la rencontre des habitants d’Astana, la capitale kazakhe, afin de comprendre leurs représentations et expériences relatives au service militaire. La majorité de ces échanges laissent entendre que le service militaire ne jouit pas d’une bonne réputation auprès des habitants de la capitale kazakhe. « Moi je n’irai pas. Chaque année il y a des centaines de garçons qui reviennent blessés . Certains meurent, d’autres qui se suicident, c’est hyper violent. Le Kazakhstan n’est même pas un pays en guerre, ça n’a aucun sens « , raconte Jordan, jeune informaticien âgé de 23 ans. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Dans les rangs de l’armée kazakhe, une violence inouïe : « Mes reins se sont déplacés à cause des coups » La conscription suscite effectivement de l’inquiétude auprès de nombreux kazakhs. Des drames survenant chaque année ont forgé une réputation de violence dans l’imaginaire collectif autour du service militaire : morts, blessures, harcèlement, suicides. Parmi les scandales les plus viraux des dernières années, le cas de Moukhtar Yerebatan, jeune homme de 18 ans, victime d’une commotion cérébrale dans le cadre de son service, avait également suscité l’indignation dans tout le pays. Après un coma de deux ans, la mort du jeune homme le 23 juin dernier avait relancé la polémique sur les violences au sein de l’armée. D’après les sources officielles, il se serait blessé à la tête en tombant dans les toilettes par accident, mais cette version est contestée par ses proches qui suspectent des violences intentionnelles. La semaine passée, la mort d’une dizaine de jeunes conscrits lors d’un accident dans la mer Caspienne a intensifié la colère et les inquiétudes des parents concernant le service militaire, ne croyant plus en la capacité de l’armée à assurer la sécurité de leurs enfants. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Dans les rangs de l’armée kazakhe, une violence inouïe : « Mes reins se sont déplacés à cause des coups » « Les nouvelles sont terrifiantes. Si j’avais un fils, en aucun cas je le laisserais rejoindre l’armée « , confie Samal, hôtesse de l’air et mère de famille à Astana. Nombreux sont les jeunes qui mettent en place des stratégies pour échapper à la conscription, souvent avec le soutien de leurs parents et de leur réseau. Ces méthodes peuvent se baser sur des dispositifs légaux, mais aussi sur des formes de corruption. Sont notamment exemptées les personnes déclarées inaptes lors de la visite médicale, et les inscrits à l’université. Timur, 22 ans, ancien étudiant en économie et commerce, raconte que beaucoup d’étudiants à l’université sont uniquement inscrits pour échapper à l’armée. Il explique les raisons pour lesquelles lui-même s’est soustrait au service militaire : « Je pense que c’est pas pour moi. J’ai pas envie de perdre un an de ma vie, c’est pas le bon moment, j’ai des projets personnels, je compte acheter un appart, voyager... « Rouslan, 26 ans, créateur de contenu, a suivi de longues études et obtenu un doctorat en anthropologie, un choix motivé à la fois par son intérêt pour la discipline et par la possibilité temporaire d’échapper au service obligatoire. « Après 25 ans, si on n’a pas encore servi, on peut être exempté en passant une formation militaire de 40 jours. C’est payant, mais les conditions sont beaucoup moins rudes, on est mieux traités que pour le service d’un an. « « Rapts » et « Kidnapping » Faute de parvenir à recruter un nombre de jeunes correspondant aux effectifs prévus annuellement, le ministère de la Défense met en place des mesures offensives. En particulier, ce que les locaux nomment des “rapts” ou “kidnappings” de jeunes, des formes de mobilisation forcées menées par la police et les militaires dans des lieux publics, sans être toujours justifiées légalement. Timour raconte que pendant les périodes de recrutement, à l’image de celle qui a débuté le 1er septembre, de nombreux jeunes évitent au maximum de fréquenter des lieux publics, par peur de se faire convoquer de force : « La police vient dans des endroits comme ça, par exemple dans le jardin botanique, où y’a beaucoup de jeunes, potentiellement ceux qui n’ont pas servi. Ça peut être un club, un billard, ou des salles de jeux vidéo, ce type d’endroits, où les mecs traînent souvent. » Lire aussi sur Novastan : Avec de nouveaux blindés, le Kazakhstan fait évoluer son armement pour une diversification prudente Un système de solidarité entre usagers s’est d’ailleurs développé sur l’application 2GIS, l’équivalent de Google Maps au Kazakhstan, pour s’entraider à éviter les lieux. Les utilisateurs peuvent se notifier entre eux et écrire des messages à propos de plusieurs lieux publics. Sur l’image, un utilisateur notifie « Police présente pour conscription, ils sont avec des camions « . Contrairement à ses amis qui réduisent leurs sorties pendant les périodes de recrutement, Timur a fait le choix de garder son mode de vie inchangé malgré le risque. « C ‘est impossible de surveiller partout où ils pourraient me trouver. Un ami est allé au magasin près de chez lui, et quand il est sorti, ils l’ont attrapé, embarqué dans une voiture et envoyé direct au bureau militaire. On peut se faire prendre n’importe où, mais je n’ai pas envie de rester enfermé chez moi constamment. J’ai peut-être de la chance « , sourit-il. Pourtant, au cours des deux dernières années, Timour a été embarqué par la police à plusieurs reprises, depuis qu’il a interrompu ses études. Pour s’en sortir, il compte surtout sur le soutien de son réseau. “ J’ai des amis, certains dans des organes d’État. Disons qu’ils ont des ressources administratives. Quand je les appelais, on me libérait directement ” explique Timour. Il relate le cas d’un ami qui a échappé de justesse à l’armée. Après avoir été embarqué par la police, il aurait été aidé par son père pour s’inscrire in extremis dans une université afin d’obtenir un sursis. D’autres, moins chanceux, ne disposent pas assez de ressources sociales et financières pour se tirer d’affaires. Si les bourses au mérite existent pour entrer dans l’enseignement supérieur, les places sont rares et la stratégie de l’inscription à l’université reste souvent coûteuse. « J’ai progressé dans tout » Malgré les controverses et les appréhensions de nombreux citoyens kazakhs, certains ayant

https://novastan.org/fr/kirghizstan/eau-.body: 16 septembre 2026 Rédigé par : Mathieu Lemoine Tags Accès abonné Asie centrale Changement climatique Kirghizstan Ouzbékistan Tadjikistan Syr-Daria à Baïkonour, Kazakhstan. Photo : Ninaras / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. Souvent présentée comme une source potentielle de conflits en Asie centrale, l'eau est aussi au cœur d'une coopération régionale ancienne et en pleine évolution. Après vingt-cinq années passées à travailler dans la région, dont près de vingt sur les questions d'eau et d'assainissement, Olivier Normand observe une transformation profonde des relations entre les États d'Asie centrale. Des héritages soviétiques au rapprochement récent entre le Kirghizstan, le Tadjikistan et l'Ouzbékistan, la gestion de l'eau raconte une autre histoire de la région. Lorsqu'Olivier Normand arrive pour la première fois en Asie centrale, en juin 2000, la région ne ressemble guère à celle d'aujourd'hui. Son premier contact avec l'Ouzbékistan est presque fortuit : une rencontre avec un Ouzbek à Moscou le conduit à participer à un projet consacré à de nouvelles techniques agricoles. Il traverse alors le pays, de Namangan à Ourguentch, en passant par Boukhara, Samarcande, Termez et Tachkent. À partir de 2003, il dirige depuis Termez un projet d'appui au ministère du Travail, avant de travailler sur différents projets sociaux. Depuis 2007, ses activités sont principalement consacrées à l'eau et à l'assainissement, notamment dans le bassin du Syr-Daria et la vallée de Ferghana. Ce qui l'a retenu en Asie centrale ? « Le sentiment d'être au centre du monde et d'assister à l'Histoire en marche », répond-il. Vingt-cinq ans plus tard, cette histoire a considérablement changé. Parmi les transformations qu'il aurait difficilement imaginées au début des années 2000, Normand cite l'ouverture des frontières, une plus grande liberté de circulation à l'intérieur de l'Ouzbékistan, la simplification du système bancaire et des taux de change, le développement d'Internet, la modernisation des infrastructures et la transformation des villes. Mais il insiste surtout sur le rapprochement entre les pays d'Asie centrale, et notamment entre ceux qui se partagent la vallée de Ferghana. Le 31 mars 2025, les présidents du Kirghizstan, du Tadjikistan et de l'Ouzbékistan se sont retrouvés à Khodjent, au Tadjikistan, pour signer un traité fixant le point de jonction de leurs trois frontières ainsi que la Déclaration de Khodjent sur l'amitié éternelle. Cette rencontre venait consacrer le règlement de différends frontaliers qui avaient longtemps empoisonné les relations régionales. Elle a également ouvert de nouvelles perspectives de coopération dans des domaines allant des transports et du commerce à l'énergie, l'environnement et l'eau. Pour Normand, le 31 mars 2025 constitue ainsi moins un accord spécifiquement consacré à l'eau qu'un symbole d'une évolution beaucoup plus large : la région apprend progressivement à gérer collectivement . . . https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/kazak.body: 2 October 2026 Daniyar Sadvakasov Edited by: Mathieu Lemoine Tags Artificial intelligence Electricity Infrastructure Kazakhstan A sign for the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, where Kazakhstan plans to develop a major cluster of AI and data centre infrastructure. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Kazakhstan has begun building a major data centre cluster in the industrial city of Ekibastuz. Its first phase will require around 50 MW of power, but the government’s longer-term ambition is to expand the site to as much as 1 GW. As the country seeks to position itself as a regional hub for artificial intelligence and computing, questions remain over whether its electricity and water infrastructure can keep pace In early 2026, Kazakhstan launched construction of its Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, in the northern Pavlodar region, following instructions from President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The first facility in the planned cluster is expected to have an energy capacity of around 50 MW. Depending on investor demand, however, the campus could eventually expand to as much as 1 GW and occupy up to 1,300 hectares. Ekibastuz was not chosen by accident. The city is one of Kazakhstan’s main energy centres and is home to the Ekibastuz GRES-1 and GRES-2 coal-fired power stations. Yet the scale of the project raises questions over whether Kazakhstan can generate enough electricity for such a large new consumer, how the data centres will be supplied with water, and what environmental pressures the development could create. What is Kazakhstan planning to build? According to the Pavlodar regional administration, the precise distribution of land between individual data centres, energy facilities and other infrastructure will be determined as project documentation is developed. The first stage includes data centre facilities, energy and engineering infrastructure, administrative buildings and AI computing infrastructure. Work is currently under way on site preparation, foundations, administrative facilities, checkpoints and the necessary engineering infrastructure. Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov inspects progress on the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz. Photo: Prime Minister of Kazakhstan’s official website. The authorities say the initial stage will require around 50 MW, with capacity subsequently increasing in phases. Additional land has been reserved to allow the campus to expand if demand from investors and technology companies materialises. Kazakhtelecom, one of the operators involved in the Data Center Valley project, told Novastan that the project envisages a hybrid cooling system combining precision air conditioning with closed liquid-cooling circuits using non-freezing liquid solutions. Construction has already begun, but public hearings with local residents have not yet taken place. The Pavlodar regional administration said hearings would be held after the necessary project documentation had been completed and the procedures required for environmental assessment had been carried out. The biggest question: electricity Connecting a new consumer with an eventual capacity of 1 GW would be unrealistic under Kazakhstan’s current energy conditions if such capacity were required all at once, according to Yerkebulan Kozhmambet, a member of the Public Council on Fuel and Energy Issues under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy. “If we are being honest, today this looks unrealistic, particularly given that the average age of our generating capacity is more than 65 years,” Kozhmambet said. A phased project would be possible, he added, provided new generation and grid infrastructure were developed at the same time. The first launch complex is expected to require 50 MW and is scheduled to enter operation in June 2027, while 1 GW represents a longer-term target rather than capacity the power system is expected to provide immediately. The scale is nevertheless considerable. According to Kozhmambet, a continuous 1 GW load would consume around 8.76 billion kWh of electricity annually. Kazakhstan’s total annual electricity consumption is approximately 110-115 billion kWh, meaning the completed Data Center Valley could theoretically account for around 7-8 percent of current national consumption. “No region today has a free reserve of this scale,” he said. The project also comes as Kazakhstan’s electricity system has faced shortages and imports, particularly from Russia during peak periods. Kozhmambet warned that if the full 1 GW capacity were introduced before Kazakhstan achieves a sustainable electricity surplus, the new data centres could absorb that additional generation and push the system back into deficit. Energy expert Asset Nauryzbayev takes a less pessimistic view. He argues that 1 GW would not necessarily pose a major problem for Ekibastuz if the development of the data centres is synchronised with new generating capacity. “If I understand the government’s intention correctly, it is based on the Soviet project to build four 4 GW power stations in Ekibastuz,” Nauryzbayev said. “In today’s conditions, the units would be 660 MW rather than 500 MW. An eight-unit station would therefore generate 5.8 GW. In those circumstances, 1 GW of consumption is absolutely not a large amount.” He also pointed to planned new gas generation in southern Kazakhstan, which he expects to reduce the country’s electricity deficit. But there is an environmental price. “This will undoubtedly create an enormous carbon footprint,” Nauryzbayev said, although he believes the price of carbon offsets is unlikely to fundamentally affect the economics of the project. Read more on Novastan : Carbon neutral by 2060? Kazakhstan’s green pledge faces a reality check There is another potential risk if data centres are completed before the generation intended to supply them. “Data centres will undoubtedly be able to pay more than ordinary consumers,” he said. “That could strongly affect the market if there is no direct link to newly built power stations. Data centres built quickly will take electricity away from ordinary consumers.” Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy says the government plans to add more than 26.3 GW of generating capacity by 2035 through modernisation, new conventional generation, renewable energy projects and nuclear power. Of this, 13.3 GW is planned through 2029. The ministry expects the country to be able to cover domestic electricity demand from 2027 onwards and subsequently develop a surplus sufficient to accommodate energy-intensive AI infrastructure and large data centres. Whether those projects are delivered on schedule will therefore be crucial to Data Center Valley’s longer-term expansion. Could water become the bigger constraint? Electricity may not be the only – or even the most difficult – resource question facing the project. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation told Novastan that it has not yet received an application to establish a water-use limit for Data Center Valley. No specific limit has therefore been set. The ministry said that the appropriate volume would be assessed once an application and supporting documents were submitted. Citing information from the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, it also said planned AI data centres in Kazakhstan would use immersion cooling with specialised liquids, which should not require large volumes of water or restrict supplies to existing users. This description differs from Kazakhtelecom’s statement that Data Center Valley will use a hybrid system combining precision air conditioning and closed liquid-cooling circuits. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Following a small river from the mountains into the Kazakh steppe, filmmaker Kristina Mikhailova set out to imagine its dreams. Five years later, the journey had become a portrait of Kazakhstan told through the voices of its women – and an intensely personal exploration of freedom, identity and belonging. A small river runs for 130 kilometres through Kazakhstan, beginning among mountain peaks and glaciers before gradually disappearing into the vast landscape below. When filmmaker Kristina Mikhailova first decided to follow the Aksay from beginning to end, she imagined making a film about the river’s dreams. Five years later, that idea had become something much larger. Along the river, Kristina interviewed around 100 women, asking each an unusual question: if you were a river, what kind of river would you be? Fifteen of them eventually became part of River Dreams , a 98-minute film in which the Aksay serves simultaneously as landscape, witness and metaphor. What emerged is not simply a portrait of a river. Through women’s stories of freedom, violence, dignity and belonging, the film became what its director describes as “a political portrait of Kazakhstan through a female perspective”. The film has since travelled internationally, receiving around 30 festival invitations and and winning the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury in the Forum section at the 2026 Berlinale . It has also drawn enthusiastic audiences closer to home, including three sold-out screenings in Kazakhstan and a packed morning screening in Kyrgyzstan, where it won Best Feature-Length Documentary Film at the UmutDoc International Documentary Film Festival in Bishkek. Yet bringing the film to a wider audience in Kazakhstan itself has proved much more difficult. Kristina says censorship has prevented River Dreams from securing the domestic release she wants. For Novastan, Kristina Mikhailova spoke with Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine about the “sisterhood of rivers”, the women she met along the Aksay, her Ukrainian grandmother’s memories, female agency and violence, her identity as a Russian Kazakhstani, and the painful experience of feeling deeply attached to a country that she sometimes feels is pushing her away. Kristina Mikhailova, director of River Dreams. Photo: Bauyrzhan Bismildin. A sisterhood of rivers Novastan: The film began with the idea of following the Aksay River for its entire 130-kilometre course. What were you looking for when you first set out? Kristina Mikhailova: When I started filming, I was very young. This was the idea for my first feature-length film: I wanted to follow the river all the way, 130 kilometres from beginning to end, and imagine what it might dream about – to film those dreams as I saw them. But after walking the entire river alone, I saw how much it changed along the way. I wanted to capture those changes and see reality through the river’s eyes, to personify it. I was working with a post-humanist approach and looking for a way to give the river a voice. That is how I came up with the idea of asking the girls who lived along the river what kind of rivers they would be. A still from River Dreams. Photo: Amir Zarubekov / River Dreams. That question immediately helped me understand the person in front of me and shape the conversation in a way that allowed her to share something very important to her. In the Kazakhstani context, very little space is often given to women’s perspectives. It mattered to me that, as a woman, I was creating such a space, and that through the film other women could have that space too. Gradually, what emerged was a political portrait of Kazakhstan through a female perspective. Why did you choose the Aksay in particular? Aksay, or Aksaika, is a very small, modest river. I wanted to film precisely this kind of inconspicuous river, because we have so many of them. Its journey is typical of many mountain rivers in Central Asia: they begin among mountain peaks and glaciers and then disappear somewhere in the steppe or flow into lakes, never reaching the ocean. By filming Aksay, I was also filming all these other rivers. I called it a “sisterhood of rivers”. It is funny because I once heard someone say that the film shows some of the negative aspects of women’s lives in Kazakhstan because I had chosen the “wrong” river – one that was too insignificant. Apparently, if I had chosen some great, “proper” river, the story would have turned out differently. I doubt it. Making female agency visible You interviewed around 100 women during the making of the film, with 15 eventually appearing in the final version. What did these encounters teach you? First and foremost, I learned about myself. Recently, I started thinking about how I changed over the five years it took to make the film. Of course, I established myself as a filmmaker, my name became known and new opportunities opened up. But something much more personal happened too: I discovered myself as a woman of Kazakhstan. I saw who I was. Through meeting other women, I realised how different we are and how many pains we share. I came to understand relationships between men and women better – and men themselves, too. For me, it was a genuine step up in my understanding of myself. One film led to so many personal discoveries. Freedom seems to be one of the central themes of the film. Did making it change the way you understood freedom and the restrictions women face? I am glad you noticed the theme of freedom because, for me, it was one of the key themes on a human level. While making the film, I realised how many layers restrictions can have. Some are so deeply embedded and so difficult even to recognise that overcoming them can sometimes seem utopian. But if we are talking about empowerment, then yes, absolutely. And women expand these possibilities for themselves. I think every one of the 100 girls I interviewed, and each of the 15 who eventually appeared in the film, helped create a safe space through her story and her willingness to share her vulnerability – a safe space for all of us within those 98 minutes. It is a space that women throughout Kazakhstan can enter. That is why I am trying so hard to secure a wide release for the film in Kazakhstan. I want every Kazakhstani woman to be able to see it. Its distribution title is Qyz Republic . The film deals with difficult experiences, including violence, but the women are never reduced to victims. Was challenging stereotypical representations of women something you consciously set out to do? I did not explicitly set out to move away from stereotypical representations of women. I had a different objective: to make female agency visible. That sounds slightly paradoxical, but there is a need for it. Above all, I wanted my girls to feel strong. I think both men and women can connect with that experience. But for girls in particular, the film creates a place where they can recognise themselves, feel seen and feel strong – where they can see themselves as capable of preserving their dignity despite everything. The culmination of this, of course, comes in the final scenes involving violence. At that point, the conflict becomes completely explicit – almost black and white. But in my view, not one of my girls looks like a victim. The river as witness The landscape itself seems to function almost like another character. How did you want the river and its surroundings to appear on screen? The landscape is definitely my silent witness – the ghost of Hamlet’s father. https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/the-l.body: 29 January 2025 Julian Postulart Edited by: Anna Wilhelmi Tags decolonisation Identity Kazakhstan Language A selection of clothes from Qazaq Republic, a popular fashion brand that owes much of its success to the ongoing identity debate in Kazakhstan. Photo by Julian Postulart. Over thirty years after the Soviet Union’s collapse, colonial influences persist in Kazakhstan. Russian remains widely spoken and serves as the primary language for interethnic communication. As language is a vital symbol of national identity, the enduring linguistic prominence of Russian poses a significant challenge to fully decolonising Kazakh identity. However, the invasion of Ukraine has spurred a young, urban middle class to confront these imperial remnants by reclaiming their native language. Russia’s colonial war against Ukraine has sent shockwaves throughout Central Asia. Moscow’s emphasis on historical, cultural and linguistic connections makes other former Soviet republics feel increasingly uncomfortable. Especially in Kazakhstan, home to a sizable ethnic Russian population, many fear that their country could be next on the Kremlin’s list. These concerns are not unfounded. Since the start of the war in Ukraine, Russian propagandists have repeatedly voiced thin-veiled threats about annexing parts of their southern neighbour. Moreover, after partial mobilisation was announced in Russia in September 2022, hundreds of thousands of predominantly young men fled across the border into Kazakhstan. Their arrival has exacerbated existing concerns, and magnified domestic tensions between social groups that identify themselves differently. Although over the past three decades, Kazakhstan’s government has attempted to forge a new national identity, Russian influence remains. Since the conquest of the Kazakh steppe in the 19th century by tsarist forces, the lands and the people inhabiting the territory of modern-day Kazakhstan were shaped by imperial rule. First by the Russian Empire, then by the Soviet Union. In the 20th century, forced collectivisation uprooted traditional lifestyles and led to famine. Countless people flocked to towns and cities in a desperate search for food and work, places which themselves were colonial spaces, dominated by imperial infrastructure and buildings. Rapid urbanisation and industrialisation have scarred the landscape and still cause pollution and environmental and health problems to this very day. The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue Russia’s linguistic legacy But apart from these more abstract, postcolonial realities , there is the pertinent yet controversial issue of language. In the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, many have grown painfully aware of the influence Russia still exerts over Kazakhstan through language. Over thirty years after independence, Russian remains the country’s main interethnic language. Political scientist Dossym Satpayev, in a piece for Chatham House, writes that Russification policies in the colonial era suppressed the Kazakh language so thoroughly that most forgot how to speak their native tongue. As the de facto official language of the USSR, speaking Russian was key to social mobility . After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the benefits of learning the Kazakh language remained negligible. Although Kazakh is the state language, and Russian a mere ‘official’ language, in reality , Russian-speakers still enjoyed significant privileges and advantages. Until recently, insufficient knowledge of spoken Kazakh was hardly considered a problem, as Russian proficiency was enough to live a comfortable life, especially in the north and in the cities, where most of Kazakhstan’s Russian-speaking population is concentrated. In education, Russian has been more advantageous for increasing the possibilities to study at renowned schools and universities in Russia, partly because of the availability of a broader range of academic resources. Similarly, career-wise, Russian speakers have traditionally had more job opportunities. By contrast, Kazakh was viewed as backward and inferior, as sociologist Azamat Junisbai remembers how, while growing up, he associated the Kazakh language exclusively as rural, uncultured and of low status. Read more on Novastan: “Alaqan” – Aida Adilbek’s decolonial documentary cinema Fear for antagonising Moscow Initially, Kazakhstan’s government made little effort to support the elevation of the Kazakh language. Policymakers were concerned that such a stance would feed into rising Kazakh nationalism, which in turn could endanger the country’s inter-ethnic stability. So, from the 1990s onwards, it chose to counter early national-patriotic movements by prioritising the development of a Kazakhstani civic identity . This civic identity, epitomised by the slogan ‘unity in diversity,’ sought to rally all people of Kazakhstan around the flag of the newly independent republic, regardless of ethnicity. However, the main threat to inter-ethnic stability did not emanate from Kazakh nationalism, nor from the country’s sizable Russian minority. As a matter of fact, Astana’s stance on the issue was long guided by the fear that, should it have followed a more ethno-national course, Kazakhstan would have risked antagonising its northern neighbour. Demographics driving change Meanwhile, it was increasingly difficult for the government to balance the national interest against grassroots calls for the strengthening of Kazakh ethnic identity. After independence, millions of Russians left Kazakhstan, dramatically changing the country’s demographic make-up. Kazakhs now form a clear majority. They are the country’s fastest – growing ethnic group, and their proportion of the total population is only expected to increase. Satpayev, in his contribution for Chatham House, argues that the strengthening of national-patriotic sentiments and movements is occurring organically. Based on demographic trends, support for a Kazakh ethnic identity will continue to grow, while the use of the Russian language is expected to decline. The Russian invasion of Ukraine catalysed societal developments resulting from these demographic developments, which are shaping current and future political preferences. Not so long ago, the debate on national identity was quite marginal , predominantly talked about among small-circles of Kazakh-speaking intellectual elites. The war has caused this discussion to spillover into public domain, with an ever-increasing number of people rediscovering what it means to be Kazakh in the context of persistent colonial legacies. Language as a decolonial tool Language possibly is the most enduring bastion of Russian influence in Kazakhstan. In an episode of RFE/RL’s Majlis Podcast, sociologist Junisbai discusses how older generations primarily engage with Russian media, which makes them more susceptible to Russian propaganda. Consequently, the idea of so-called benevolent colonialism still is widespread among the elderly. Many believe that Kazakhstan owes much to foreign rule, such as industrialisation and modernisation. Read more on Novastan: Pressure from Russia increases on Central Asian media outlets This sentiment is not shared with younger generations. They have no living memory of the Soviet Union, and seek to undo the final vestiges of Russian and Soviet colonialism in pursuit of a new Kazakh identity. For them, language is a tool for decolonisation. On the streets, for example, this is reflected in the growing popularity of fashion brand Qazaq Republic. This company, famous for its trendy clothing and other merchandise with patriotic Kazakh and English language slogans, owes much of its success to ongoing societal developments.
