https://novastan.org/en/politics/night-t.body: 6 June 2024 Julian Postulart Tags Regional politics Tajikistan Trains Uzbekistan A truck driving on a dusty road between Jizzakh and Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Photographed from the Tashkent-Dushanbe night train. Picture by Julian Postulart. For many years, relations between Tajikistan and Uzbekistan have been fraught with tension. Some analysts even dubbed the ties between the two countries a Central Asian ‘cold war’. But luckily, things are slowly improving. The return of the Tashkent-Dushanbe night train is a testament to this bilateral thaw. The new rail service connecting both capitals is, in many ways, a miniature of the past, present, and future of Uzbek-Tajik relations. “Your phone, please”, one officer demands. As the only man in the kupe , a train compartment, the border guards summoned me into the corridor. Reluctantly I let the officer scroll through the pictures I took during my brief visit to Uzbekistan. Pornography, photos of government buildings, military installations – whatever he is looking for, the man finds none. As he returns my phone, some of his colleagues enter the train to look for contraband and other prohibited items. Luggage is thoroughly searched, as well as the train’s interior. Some ceiling panels are removed and part of the flooring is opened up to examine if anything is hidden underneath. Despite Uzbek authorities having relaxed customs procedures over the past years, the border crossings with Tajikistan remain an uncomfortable exception. But relations between the two countries have improved significantly over the past few years. Travelling aboard the direct Tashkent-Dushanbe night train shows the slow fruition of this regional detente . The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue 15:47 – Tashkent Some thirteen hours earlier, my travel companion and I boarded the train at Tashkent’s central station. It was mid-May and with temperatures well over thirty degrees Celsius, our kupe was unbearably hot. Although the ticket agent had promised us air-conditioning, the one in our wagon was not working this afternoon. With sweat dripping down my back, a young Tajik mother asked if I could help her store her large suitcase. Nodira and her toddler son would be our cabin companions for the night, travellig to Dushanbe for a family visit. Although Tajik by birth, Nodira often pendles between Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Her husband owns a suitcase shop in Tashkent, yet she prefers the tranquil mountains of native Tajikistan over the hustle and bustle of the Uzbek capital. For a time, Nodira thought of running her own business as a professional make-up artist on Instagram, though it was no longer acceptable after becoming a married woman, she tells us. Ever since, Nodira has embraced a more conservative lifestyle, focusing on religion, her three children, and running the household. Tajik society is deeply patriarchal and gender roles remain traditional. However, for Nodira, social media has an important emancipatory function. It helps her learn a little English and connect with the outside world through her followers, mostly in Russian. In fact, she has become quite the influencer since our meeting on the sweltering night train. Thousands of people watch her videos in which she prepares classic Central Asian recipes in her kitchen. 20:40 – Samarkand Just after sunset, we made a brief call at Samarkand. The city’s magnificent architecture still reflects its historical significance as a leading centre of Persian civilisation. But Samarkand’s legacy is also highly contentious. For centuries, the Tajik language – a variety of modern Persian – has been Samarkand’s lingua franca. However, this position has come under increasing pressure since Uzbekistan’s independence. Eurasianet writes that former President Islam Karimov seemed intent on erasing the city’s Tajik roots. Many in Tajikistan, however, still see Samarkand as inextricably linked to their ethnic and cultural identity. The issue of Samarkand dates back to the 1920s when the city was made part of the Uzbek SSR under the Soviets’ policy of national delimitation. In 2009, Tajik President Imomali Rahmon told journalists that in a brawl with Karimov, he had threatened to take back Samarkand by force. Interestingly, a significant number of Tajik speakers in Uzbekistan hold more nuanced views about their ethnicity. Research about this topic found that “ many people speak a language as their vernacular language while identifying themselves with the ‘other’ ethnic group in daily life. ” In the same study, Persian-speaking respondents from Samarkand primarily see themselves as Samarkandi, rather than Tajik. On the other hand, for people like Nodira who are multilingual and have mixed families, local, national, and ethnic identities overlap. The new rail connection also has a significant symbolic function as a token of regional interconnectedness. In many ways, the hard border between Uzbekistan and Tajikistan was a historical anomaly, in that it divided a continuous cultural and linguistic space. 05:53 – Border After the Uzbek border guard returns my phone and the customs officials exit the train, we ride into no-man’s land. As we accelerate, I notice that at some point during the night, we have traded our silent, electric locomotive for a noisy diesel enginge. A gust of black smoke occasionally enters through the open windows – an unfortunate tradeoff for ventilation against the heat. As the train pulls out of the Uzbek customs zone, we pass high walls and concrete barriers, manned guard towers, and barbed wire. Suddenly, this militarised border zone gives way to green fields, off-roading Ladas, and even some rice paddies. Despite the early hour, whole families are out working the land. Some wave to the passing train. Indeed, a passenger train on these tracks remains a rare sight. Since independence, ordinary Uzbeks and Tajiks have been caught in the crosshairs of bilateral tensions. Lengthy examinations and searches, considerable red tape and frequent border closures had a significant impact on travel and trade. Relations between the two countries were mired in suspicion and distrust. Uzbekistan even had parts of the border area mined, allegedly to prevent militant Islamist groups from entering the country. Hundreds of people, mostly local farmers, were killed or injured in landmine explosions. After Shavkat Mirziyoyev succeeded Karimov in 2016 as president of Uzbekistan, clearing the minefields was a top priority in his pursuit of better ties with Tajikistan. Read more on Novastan: Moscow attacks highlight Tajikistan’s radicalisation problem With most of the obstacles removed, the task remains to rebuild the political, economic, and cultural ties that were virtually destroyed over the past 30 years. The return of the Tashkent-Dushanbe night train, as the first passenger rail connection between the two capitals since the collapse of the Soviet Union, is a testament to this ambition. 09:41 – Dushanbe On April 18 this year, Mirziyoyev and Rahmon signed a ‘Treaty on Allied Relations’ in Dushanbe. The treaty consists of 28 documents covering various areas of cooperation, ranging from cross-border trade to food safety, and from fostering intercultural exchange to transport and communication. In a statement, the President of Uzbekistan declared that bilateral relations between the countries had “risen to an unprecedented level” . Uzbek news website Darya.uz wrote that developing new transit corridors was among the leaders’ priorities. The Diplomat previously reported that, since coming to power, Mirziyoyev has pushed for new rail projects to bolster regional integration. Read more on Novastan: Railway between Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to be electrified But it might take some time before this treaty will bear fruit. For now, Dushanbe is all but a regional transport hub. The railway station of Tajikistan’s capital city ha

https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/kazak.body: 4 July 2023 cbabakoulov ascripka Translated by Abby Scripka Tags climate water shortage Since May 2023, the capital of Kazakhstan is suffering from a severe water crisis, as a result residents are now facing a shortage of drinking water. According to the government, across the country there are more than 600,000 Kazakhstanis that do not have access to drinking water. By 2050 the Republic of Kazakhstan may join the category of countries “ in dire need of water. ” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed holding an anti-crisis summit in Kazakhstan under the backing of the UN to solve the water problem. According to the monitoring group “Energyprom” – migration influx, rapid population growth and large-scale construction in the capital of Kazakhstan has exceeded the available capacity of the pumping stations. Therefore, on March 28, 2023, the city water supply service “ Astana Su Arnasy ” resorted to introducing an hourly water schedule to citizens. On May 23, residents of a residential complex expressed their dissatisfaction due to the lack of water by blocking the road. On June 10 the situation was resolved and authorities assured that the problem would be solved by the 30 of June as they are launching a new pumping and filtering system. Meanwhile the publication “KazTAG” reported that the water source for Astana is designed for only 500,000 people while the city has 1.3 million inhabitants. The mayor of Astana has connected the water shortage with the population growth and the active irrigation of agricultural land. The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue Aset Kaliyev, Directory of the Water Security Centre at the international scientific complex “Astana,” told “Inbusiness.kz,” that one of the causes of the water shortage in the capital was the failure of developers to follow the general plan for city construction, “ Having departed from the general plan, in Astana, with the approval of officials, densification and infill construction began. In turn, the infill developments began to cut into existing neighbourhoods, which already had their own load on the engineering networks. Since then, everything went “crooked and tangled”. According to Nursultan Kerimkulov, head of the Water Supply and Sanitation Department, the lack of water will affect the development of construction in the city, but the quality of drinking water will not be affected. Read more on Novastan: The recession of the Tian Shan glaciers and other recent studies On April 19, 2023, at a meeting on socio-economic development of the country President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev noted , that by 2050 Kazakhstan may enter the category of countries in dire need of water. The President said that the infrastructure of large cities is not able to meet the increasing demand each year. “Even in Astana itself, there has begun to be a shortage of water. One of the main reasons is the increase in construction. If we are not frugal, we will not be able to eliminate the deficit, even if we launch new facilities that provide clean water, ” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was quoted by the Kazakhstani news outlet “Tengrinews.” Read more on Novastan: A disappearing river: the fate of the Ural The problem of water shortages in Astana is not only related to the lack of design capacity of networks and pumping stations, but also to the direct shortage of water sources. Apart from the Astana reservoir, there are no alternative water supply options. Currently, the Ministry of Ecology of Kazakhstan is considering several options to solve the problem: construction of facilities to replenish the reservoir, laying a water pipeline and taking water from the Irtysh-Karaganda water canal. The crisis of water scarcity in the cities and provinces of Kazakhstan will only get worse According to the deputy director of public utilities of Kazakhstan, the provision of centralized water supply in Kazakhstan in 2022 was 96.8%. At the same time, more than 600,000 people, meaning the remaining 3.2%, are in need of drinking water. Experts draw attention to bureaucratic complications that arise between government agencies at different levels and hinder the timely resolution of problems. For example, the government’s Geology Committee is responsible for water resources in Kazakhstan, while the Water Resources Committee controls pipeline infrastructure. Other local executive bodies manage network design and construction. However, not every region does the necessary work without delays. Marat Karabayev, Minister of Industry and Infrastructure Development of Kazakhstan, made a statement at a recent government meeting. Read more on Novastan: Climate change could lead to ever more fluctuated temperatures in Central Asia The water sector also faces significant problems of deterioration of main pipelines and urban water pipelines. Overall, the degree of wear and tear on the country’s water supply networks is 43% . However, this figure does not reflect the scale of problematic networks in all regions. The highest level of infrastructure wear is seen in Almaty (58%), East Kazakhstan (54%), Akmola (52%), Abay (51%) regions and Almaty region (57%). In contrast, Atyrau region boasts the lowest level of pipeline wear and tear – 29%. In 2023, a significant budget of 544 million Euros was allocated by the authorities for the construction and reconstruction of water supply and sewerage systems throughout Kazakhstan. The government of Kazakhstan plans to provide water to 1,395 villages and 25 cities that do not have full access to water by 2025. Summit in Kazakhstan with back from the UN to solve the water problems On June 8 and 9, 2023, the Astana International Forum was held in the capital, which was attended by the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and the heads of several other states, including the Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov. At the meeting, the President of Kazakhstan proposed to hold a regional climate summit in Kazakhstan in 2026, under the supervision of the UN and other international organizations. “Our country offers tremendous opportunities for a green economy and become a centre for renewable energy. However, time is not on our side. To decarbonize and create a green economy at the necessary speed, we need resources and partnerships ,” the official website of the head of state “Akorda” quotes Tokayev’s proposal. Read more on Novastan: Kazakhstan: replenishing the Aral Sea’s fish stocks To prevent an environmental catastrophe in the region, the country is calling for increased international support for the Aral Sea Rescue Fund. “The problem of water and climate change are closely linked. Central Asia is a region where water security can only be achieved through close cooperation and effectively selected joint measures,” concluded the President. https://novastan.org/en/culture-sports/s.body: 13 June 2024 Florian Coppenrath Edited by: Julian Postulart Translated by Anna Wilhelmi Original Tags Bishkek Music Postpunk Review "Swinaja Poputka" cover of the third album by Vtoroi Ka Bishkek musical duo Vtoroi Ka has recently dropped its third album: carnivalesque postpunk in a world where nothing is as serious as it seems. Novastan’s review. “ These post-Soviet cities have already seen quite some nonsense/ But after seeing our Kyrgyz squad up close/ the lockdown has been abruptly enacted for some reason “, says the chorus of the single “Vstrechyaite Govnyukov” (“Welcome the shitheads”) , released in February 2023. The retro-aesthetic video shows an exuberant wedding party stirring up the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek. The audience has been warned: the “shitheads” are coming to cause a lot of trouble. The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue “Shitheads” – Govnyuki in Russian – is what Sultan and Ilya of the duo Vtoroi Ka, currently one of the most exciting music groups in Central Asia, call themselves. They adopted the term from a video blogger who mocked them with it and turned it into something positive. As Sultan says in a long interview with the online magazine SRSLY: “ [We are] two shitheads. We’re explorers. The kind that aren’t afraid to try things and are constantly on an artistic quest .” At the beginning of May, Vtoroi Ka released their third album, Svinaya Poputka, a mysterious title that could literally be translated as “ piggy ride ” – a not entirely inaccurate description of the listening experience. It opens with the inviting bass line of “ Teni ot pal’m ” (“ Palm Shadow “): “ Come take me quickly to where the palm shadows are...” A cheerful Joy Division The song, which was released in June 2022 together with a music video filmed in Bishkek and on Lake Issyk-Kul, is the duo’s most successful hit to date. A total of six of the eleven tracks on the album had previously been released as singles, all with funny and colourful videos. Die-hard fans of the group will therefore recognize some of the songs, but in any case Svinaya Poputka offers a musically delightful half hour. https://youtube.com/watch?v=qyTjfhJpEAI%3Fsi%3D-nAQ6fToq_MT9v7e “Palm Shadow” Since their debut album “ Den’ Zavisimosti ” ( “Dependence Day” , 2020), which was still clearly a rap album, Vtoroi Ka seem to be moving further and further back into the musical past. The second album, “Serial” (2022), features excursions into the alternative teen rock of the 2000s, and the most recent tracks are full of allusions to the post-punk of the 1970s and 1980s. However, the characteristic sound of bass, drum computer and synthesiser, which according to one critic is sometimes even reminiscent of the late Soviet cult band Kino around Viktor Tsoi , does not underpin a dark soundscape as is so often the case. “ Vtoroi Ka play post-punk, but their music doesn’t have the depressive vibe so typical for the genre, ” emphasises hip-hop magazine The Flow. On the contrary: Svinaya Poputka is full of colourful irony – a kind of cheerful Joy Division, as those who grew up with English-language music might say (especially as Sultan’s bass voice is not so dissimilar to that of Ian Curtis). Read also at Novastan: Inside Bishkek’s Metal Boom: Portrait of a Music Pioneer in Kyrgyzstan Musical references and quotations can be found in abundance, whether in the lyrics themselves (“ An old cassette, vernissage in the loudspeakers “) or in the musical elements. The reels that Sultan and Ilya use to promote their music on social media are like building instructions. For example, for Dura (dummy), their latest single: “ Oh, try singing like Zhanna Aguzarova “ , an eccentric Russian-speaking singer who was particularly successful in the late 80s. Sex, drugs and gangster romance While Svinaya Poputka takes listeners back to the 80s musically, its content primarily relates to the first decade of independence after the end of the Soviet Union. In the words of another reviewer: “ The main characters in these songs are bandits and shitheads from the times of the wild 90s, such country road romantics”. This is symbolised by the “ Tonirovannyi Kaban ” ( “Tinted Boar” ), which is enthroned on the album cover with Bishkek’s skyscrapers and a “ Kosh Kelingizder ” sign (Kyrg. for “Welcome” ) in the background. On closer inspection, you can also recognise a “ pig duck ” on the sign, the signature of graffiti artist Cherv1, which adorns many a wall in Bishkek. Kaban – Russian for wild boar – is the popular name for the Mercedes W-140 , a status symbol particularly popular among the nouveau riche and mafia of the post-Soviet 1990s. However, the bonnet is emblazoned with a pig’s snout instead of the usual star. The single of the same name, in which Sultan and Ilya stage themselves as music dealers, is also dedicated to the “ Tonirovannyi Kaban “: Bakai Kolchaev, director of the Bishkek music label Infinity Music , which also distributes the music of Vtoroi Ka, plays the role of a mob leader in the music video. “Tinted Boar” But unlike the Russian cult series Brigada , which definitively associated the “ Kaban ” with the criminal 90s, Svinaya Poputka is not so serious. “ We don’t want to be taken seriously – like Skryptonite . We want to be simpler, with irony. Sometimes serious, but with a bit of fun, ” says Ilya, summarizing the group’s approach. Through music, colourful imagery and witty language the actually serious references turn into carnivalesque. A typical example for this is the music video “Dura” (“Dummy”) , whose bizarre characters seem to come from Alice’s Wonderland. At the same time, the piece is peppered with allusions to the world of erotic webcams, an equally l ucrative and dodgy business in Kyrgyzstan, and a recurring motiv in Vtoroi Ka’s work. Dura ‘s text speaks of “her” admirers (“ Ukhazhory “), who “ give her money wholeheartedly and so earnestly “, while she repeatedly goes “on air”. The same applies to the extremely danceable “ Ona sovsem odna ” ( “She is all alone” ): “ Her body is a glossy comic for adults “, and further: “ All admirers are wild, with brisk movements, unarmed/ In the chat, uncles over 40 are frolicking “. “Dummy” The underworld of Vtoroi Ka with its very likeable characters, always on the lookout for the next “Dvizh” , the next adventure, is romantic. In “ Boomerang”, a couple hides from unclear dangers in cosy togetherness in anticipation of the next Dvizh : “ Here we are an easy target/ Let’s leave these rooftops “, whether meant metaphorically or literally. “ We don’t have to die ye t”, it says, as in “Teni ot Pal’m”, which tells of a girl who has become a “ great shooter “, probably not without allusion to Luc Besson’s Leon – The Professional. Obviously, if you die, you can’t have fun anymore. Intoxication and artificial paradises run through the album like another leitmotiv. The place of longing, where the palm trees stand, is one “ where a kilo of junk for the nose costs a thousand “. Or “ Pomyat “( “Crumpled” ), a wild piece about the state “ when there is nothing to recharge yourself with “. “Bong” stands out in particular with its rock’n’roll rhythm – and is, unsurprisingly, dedicated to the water pipe, which, according to the lyrics, should definitely feature in Vtoroi Ka’s Stage Riders (or that of their fictional characters?). Flawless craftsmanship Svinaya Poputka impresses no less with its detailed and flawless production, all handcrafted by Sultan and Ilya, who, by their own admission, like to control “ everything from start to finish ” when it comes to their songs. Without overloading their songs, they manage to surprise you – even on the hundredth listen – with a noise in the background, an imaginative rhyme or a particularly successful transition. The tracks are entertaining, all around two and a half minutes long, with snappy intros – and therefore fit perfectly into the streaming

Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan A four-day expedition to Kyrgyzstan’s Adygene glacier brought seven women into the field with glaciologist Gulbara Omorova. For filmmaker Tynymgul Eshieva, the journey is part of a larger effort to document both the rapid transformation of Kyrgyzstan’s glaciers and the women working to understand them. In August, seven women set out into Kyrgyzstan’s Ala-Archa gorge for a four-day expedition. Some were experienced hikers; others had never undertaken a high-altitude trek of this kind. Their destination was the Adygene scientific station, around 11 kilometres into the mountains. They were not going simply to see a glacier. From 16 to 19 August, the participants worked alongside Kyrgyz glaciologist Gulbara Omorova, installing ablation stakes to measure melting, recording glacier movement with GPS and carrying out bathymetric measurements on lakes below the ice. Behind the expedition was documentary filmmaker and producer Tynymgul Eshieva. She is developing The Voice of the Glaciers ( Мөңгүлөрдүн үнү ), a feature-length documentary centred on Omorova and her work in Kyrgyzstan’s mountains. The film is still in development and is currently expected to be completed in 2028. But Eshieva has already been filming a landscape that is changing fast enough for those returning to it to see the difference with their own eyes. “We filmed the teaser in June last year, and then we went back for the expedition in August this year,” Eshieva told Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine. “The glacier looked completely different. You don’t need instruments to see it. You can see with your own eyes how rapidly it’s disappearing.” A glacier changing within a lifetime The measurements reinforce what the eye can see. During the expedition, around 1.4 metres of surface lowering was recorded near the glacier terminus over approximately one month. Over an entire ablation season, melting in the lower sections can amount to several metres. A field briefing during the expedition in Ala-Archa. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Omorova’s longer-term research paints an even starker picture. The Adygene glacier system comprises three glaciers – Bolshoy Adygene, Panfilov and 30-let VLKSM. Bolshoy Adygene has decreased in area from approximately 3.5 square kilometres in 1962 to 2.8 square kilometres in 2025, a loss of around 20 percent. More strikingly, the annual rate of area loss has accelerated from 0.006 to 0.033 square kilometres per year. The smaller glaciers are retreating too. Between 1977 and 2024, Panfilov lost around 20 percent of its area and 30-let VLKSM around 29 percent. For Eshieva, however, seeing the process at close range changed the meaning of such figures. “It’s completely different to see it with your own eyes,” she said. “You can read the news, follow websites, see the numbers online. But when you go there, when you stand on the glacier and feel it, it’s something else.” What struck her just as strongly was the work required to produce those numbers. “She carries heavy equipment up the mountain. She takes the measurements again and again, with total commitment,” Eshieva said of Omorova. “It’s slow, repetitive work, sometimes even boring, but it’s absolutely necessary. Without people like her doing it year after year, we simply wouldn’t know what is happening.” The woman behind the measurements Eshieva has known Omorova since the mid-2000s. Long before either woman imagined making a documentary together, they talked, hiked and even climbed a peak near Bishkek. Expedition participants make their way towards the glacier. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Eshieva only began documentary filmmaking in 2023. While editing her first feature documentary, also about a woman activist, she began searching for another project. She hopes to complete that film next year. The catalyst came through social media. The Adygene research station had been robbed and scientific equipment stolen. Omorova appealed publicly for help. People who had never visited a glacier responded, crowdfunding enough money to replace what had been lost. “That was the moment I thought: this could be a film,” Eshieva recalled. “Here is a woman who fights for her science, for the environment, for justice, and she doesn’t wait for anyone to do it for her. And ordinary people answered her call.” She began filming. Omorova’s route into glaciology itself began far from the ice. Trained in sociology, she travelled to villages to interview residents about social issues. During a visit to Batken, farmers told her about shortages of water. Already an experienced mountaineer with training in alpinism, she began asking why. That question eventually took her towards glaciology and the Adygene station. It also illustrates one of the central realities of glacier retreat: what happens high in Kyrgyzstan’s mountains does not remain there. Read more on Novastan : The recession of the Tian Shan glaciers and other recent studies From the glacier to the valley As glaciers retreat, they transform not only water availability but the landscape around them. Omorova’s monitoring has identified 16 new moraine-glacial lakes in the Adygene complex since observations began in 1977. Some glacial lakes can become unstable, making continuous observation essential. During the August expedition, the participants went out by boat to conduct bathymetric measurements using an echo sounder. By measuring water depth at different points, researchers can map the lake and track how it changes. Monitoring can also involve automatic loggers recording water levels and temperatures, water-column profiling and examination of the moraine dams holding back the lakes. Read more on Novastan : Life by the river: the Naryn in Kyrgyzstan The relationship between melting ice and downstream risk is complex. A lake that appears stable today may change as the glacier, surrounding terrain and permafrost evolve. The purpose of monitoring is therefore not to predict an outburst from a single measurement, but to observe the glacier-lake system continuously and identify changes that may eventually become warning signs. Expedition participants rest beside a mountain stream in Ala-Archa. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Eshieva did not originally set out to make a film about the relationship between glaciers and water. “When I started, my idea wasn’t to connect what happens up on the glacier with what happens down below,” she said. “But the more I filmed, the more I saw that they are deeply connected.” Whether that relationship ultimately becomes central to the documentary remains open. “People often ask me at pitching forums: is this a film about water? For now, it isn’t,” she said. “Documentary is a long process. You follow a person’s life, sometimes for two or three years, sometimes ten. I don’t know yet where it will go.” Seven women on the ice The August expedition itself emerged partly from necessity. Eshieva had initially envisaged a camp for aspiring ecologists, selected through an open call and led by Omorova. But by August, funding for the film had not materialised and the summer field season was slipping away. “I felt I had to do something,” she said. She changed the plan, crowdfunded an expedition and invited women interested in learning about glaciers to join. There was no competitive selection process. Participants simply had to be willing and able to commit to four days in the mountains. Seven ultimately went. Their backgrounds and levels of mountain experience differed. https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/germa.body: 4 October 2026 Mathieu Lemoine Tags Kazakhstan Russification Soviet Germans Lena Wolf, author of May the Universe Be Your Home! Growing up German in Kazakhstan. Photo courtesy of Lena Wolf. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Born in Latvia and raised in Kazakhstan, Lena Wolf grew up with fragments of a history that Soviet society rarely discussed openly. In her graphic memoir, she retraces the deportation of her German family to Kazakhstan, their struggle to preserve language and identity, and her own journey from Aktobe to Germany. For our readers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan: Lena Wolf’s e-book is now available at reduced regional prices on Google Play Books in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. Available in English and Russian . For much of her childhood, Lena Wolf believed that all Germans came from Kazakhstan. Aktobe was home. Her grandmother cooked German dishes alongside baursaki and manti, organised clandestine religious gatherings and spoke German to her grandchildren, even when they answered her in Russian. Around them lived families whose own histories had been shaped by deportation, repression and displacement. Yet Wolf also learned early that being German could set her apart. “I don’t think I really understood what being German meant to other people until I was called a fascist for the first time,” she recalls. “I was probably about six.” Decades later, Wolf began piecing together the family history that had reached her in fragments behind closed doors. The result was a graphic memoir illustrated by Christoph Heuer, tracing almost two centuries of migration, persecution and repeated attempts to build a home. Migration of German communities to the Russian Empire from the eighteenth to the nineteenth century. Her grandmother Emilia was 25 when she was deported to Kazakhstan in 1941 with two young children. Like many Soviet Germans, the family initially believed the displacement might be temporary. “They left behind their houses, land, animals – everything – still hoping they would return,” Wolf says. They never did. Forced deportation routes of Soviet Germans in 1941, including destinations in Kazakhstan and Siberia. Even after Stalin-era special-settlement restrictions were lifted in 1955, Soviet Germans were not allowed to return to the areas from which they had been deported. Emilia eventually built a new life in Aktobe. “Kazakhstan did become home for her, partly because she knew she could never return to her village in Ukraine,” Wolf says. “She found her people there and had her family around her.” The contradiction would become central to Wolf’s understanding of her family history: Kazakhstan was both a place of forced exile and the country in which several generations of the family made their lives. “Somewhere along the way, she too became a German from Kazakhstan.” German communities in the Soviet Union and its successor states after 1945. Growing up German in Soviet Kazakhstan For Wolf herself, Kazakhstan carried no such ambiguity during childhood. “For me, Kazakhstan was simply home. I didn’t know anything else,” she says. “In fact, when I was very little, I thought all Germans came from Kazakhstan.” Read more on Novastan : Beyond any borders: a new multicultural generation in Kazakhstan Her family’s German identity nevertheless remained clearly marked in Soviet society. Official documents continued to identify Soviet Germans as nemets or nemka , even as German-language education, religious life and much of the community’s institutional culture had been suppressed. “You were expected to stop being German, but you were never allowed to forget that you were German,” Wolf says. In her family, survival meant avoiding attention. Her father’s advice was encapsulated in the Russian expression тише воды, ниже травы – “quieter than water, lower than grass.” “Don’t attract attention. Don’t stand out. That was how you survived.” Wolf remembers the word “German” being routinely associated with “fascist”, decades after the Second World War. Soviet Germans’ own experience of deportation and repression was largely absent from the history taught in schools. “When you don’t know the history, you fill the gaps with your own explanations,” she says. “So people assumed that because we had been deported, we must have been guilty. The deportation itself became proof of our guilt.” As a child, she even changed her surname when helping an elderly Soviet woman whose husband and son had died during the war. “I invented another name for myself: Volkova instead of Wolf.” The Russian name, she says, became a form of protection. When Russian became the common language Language is another thread running through Wolf’s memoir. Her grandmother spoke German to her; Wolf usually answered in Russian. She later recognised almost exactly the same pattern among Kazakh families: grandparents speaking Kazakh while younger generations responded in Russian. “When that happens, it isn’t only language that gets lost,” Wolf says. “Stories, traditions and knowledge can no longer be passed on in the same way.” She remembers receiving some Kazakh-language teaching at school but says it was far too limited for children to become proficient. Russian, meanwhile, dominated education, television and popular culture. “You didn’t necessarily have to force children to speak Russian,” she says. “Education, television, culture and opportunities were in Russian, while Kazakh was often seen as old-fashioned or backward. Of course children were going to choose Russian.” Read more on Novastan : The Lexicon of Kazakh Decolonisation Looking back, she says she is glad to see the Kazakh language gaining greater prominence today. A garden as survival – and as home One image reappears throughout Wolf’s family history: the garden. Her ancestors had originally migrated eastward to work the land. After deportation, a garden helped her grandmother and a neighbour survive wartime shortages. Decades later, during Wolf’s own childhood in Kazakhstan, home-grown food helped sustain the family when Soviet shops were empty. But the garden came to represent more than food. Wolf recounts the story of her father, whose mother was sentenced to the Gulag after attempting to leave the deportation zone and return to Ukraine. He was sent to an orphanage in Zaporizhzhia shortly after the war. One teacher once invited him to her home for dinner. While she cooked, he played in the garden with her son. “He remembers standing there among the flowers and plants and realising, for the first time, that the world was beautiful,” Wolf says. The memory remained with him throughout his life. Now 91, he can no longer maintain a large garden but still cares for flowers on his balcony in Offenbach, Germany. “Perhaps that is what a garden means in our family,” Wolf says. “It feeds you when there is nothing to eat, but it also gives you beauty when there isn’t much beauty around you. And wherever you end up, you can plant something and make that place your own.” A ‘return’ to a country they did not know In 1989, Wolf and her family left Kazakhstan for Germany. Officially, such migration was often presented as a return to an ancestral homeland. In practice, Wolf discovered that Germany was another unfamiliar country. “What surprised me most was that in Germany I wasn’t seen as German,” she says. “After everything our families had gone through in the Soviet Union because they were German – persecution, discrimination and sometimes literally fighting for survival – we arrived in Germany and suddenly we were foreigners.” At 17, Wolf initially tried to assimilate as completely as possible. She stopped speaking Russian, avoided food associated with her Soviet childhood and even began using the name Helene. I

Oktober 2026 jschupp Schlagwörter Azamat Omarov Pressefreiheit Satire Azamat Omarov hatte in der Vergangenheit wiederholt Witze über die kasachstanische Regierung gemacht. Im September verurteilte ihn ein Gericht in Astana zu dreieinhalb Jahren Haft auf Bewährung. Photo: Instagram/Collage. Wer in Kasachstan Witze über die Regierung reißt, kann wegen „ Anstiftung zur Zwietracht” vor Gericht landen. So wie der Satiriker Azamat Omarov. „Ich sehe, dass euch die Witze über Toqaev gefallen haben, also kommt hier der nächste:” , sagt der kasachische Satiriker Azamat Omarov in die Handykamera, er läuft unter kahlen Baumreihen entlang. „Treffen sich die einheitliche Zeitzone, das neue Steuergesetzbuch und die neue Verfassung – und zack wird scharf geschossen!” Omarov stellt hier – für Kasach:innen offensichtlich – die jüngsten Reformen der Regierung ihrer brutalen Handhabung der Proteste von 2022 gegenüber. Es sind Witze wie dieser, veröffentlicht auf seinem YouTube-Kanal Akhual Segodnya [die heutige Lage, Anm. der Redaktion], die den Satiriker ins Visier der Behörden gebracht haben. Unterstützt Novastan – das europäische Zentralasien-Magazin Als vereinsgetragene, unabhängige Plattform lebt Novastan vom Enthusiasmus seiner ehrenamtlichen Mitarbeiter:innen – und von eurer Unterstützung! Novastan unterstützen Am 18. Juli 2026 nehmen Polizeikräfte Omarov in Astana fest und durchsuchen seine Wohnung. Nach zwei Monaten Untersuchungshaft kommt es zum Prozess. Omarovs Satire, so die Anklage, habe „soziale, nationale, stammesbezogene, rassistische, klassenbezogene oder religiöse Zwietracht“ gesät, strafbar unter Artikel 174 des kasachstanischen Strafgesetzbuches. Konkret hatte sich die Anklage laut dem Kazakhstan International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law auf ein Video vom Januar 2026 berufen, in dem Omarov die Führung des Landes kritisiert hatte. Lest auch auf Novastan: Verurteilt wegen lustig – Fünf Jahre Haft für Temirlan Ensebek Durch eine Verfahrensvereinbarung kommt Omarov Mitte September schließlich frei. Die Einigung: Omarov bekennt sich schuldig und entgeht so einer Haftstrafe, die nun über dreieinhalb Jahre zur Bewährung ausgesetzt wird. Fünf Jahre darf er keine neuen Inhalte mehr verbreiten, sich nicht politisch oder sozioökonomisch engagieren. Nur um der Haft zu entgehen, habe Omarov sich schuldig bekannt, sagte sein Anwalt Tölegen Şaıkov nach dem Prozess. „Durch diesen Artikel (174) landen viele Leute im Gefängnis. So absurd es ist, er existiert und funktioniert.” Man könne nicht genug betonen, wie ungerecht dieses Urteil sei, schrieb Mihra Rittmann, Senior Advisor bei der NGO Human Rights Watch , Mitte September in einem Beitrag über den Fall. Kasachstanische Behörden nutzten die vage Formulierung von Artikel 174 schon lange, um unliebsame Stimmen zum Schweigen zu bringen. Erst 2025 hatte ein Gericht in Almaty den Satireblogger Temirlan Ensebek unter eben jenem Artikel der „Anstiftung zur Zwietracht” schuldig befunden. Amnesty International stufte seine Strafverfolgung als politisch motiviert ein. Lest auch auf Novastan: Internationale Resonanz zum Fall Temirlan Ensebek Um die Pressefreiheit ist es in Kasachstan schlecht bestellt. 2026 belegt das Land im World Press Freedom Index Platz 149 von 180. Der Index wird von der NGO Reporter ohne Grenzen erstellt. Sie begründen ihre Einstufung damit, dass die Regierung alle verfügbaren Mittel nutze, um unliebsame Berichterstattung einzuschränken. Das scheint insbesondere für die sensible Mischform der Satire zu gelten, für die sich Artikel 174 als probates Gegenmittel etabliert hat. Der Zeitpunkt von Azamat Omarovs Festnahme – etwa ein Monat vor den ersten Wahlen des neuen kasachstanischen Parlaments – fällt zudem in ein breiteres Muster. Zwischen Juni und August 2026 wurden gegen mindestens drei weitere unabhängige Journalist:innen Strafverfahren eingeleitet, eine von ihnen wurde verurteilt. Im Gespräch mit der Menschenrechtsorganisation CIVICUS sagte die kasachstanische Journalistin Nazira Därimbet, dass Behörden insbesondere vor großen politischen Ereignissen wie der Kurultai-Wahl darauf aus seien, unbequeme und unabhängige Stimmen zum Schweigen zu bringen. Auf YouTube ist der Kanal Akhual Segodnya nicht mehr zu finden, Omarovs Satire ist gelöscht. Dass irgendwo in Kasachstan jedoch weiterhin Witze über die Regierung von Qasym-Jomart Toqaev gemacht werden, lässt sich nicht verhindern. Doch autokratische Regime wie das Kasachstanische setzen für ihre Machterhaltung auf Kontrolle: Der politische Diskurs soll in staatlich geregelten Bahnen verlaufen. Auf Satire wie die von Omarov reagiert der Staat repressiv: Es soll verhindert werden, dass der Diskurs seine Bahn verlässt – und potenziell die Legitimationsgrundlage des Regimes unterminiert. Artikel 174, in all seiner Vagheit, hat sich dabei als probates Mittel erwiesen. Long-distance drivers often spend extended periods living and sleeping in their vehicles between assignments. Photo courtesy of Alex. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan For three years, a truck driver from Kyrgyzstan has been working across the European Union, sleeping, cooking and living inside his vehicle for months at a time. His story reveals both the opportunities and the precarious realities faced by Central Asian drivers working far from home. Alex is sitting on the bed inside the cabin of his truck, his head almost touching the ceiling. “I can’t stand,” he says as he films the cramped space around him. On the bed beside him, he chops a cucumber next to a box of garlic. Between his legs, a gas stove supports a kazan filled with pearl barley, meat, potatoes and garlic. The truck is not only his workplace. For much of the year, it is also his kitchen, bedroom and living room. In another video, Alex opens the small refrigerator squeezed into the cabin. It is packed with salted fish fillets and what he estimates to be between 10 and 15 kilograms of meat. Above it sits a basket of dry goods: rice, pearl barley, salt and soy sauce. When the weather is good, he cooks outside in the truck park. When it is not, everything happens inside. Alex prepares a meal inside the cab of his truck, where he also sleeps and spends much of his time while working across Europe. Photo courtesy of Alex. Alex, a pseudonym, is in his early forties and comes from Kyrgyzstan’s Talas region. For the past three years, he has worked as a long-distance truck driver in the European Union. The wages are considerably higher than those available to him at home, but getting to Europe was difficult, and life on the road has proved far more precarious than the promise of European employment might suggest. Losing money before reaching Europe Alex’s path into European trucking began with failure. On his first attempt to find work abroad, he says he lost between 60,000 and 70,000 Kyrgyz som to a posrednik , or middleman, in Slovakia. He obtained the contact through an acquaintance. According to Alex, the intermediary promised to arrange a work visa, contracts and other documents. “The money was burned,” he recalls. He tried again and lost money a second time, though less than on the first occasion. It was only on his third attempt that he found a viable route. Rather than relying on another intermediary, Alex contacted a Lithuanian logistics company directly through WhatsApp. According to him, the company prepared a contract, invitation letter and the other documents he needed. Within two or three months, the process was complete, and his principal expenses were administrative fees and flights. The experience left him deeply suspicious of intermediaries. Although some of his criticism is based on what he has heard from other drivers rather than his own experience, he believes agencies can withhold information or charge workers for poorly explained services. His experience reflects concerns documented more widely among migrant truck drivers. Research on the European road transport sector has described cases in which drivers paid high recruitment fees, faced unexpected charges after arrival or were misled about working conditions. Other research on Central Asian migration to Europe has similarly identified weaknesses in recruitment systems, including inadequate contract verification and limited pre-departure information. A truck that doubles as a home Once Alex started working in Europe, the realities of the job became clearer. He has worked for companies based in Lithuania and Czechia, driving across large parts of the European Union. Alex says he initially started on around €85 per day, but once he moved into vehicle transport – the work he now specialises in – his pay rose to around €100-€120 per day, sometimes reaching €130. His current Czech employer, he says, allows him to work for considerably longer periods and with fewer expenses than his previous Lithuanian company. By comparison, the Lithuanian employer operated what Alex describes as a “cadence” system, with drivers moved in and out of different routes and countries by minibus. “They split drivers up across Europe, over to Germany, France, Italy and Belgium,” he says. One driver would arrive with his belongings and continue the work while another returned home in the same minibus. The financial attraction of Europe is obvious to him. “In Kyrgyzstan a driver’s salary is roughly $800 per journey,” Alex says, but a single trip can mean collecting cargo in China and returning to Kyrgyzstan, or driving from Kyrgyzstan through Kazakhstan and onwards to Russia. On those routes, “nothing is provided”, he says. Repairs, tyre changes and other costs may have to be handled by the driver. Border queues can also consume days. Drivers may wait two or three days, or sometimes as long as a week, he says, while spending part of their earnings on food and other expenses along the way. By contrast, he considers trucking in the EU better paid and, in some respects, easier. But that income comes with a lifestyle dominated by the vehicle itself. Even buying groceries can become an expedition. In one video recorded in Germany, Alex walks back from Lidl carrying a full shopping bag. On that occasion, the supermarket was only 2.5 kilometres from where he had parked. At other stops, he says, drivers may have to walk five or even ten kilometres to reach a large shop. Truck parking determines much of daily life. Drivers cannot simply take their vehicles into many city streets, while roadside facilities do not always provide the food or services they need. Finding somewhere to stop is itself a recurring problem. Alex has filmed parking areas where trucks double-park, occupy exits or line the roadside because designated spaces are full. “The number one problem is always parking,” he says, especially in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and Czechia. Spain and France are somewhat easier, though he says parking around Lyon and Paris can also be difficult. Basic facilities vary considerably. Alex carries his own water and has recorded truck stops without showers. “The most important thing,” he says, “is that it has a toilet.” Sleeping where you work Alex says he rarely stays in a hotel or hostel while on the road. Most nights, he sleeps in the bed built into the truck cabin. That can mean spending entire days and nights inside the same few square metres. The truck becomes somewhere to eat, sleep, exercise, store food and wait between assignments. At night, security is another concern. Alex loops the seatbelts through the interior door handles in an attempt to make it harder for thieves to force open the cabin while he sleeps. He says he has not personally experienced a break-in, but learned the technique from other drivers and from stories circulating among them. EU rules prohibit drivers from taking their regular weekly rest period of at least 45 hours inside their vehicles. Suitable accommodation outside the truck should instead be provided, with the cost covered by the employer. Alex is familiar with the rule. “For 45 hours the driver must rest and the company must provide him with a proper room so that he can go in there and sleep and rest,” he says. But according to him, that often does not happen. “No one arranges hotel accommodation. The driver is the one who has to sort it out,” he says, adding that in his experience only a minority of companies consistently comply. Support Novastan Producer Azimjon Rahimjonov discusses Lola Animation, the making of Share Happiness, the growth of Uzbekistan’s animation sector and the studio’s ambitions to reach international audiences. Azimjon Rahimjonov’s career in film began on the side of a road in Tashkent. He was 19 and trying to hail a taxi early one morning when he met an experienced cinematographer named Humoyun. The encounter proved unexpectedly consequential: Humoyun took him on as an apprentice at a small studio that mainly filmed weddings, introducing him to editing and cinematography. Rahimjonov had already been fascinated by directing from a young age, long before he knew what the profession was called. He remembers seeking out complicated films and imagining himself behind the camera. Over time, he worked across editing, cinematography and directing, learned from Uzbek filmmaker Abdukarim Mirzayev and eventually worked in television as an editing director. His path later took him to Istanbul, where he studied at the Hassan Bin Sabit Cinema Academy. After returning to Tashkent, he joined Najot Ta’lim at a moment when its founder, Temurbek Adhamov, was supporting a grant programme for young people interested in animation. Adhamov told him something Rahimjonov still remembers: “One day, you will become the person who guides the young people who create this animation.” “That was how I entered the world of animation,” Rahimjonov tells Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine. What drew him increasingly towards the medium was its potential influence on children. “I believe that animated films created for children can have a profound influence on their worldview and upbringing.” A sentence on a building in Tashkent The idea for Lola Animation’s short film Share Happiness emerged from another apparently ordinary encounter in the Uzbek capital. Several years ago, shortly after returning from Türkiye, Rahimjonov was taking one of his regular long walks through central Tashkent. On one of the city’s most expensive streets, he noticed a luxury building under construction carrying the slogan “Share Happiness.” Poster for Share Happiness, an animated short produced by Lola Animation. Image: courtesy of Lola Animation. Standing beside it was a bearded man who appeared to be homeless. “He was looking at the building with admiration,” Rahimjonov recalls. “There was something childlike and sincere in his expression. It felt as though he, too, wanted to enter that house and live there.” The image stayed with him. When his team later decided to make a short animated film as a way of building practical experience, Rahimjonov returned to the idea. The first version of the story followed a girl and an older man who secretly entered a luxurious home and pretended to be its owners. As the project developed, the setting shifted from a house to an amusement park. The broader context also influenced the screenplay. With wars and conflicts intensifying internationally, Rahimjonov found himself thinking increasingly about children whose circumstances deny them experiences that others take for granted. The result was an eight-minute film about a homeless girl who dreams of entering an amusement park and the security guard whose encounter with her recalls his own childhood. A still from Share Happiness, which follows a homeless girl dreaming of entering an amusement park. Image: courtesy of Lola Animation. “The central idea behind Share Happiness is that no child should ever feel like an outsider,” he says. “Regardless of where they live in the world, every child deserves to be happy and to experience a full and meaningful childhood.” The film explores childhood dreams, inequality and the tension between rules and conscience. Its title, Rahimjonov says, ultimately expresses a simple idea: happiness acquires meaning when it can be shared. Making the same film twice The finished film hides how difficult its production was. Rahimjonov says, quite literally, that the team made Share Happiness twice. The first production brought together roughly 20 to 25 young people who had completed an animation grant programme. Many were still learning the fundamentals of professional modelling, animation and rendering. Shuhrat Asayev worked as the project’s art director, alongside artists including Elyor Rahmatullayev and Shohsanam Quryozova, layout artist Muhammadyusuf Yo‘ldashev and lead animator Ilhom Karimov. “We hardly knew how to do anything at a professional level,” Rahimjonov recalls. But that inexperienced group became the basis of what would develop into Lola Animation’s creative team. Rahmatullayev, for example, is now the studio’s art director. The first render alone took eight months to arrive. “When we finally saw it, we were so excited that some of us actually cried,” Rahimjonov says. “We were saying, ‘Are we really making something this amazing?’” Production continued for around a year and a half. Yet when the rendering process was finally finished, Rahimjonov looked back at what the team had made and concluded that it was no longer good enough. By then, the animators themselves had improved dramatically. The directing, visual style and technical quality that had once seemed exciting now appeared inadequate beside what the team had learned to produce. So they discarded the entire eight-minute film. Rather than patching individual sequences, the team started again from scratch. It was an expensive decision in time and effort, but for Rahimjonov it also demonstrated how quickly the studio had developed. The final Share Happiness became not simply a film but a record of a team teaching itself how to make professional animation. Uzbek creators, universal story Despite being produced in Uzbekistan, Share Happiness was deliberately not designed as an explicitly Uzbek story. Rahimjonov says the decision was intentional. “I wanted it to be understandable and relatable to audiences around the world,” he explains. “Whether the viewer is American, Parisian, Russian, African or Uzbek, Muslim or non-Muslim, I wanted everyone to be able to find a feeling or idea that resonates with them.” Rather than foregrounding traditional motifs or identifiable elements of everyday Uzbek life, the team chose to concentrate on childhood, inequality and compassion. “I believe that human values transcend national and geographical boundaries,” he says. For Rahimjonov, however, universality does not mean detachment from Uzbekistan. It reflects his ambition to create from Uzbekistan while participating in conversations that are global rather than geographically confined. “In a way, the film also reflects my personal perspective as an artist on today’s capitalist world.” Building an “Uzbek Animation Factory” Lola Animation describes itself as the “Uzbek Animation Factory.” The phrase captures the scale of its ambitions. Rahimjonov does not see the studio’s mission simply as producing individual cartoons, but as helping create an animation ecosystem capable of developing talent, telling local stories and competing internationally. “Our goal is to contribute to building a future where human values come first by creating animated films that are engaging, thought-provoking and promote humanity,” he says. September 2026 bstoeckl Schlagwörter Bayern Berlin Deutschland Frank-Walter Steinmeier Friedrich Merz Markus Söder Qasym-Jomart Toqaev Bundeskanzler Merz hat am 29. September Kasachstans Präsidenten Toqaev im Kanzleramt empfangen, Photo: Akorda.kz Wirtschaftliche Zusammenarbeit, Energie und der Ukrainekrieg standen im Mittelpunkt des Staatsbesuchs des kasachstanischen Präsidenten Qasym-Jomart Toqaev, der sich am Dienstag (29.9) in Berlin mit Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier zu Gesprächen traf. Auch ein Besuch des Deutsch-Kasachischen Wirtschaftsforums stand auf der Agenda des kasachstanischen Präsidenten. Der Staatsbesuch stellte das erste Treffen zwischen Toqaev und Merz dar. Der Kontakt auf höchster politischer Ebene zwischen den beiden Ländern hat in den letzten Jahren Fahrt aufgenommen: 2023 fand der erste “Z5+1”-Gipfel statt, dessen Zweitauflage ein Jahr später folgte. Im Februar dieses Jahres trafen sich schließlich die Außenminister der sechs Teilnehmerstaaten. Wirtschaftliche Roadmap: Know-How gegen Energie Während einer gemeinsamen Pressekonferenz im Anschluss an das Treffen im Kanzleramt kündigten Merz und Toqaev eine “ Wirtschaftliche Roadmap ” für den Zeitraum 2026 – 2028 an, die “ die industrielle, technologische und rohstoffbezogene Entwicklung ” beider Länder voranbringen soll. Deutschland zielt hierbei vor allem auf einen vereinfachten Zugang zu kasachstanischen Rohstoffen und Energieträgern, die angesichts der Sanktionen gegen Russland und der Lage am Persischen Golf extrem wichtig für die deutsche Wirtschaft sind. Kasachstan hofft derweil, von deutschem Know-How und deutscher Technologie zu profitieren. “ Wir haben uns auch auf die Förderung gemeinsamer Analysen für unsere Lieferketten geeinigt. Wir wollen uns enger verbinden. Dafür wollen wir resiliente Logistikketten und den Mittleren Korridor weiter ausbauen. Kasachstan leistet schon heute einen wichtigen Beitrag zur europäischen Ölversorgung. Der deutsch-kasachische Energiedialog beweist hierbei seinen großen Wert ”, erklärte Merz während der Pressekonferenz. Zudem betonte er die Wichtigkeit der Roadmap für den Mittelstand, um “ verlässliche Rahmenbedingungen für Unternehmen beider Seiten [zu] eröffnen, beispielsweise bei der Anerkennung von Standards. ” Unterstützt Novastan – das europäische Zentralasien-Magazin Als vereinsgetragene, unabhängige Plattform lebt Novastan vom Enthusiasmus seiner ehrenamtlichen Mitarbeiter:innen – und von eurer Unterstützung! Novastan unterstützen Kasachstan repräsentiert 80 Prozent des deutschen Handels in Zentralasien und ist damit der wichtigste deutsche Handelspartner in der Region. Im Laufe der letzten vier Jahre hat sich das Handelsvolumen zwischen den beiden Ländern nahezu verdoppelt und beträgt derzeit knapp 8 Milliarden Euro. Laut Michael Harms , dem Geschäftsführer des Ost-Ausschusses der Deutschen Wirtschaft, “ bietet [das Land] hervorragende Chancen für deutsche Technologieanbieter und Investoren und trägt zugleich zur Diversifizierung von Energie- und Rohstofflieferungen nach Europa bei. ” Um das Potenzial der bilateralen Handelsbeziehungen komplett auszuschöpfen, ist es Harms zufolge essentiell, „ die hohe politische Aufmerksamkeit in konkrete Projekte und langfristige Investitionen umzusetzen. “ Kasachstan möchte deutschen Mittelstand anziehen Der kasachstanische Präsident Toqaev betonte auf der Pressekonferenz das Interesse seines Landes, Vertreter des deutschen Mittelstandes vom Aufbau von Produktionsstätten in Kasachstan zu überzeugen. “ Unser Ziel besteht darin, die Investitionszusammenarbeit mit der deutschen Seite auf ein qualitativ neues Niveau zu bringen. Wir sind sehr an langfristigen Aktivitäten der Vertreter der deutschen Wirtschaft interessiert. Wir legen sehr viel Wert auf die Zusammenarbeit in den Bereichen von Energie, Maschinenbau und Chemie. [...] Wir sind uns sicher, dass das Potenzial bei Weitem nicht ausgeschöpft ist. Deutschland hat einen sehr starken Mittelstand, [...] ”, so das kasachstanische Staatsoberhaupt. Lest auch auf Novastan: Österreich und Usbekistan schließen Migrationsabkommen Zuvor hatte sich Toqaev im Verteidigungsministerium mit Frank-Walter Steinmeier getroffen, um im Rahmen des Deutsch-Kasachischen Wirtschaftsforums im Beisein von 300 Handels- und Wirtschaftsvertreter:innen neue Projekte in den Bereichen Industrie, Energie, Rohstoffe sowie Transport und Logistik zu besprechen. Die zwei Staatsoberhäupter unterschrieben im Anschluss an das Forum 37 bilaterale Projekte mit einem Gesamtvolumen von 1,8 Milliarden Euro. Diese Projekte umfassen die Bereiche Kritische Rohstoffe, Wertschöpfung, Landwirtschaft, Energieinfrastruktur, Automatisierung, Werkzeugmaschinenbau, Industrierobotik und Digitalisierung. Ukrainekrieg: Merz entschlossen, Toqaev vorsichtig In Bezug auf den Krieg in der Ukraine betonte Merz, dass ein Frieden nur mit Vertreter:innen der EU am Verhandlungstisch gelingen könne und Deutschland der Ukraine weiterhin politische, wirtschaftliche und militärische Hilfe leisten werde, solange der Krieg andauert. Er dankte Präsident Toqaev dafür, “ dass er auch mit Präsident Putin darüber spricht, wie wir zu einem Ende dieses Krieges kommen können. ” Kasachstans Präsident äußerte sich verhaltener und bezeichnete den russischen Präsidenten Vladimir Putin als “ eine herausragende politische Persönlichkeit ”, die “ über die notwendigen Charaktereigenschaften für die Rolle als Staatsoberhaupt eines sehr großen Landes mit einer komplexen Geschichte [...] ” verfügt. Er sprach sich für “ ein Einfrieren der Kampfhandlungen auf dem Territorium der Ukraine ” aus, um sich “ dann in die Richtung von Diplomatie und Verhandlungen begeben ” zu können. Kasachstans Präsident Toqaev und Bayerns Ministerpräsident Söder bei ihrem Treffen am 30.09.2026 in München, Photo: Akorda.kz Am Mittwoch (30.09) flog Toqaev nach München, wo er sich mit Mitgliedern der bayerischen Regierung und des Landtages traf. Außerdem nahm er an der Eröffnung des “ Bayerisch-Kasachisches Technologieforums ” teil, auf dem die Zusammenarbeit in den Bereichen Digitalisierung, KI und Wirtschaft diskutiert wurden.
