https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/08/cent.body: Agriculture Governance Central Asia Central Asian countries approve water withdrawal limits for 2026–2027 Specialists discussed water distribution and accounting. Sayfiddin Karaev , asia+ 08.10.2026 14:23 Telegram Facebook WhatsApp Copy URL Central Asian countries have approved water withdrawal limits and reviewed forecast reservoir operating regimes for the 2026–2027 non-vegetation period in the Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins. The decisions were made at the 95th meeting of the Interstate Commission for Water Coordination (ICWC), held on October 7 in Turkmenbashi, Turkmenistan. Tajikistan was represented by Daler Abdukholiq Abdurazozzoqda, head of the Main Department of Water and Energy Policy at the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources. The participants reviewed the use of water withdrawal limits and compliance with reservoir operating regimes in the Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins during the 2026 vegetation period. Following the discussions, the commission approved water withdrawal limits for the countries of the region for the 2026–2027 non-vegetation period. It also took note of forecast operating regimes for reservoir cascades proposed by water management organizations responsible for the Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins. Specific water withdrawal volumes for each country, including Tajikistan, are contained in annexes to the ICWC meeting protocol. The forecast operating regimes for reservoirs in both river basins are also included in the documents. The data are expected to be made public at a later date. Chardara reservoir receives more water than forecast According to Kazinform , no major water supply problems were reported in the Syr Darya basin in 2026. About 3.69 billion cubic meters of water flowed into the Chardara reservoir in southern Kazakhstan, around 840 million cubic meters more than forecast. A further approximately 10 billion cubic meters of water is expected to enter the reservoir during the 2026–2027 autumn-winter period. Discrepancies found in Amu Darya flow measurements The meeting also addressed discrepancies in water flow measurements at the Kerki gauging station on the Amu Darya. The participants found that different flow readings were recorded despite identical water levels. The commission instructed specialists to identify the causes of the discrepancies and take measures to ensure accurate measurements. The participants also stressed that the needs of all water users in the upper, middle and lower reaches of the Amu Darya should be taken into account when distributing the river’s water resources. Automated water metering planned for Syr Darya Central Asian countries also plan to introduce an automated water metering system in the Syr Darya basin. According to Kazinform , a working group meeting will be held to develop a corresponding action plan. The ICWC meeting also reviewed implementation of decisions adopted at the International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea summits held in 2018, 2023 and 2026. The commission noted progress by the countries of the region in implementing the fourth Aral Sea Basin Program, introducing water-saving technologies, addressing the effects of climate change and strengthening cooperation in the water sector. The next, 96th meeting of the ICWC will be held in Uzbekistan. Its date and venue will be announced later. Join us on social media! https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/08/inte.body: Communication Governance News Tajikistan introduces new CMR requirement for international freight carriers Carriers are now required to obtain a consignment note (CMR) bearing the distinguishing mark of the Ministry of Transport. The CMR document itself remains unchanged. Payrav Chorshanbiev , asia+ 08.10.2026 10:08 Telegram Facebook WhatsApp Copy URL Tajikistan has introduced a new requirement for companies and sole traders transporting goods internationally: their CMR consignment notes must now bear the distinguishing mark of the authorized state body responsible for road transport. The requirement was introduced by an order signed by Transport Minister Azim Ibrohim on September 25, 2026, amending the instructions governing the issuance, completion, use and processing of consignment notes. The document has been published on the legal information portal of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Justice. Compliance will be monitored by the State Service for Supervision and Regulation in the Field of Transport under the Ministry of Transport. What has changed? CMR is the standard international consignment note used for road freight transport. The new order does not introduce a new type of document or replace the existing CMR. Instead, it adds a requirement to clause 23 of the existing instructions stating that legal entities and sole traders transporting goods on international routes must obtain a CMR sheet bearing the distinguishing mark of the authorized road transport body. The amendments also require the word “sheet” to precede the abbreviation CMR in two chapters of the instructions. The order does not specify what the distinguishing mark should look like or how it should be placed on the CMR. Previous issues with CMR documents The availability and use of international CMR documents had previously been raised by the Ministry of Transport. Transport Minister Azim Ibrohim had instructed relevant ministry units to review the procedures for distributing and using international CMR waybills and consignment documents. They were also tasked with taking steps toward introducing electronic waybills and consignment documents. The latest changes come as Tajikistan has been gradually easing conditions for international road freight transportation. In 2024, for example, Tajikistan’s parliament ratified amendments to an agreement with Uzbekistan allowing freight vehicles to transit through the territories of both countries without special permits. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/08/uzbe.body: Governance Society News Uzbekistan to raise electricity consumption allowance for households without gas The authorities also intend to expand assistance to families in need with paying for energy resources and utility services. asia+ 08.10.2026 09:35 Telegram Facebook WhatsApp Copy URL Uzbekistan will increase the baseline electricity consumption allowance from 200 to 350 kWh for households in areas without gas supplies during the 2026–2027 heating season, as part of a package of measures to support low-income families. The decision was approved on October 6 at a meeting chaired by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on measures to strengthen social protection during the autumn-winter period, Fergana news agency reported, citing the presidential press service. The meeting reviewed proposals to expand existing support mechanisms covering electricity, gas, coal and utility costs. The measures include a proposal to provide low-income families with a one-time financial payment in December. Authorities also proposed raising the per-person income threshold used to determine eligibility for reimbursement of electricity, gas, coal and utility costs for low-income families not included in the Social Register. The threshold would increase to 1.43 million soums (about $119), potentially extending support to an additional 166,000 families. Another proposal would extend until April 1, 2028, the period during which households can receive compensation for part of the cost of electricity and gas consumed above the established baseline. About 470,000 families are expected to benefit from this measure over the course of a year. The government also plans to continue insulating 3,000 homes in mahallas with difficult living conditions and equipping them with energy-saving appliances. Mirziyoyev instructed the government to ensure timely funding for the measures, target assistance at low-income households and strengthen oversight to ensure that eligible families receive the support. According to the authorities, the additional measures are needed amid geopolitical tensions, higher global energy and commodity prices, and disruptions to supply chains and logistics. These factors are increasing inflationary pressures, the presentation noted, while reducing household expenses and providing targeted assistance to low-income families remain key priorities. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/28/ches.body: Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE “With this kind of team, we’ll have many more victories to come”: Uzbekistan’s road to Chess Olympiad gold Uzbekistan won the home Chess Olympiad in Samarkand with 20 points, losing only to Germany. Three players won individual medals. Gazeta reviews the team’s road to its second Olympic gold, Uzbekistan-2's breakthrough and the results of the women’s teams. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 28 September 2026, 23:24 Sport In its interim review after six rounds of the Samarkand Chess Olympiad, Gazeta wrote that the “cautious optimism” of the national team’s captain Rustam Kasimdzhanov was proving justified: Uzbekistan’s first men’s team had won every match and was leading the Olympiad outright. In the end, the optimism turned out to be even too cautious: the team won 10 of its 11 matches and became Olympic champion for the second time in four years. In the final review, we look at how all of Uzbekistan’s men’s and women’s teams performed and who stood out at the tournament. After the tournament, Javokhir Sindarov said that winning at home gave the achievement special significance. “We feel fantastic. We are very happy to win Olympic gold in our own country and very proud to become champions at home, when everyone is supporting you,” he said . Advertising on Gazeta Sindarov’s preparation and participation in international tournaments, including the Chess Olympiad, as well as work with coaches, are supported by the National Bank of Uzbekistan . After the Olympiad, he will begin preparations for his World Championship match against Dommaraju Gukesh in Geneva. National team Starting rank Final position Match points Uzbekistan, men 3 1 20 Uzbekistan-2, men 30 18 15 Uzbekistan-3, men 55 60 13 Uzbekistan, women 13 13 15 Uzbekistan-2, women 43 35 14 Uzbekistan-3, women 65 47 13 The home Olympiad will be remembered not only for the first team’s gold. Uzbekistan-2, seeded 30th, was among the medal contenders going into the final two rounds and eventually finished 18th. On the third team, Asrorjon Omonov started the tournament with seven consecutive wins. In the women’s tournament, the main team finished exactly where it had started — 13th. Both reserve teams, however, improved on their starting positions: Uzbekistan-2 climbed from 43rd to 35th, while Uzbekistan-3 rose from 65th to 47th. Seven consecutive wins The main men’s team began the Olympiad as the third seed, behind the United States and India. Uzbekistan was represented by Nodirbek Abdusattorov (2762), Javokhir Sindarov (2778), Nodirbek Yakubboyev (2685), Shamsiddin Vokhidov (2654) and Mukhiddin Madaminov (2611). The team’s average rating was 2720. The first two rounds went as expected: Jamaica were crushed 4−0, while Peru were beaten 3.5−0.5. However, the second match already produced one of Uzbekistan’s most spectacular individual games of the tournament: Sindarov finished his attack against Diego Quillas with a striking queen sacrifice, after which the Peruvian king was caught in a mating net. Prime minister Abdulla Aripov and Javokhir Sindarov. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE. After the Olympiad, Sindarov smilingly explained that the spectacular move was partly a choice in favor of entertainment. “At the end I thought: okay, let’s play for the video, for the content, for reels. But actually, it was a simple move. I wouldn’t say there was anything crazy about it,” he recalled. The level of opposition then rose sharply. Uzbekistan defeated Austria 3−1, Türkiye 2.5−1.5 and Hungary 4−0. In the match against Hungary, all four Uzbekistan players won — including against Richard Rapport and Peter Leko. By the sixth round, the hosts had not lost a single individual game. The first truly crucial match was against India, the 2024 Olympic champions. Three games ended in draws, so everything came down to the third board, where Yakubboyev faced Nihal Sarin. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Uzbekistani player’s position was worse for a long time, and he also had significantly less time on the clock. But Sarin was the first to make a mistake under pressure and allowed a tactical blow. Yakubboyev’s victory gave Uzbekistan a 2.5−1.5 win and sole possession of first place after six rounds. Yakubboyev himself later called the match probably the most important of the entire Olympiad. “The match against India was, I think, the most important for us because it had a major impact on the whole standings. After that, we could really fight for a medal. If we had lost that match, I think everything could have turned out completely differently,” he said. The entire team watched the decisive game. “We were all watching like crazy. After the knight move to e6 [the opponent’s mistake that led to the loss of his queen — Gazeta ], we just went wild. Everyone was screaming in our chat,” the players recalled. Later, Mukhiddin Madaminov admitted that the first rounds of the home Olympiad had been psychologically difficult for him, but that the team’s confidence noticeably increased after the match against India. “At the beginning of the tournament, it was very difficult for me. In the first two rounds, I felt a lot of pressure. But then I started playing, and I became more confident. The match against India was also very important. After that, I think we really believed that we could win,” he said. China Nodirbek Abdusattorov. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta After the rest day came an even tougher test — China. Two Nodirbeks proved decisive: Abdusattorov defeated former world champion Ding Liren, while Yakubboyev beat Yu Yangyi. Sindarov and Madaminov drew their games. Uzbekistan won 3−1, extending its winning streak to seven matches and moving two match points clear of its closest pursuers. The first and, as it later turned out, only team defeat came in the eighth round. Germany ends the streak Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE Germany defeated Uzbekistan 2.5−1.5. Brothers Frederik and Rasmus Svane beat Yakubboyev and Vokhidov. Sindarov defeated Matthias Bluebaum, while Abdusattorov saved a difficult game against Vincent Keymer, but that was not enough. Until that point, Uzbekistan’s players had not lost a single individual game in seven rounds. After the tournament, Abdusattorov admitted that playing at home had been more difficult because of the expectations. “Of course, we felt some pressure because we were playing in our own country. It is always a little more difficult. We remembered how India played at home in Chennai: they were very close, but at critical moments they became nervous and could not win the whole tournament,” he said. The defeat made the race for gold extremely tight again: Uzbekistan and Germany were level on match points, while eight more teams were just one point behind. Uzbekistan responded the very next day against the top-seeded United States. The Americans took the lead after Wesley So defeated Sindarov — the only loss suffered by Javokhir at the entire Olympiad. However, Abdusattorov defeated Fabiano Caruana, while Yakubboyev beat Hans Niemann. A draw on the fourth board secured a 2.5−1.5 victory for Uzbekistan and returned the team to sole possession of first place. Confident win over Armenia and decisive Madaminov Mukhiddin Madaminov. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta The penultimate round could have been particularly difficult. Uzbekistan faced Armenia, a team that had not lost a match at the Olympiad before facing the hosts. With the black pieces against Aik Martirosyan, Nodirbek Abdusattorov unexpectedly chose the Scandinavian Defense (1.e4 d5). He later said that he had told the team about his choice around 20 minutes before the game, and his teammates initially could not believe it. The idea worked: Abdusattorov gradually outplayed his opponent and won. The game between Sindarov and Robert Hovhannisyan was even sharper. Javokhir sacrificed an exchange early, receiving a knight and two pawns for the rook, and transferred the game into a complicated middlegame. Hovhannis

The project is being implemented jointly with BI Group. A total of 18,000 new school places are expected to be created by the start of the next academic year. A separate project has also been developed to build 16 modern kindergartens. Photos. O‘zbek tilida Ўзбек тилида На русском языке 2 October 2026, 16:25 Society Construction of 12 modern schools began simultaneously in Tashkent this week, the city hokimiyat (mayor's office) announced . The project is being implemented jointly with the construction company BI Group. The new schools will be built in 11 of the city’s 12 districts, excluding Bektemir. Two schools will be constructed in Yangihayot district. Construction is expected to take eight months. A total of 18,000 new school places are expected to be created by the start of the next academic year. Advertising on Gazeta “These will be schools of a new format — technologically advanced, ergonomic, comfortable and inclusive. Three types of designs have been developed, taking into account modern architectural solutions and the necessary infrastructure,” the Tashkent city hokimiyat said. Tashkent deputy hokim (mayor) Durdona Rahimova said the schools would have capacities ranging from 1,500 to 2,000 students each. According to portfolio director for Central Asia at BI Group Nurbol Shalkenov, the schools have been designed in line with international standards and modern teaching practices. They will be five stories tall and consist of seven educational blocks that can be attached to existing schools. A separate project has also been developed to build 16 modern kindergartens. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/24/cott.body: Photo: Madina A'zam / Gazeta Uzbekistan to monitor working conditions of cotton pickers from 25 September Uzbekistan will begin monitoring the working conditions of cotton pickers from 25 September. Monitoring teams will visit randomly selected farms, check employment contracts and wage payments and investigate reports of possible violations of workers' rights. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 24 September 2026, 13:13 Society The national monitoring of working conditions for cotton pickers during the 2026 season will run from 25 September to 31 October . Its aim is to prevent child and forced labor in the fields. The Federation of Trade Unions of Uzbekistan announced the launch of the monitoring last week. The monitoring teams include 65 specialists — five from each region. They represent sectoral trade unions and the federation’s labor inspectors, as well as the Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the National Association of Non-Governmental Non-Profit Organizations. Every Monday and Saturday at 7:00, team leaders receive random GPS coordinates for up to three locations in their region. They leave for inspections at 9:00. Data and photo reports are submitted to the federation daily. Since 15 September, the federation and its regional branches have established round-the-clock duty services for the entire season. Workers can report violations of their labor rights by calling the short number 1092, via the Federation of Trade Unions' website or its Telegram bot . A total of 200 banners have been placed across Uzbekistan, with another 10,000 posters being prepared. 200,000 leaflets containing information on workers' rights will also be distributed among cotton pickers. Advertising on Gazeta “The current situation cannot even be compared with 2020, let alone with the situation a decade ago. Previously, there was no administrative or criminal liability for forced labor. Now, the Administrative Code has been strengthened, and a separate article has been added to the Criminal Code,” deputy chairman of the Federation of Trade Unions Bakhtiyor Makhmadaliev said. According to him, the Federation of Trade Unions has not recorded cases of child or forced labor during its monitoring in recent years. The main problems identified include delayed wage payments, work without contracts and inadequate working conditions. Monitoring continues partly because international organizations place greater trust in results obtained by non-governmental organizations. Katerina Gorbunova, a representative of the Better Cotton Initiative program in Uzbekistan, said the need for such monitoring would disappear only with the introduction of mechanization. The organization certifies more than 20% of the world’s cotton and has conducted its own monitoring of working conditions in Uzbekistan since 2022. “Take large farms in the United States or Brazil: a 10,000-hectare farm may have just three workers, so monitoring simply does not make sense. But when the same 10,000 hectares require 5,000 temporary workers, it is a completely different situation,” she explained. According to Gorbunova, a significant share of the population is involved in manual cotton picking during the cotton season. Three or four years ago, around 2 million people were mobilized to pick cotton each year, most of them working informally. Informal employment is common in agriculture worldwide, not only in Uzbekistan. The sector generally carries greater labor-rights risks than any other. Therefore, Gorbunova describes monitoring not as a punitive tool, but as a form of support for workers and a way to educate farmers. Farmers, as employers, generally have limited knowledge of labor legislation, and monitoring gradually helps them learn the relevant requirements. The results of last year’s monitoring show the types of violations faced by cotton pickers. The Federation of Trade Unions did not identify any cases of child or forced labor in 2025. At the same time, inspectors recorded: 166 cases of delayed wage payments, affecting 8,752 cotton pickers; 227 cases of work without an employment contract, affecting 9,075 people; 1,222 cotton pickers working at 24 farms and clusters without adequate working and rest conditions. All identified wage arrears were fully repaid, Makhmadaliev said in response to Gazeta’s question about how such disputes are resolved. “Regarding wage payments, it was established that 8,752 cotton pickers had not received their money on time. Our inspectors worked with the heads of the farms to resolve the issue, and the arrears were fully repaid. If a violation is not resolved on site, the materials are submitted to the State Labor Inspectorate for fines. If this also fails to produce a result, the case is referred to the prosecutor’s office, which oversees compliance with the law,” he said. Minimum working-condition requirements are approved every August by the Republican Tripartite Commission on Social and Labor Issues, which includes representatives of the government, trade unions and employers. Under these requirements, field camps must have toilets, showers, hot meals and clean drinking water. The State Labor Inspectorate under the Ministry of Employment and Poverty Reduction also conducted its own inspections during the previous season. Inspectors visited 986 farms and fined 116 officials a total of 397.44 million soums for non-payment of wages. The inspectorate’s hotline 1176 and Telegram bot received 222 complaints about delayed payments. As a result, 1.785 billion soums in unpaid wages was recovered for cotton pickers. The overall results of the 2026 monitoring season will be presented in December. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/25/glob.body: Photo: Shuhrat Latipov / Gazeta Tashkent ranks 343rd in 2026 Global Cities Index Tashkent rose 128 places in the 2026 Global Cities Index by Oxford Economics, ranking 343rd among the world’s 1,000 largest cities. The capital scored highly for human capital and the economy. The environmental and governance indicators also slightly improved. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 25 September 2026, 13:43 Society Tashkent ranked 343rd out of the world’s 1,000 largest cities in the 2026 Global Cities Index , compiled by the Oxford Economics research firm. The capital of Uzbekistan climbed 128 places over the year, up from 471st last year. Oxford Economics also included Tashkent among 28 Cities to Watch — cities showing strong momentum and potential for significant progress in the coming years. “Tashkent is becoming one of the most promising urban economic centers in Central Asia. Before the collapse of the Soviet Union, Tashkent was a major industrial city... However, after gaining independence and entering international markets, the city’s economy became more diversified. Today, Uzbekistan’s capital is experiencing steady growth, accompanied by a construction boom and an inflow of investment into various sectors of the economy. In addition, unlike many other cities in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, the city has seen sustained population growth,” the ranking said. The city’s geographic location and skilled workforce are among its main strengths, according to the ranking. At the same time, Oxford Economics noted that low GDP per capita increases the risk of a “brain drain” to wealthier countries. Another major issue requiring attention, according to the ranking’s authors, is environmental pressure, particularly water scarcity. Tashkent’s indicators The ranking covers five categories: economics, human capital, quality of life, environment and governance. Each category is scored on a 0−100 scale, with the results combined into an overall score. Advertising on Gazeta In the Economy category, Tashkent scored 54.7 points and ranked 188th globally (top 20%; previously 558th). Oxford Economics assesses the size, structure and growth rate of a city’s economy, considering both historical performance and future prospects. In Human Capital, Tashkent scored 61.5 points and ranked 108th globally (top 20%; previously 123rd). The category measures the size and quality of a city’s skilled workforce, as well as its ability to attract, develop and retain skilled professionals. In Quality of Life, Tashkent scored 47.5 points and ranked 644th globally, placing it in the bottom 40% of the ranking (previously 565th). The indicator measures residents' wellbeing and satisfaction, as well as living conditions, including people’s financial situation, health and access to urban infrastructure. In Environment, Tashkent scored 45.1 points and ranked 806th globally, placing it in the bottom 20% of the ranking (previously 872nd). The indicator measures a city’s ability to balance development with environmental protection, as well as its exposure to environmental risks. Tashkent received its lowest score among the five categories for Governance — 40.2 points, ranking 825th globally and placing it in the bottom 20%. However, its position improved by 15 places from last year, when it ranked 840th. The indicator reflects the resilience of urban institutions, the quality of regulation and the stability of conditions for residents and businesses. “Effective governance underpins a city’s ability to plan, invest and meet the needs of residents and businesses,” the ranking explained. In December 2025, president of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev instructed officials to move Tashkent into the top 300 cities with sustainable environmental conditions in the Global Cities Index. Plans included creating artificial water bodies and expanding green areas. Top cities The leading positions in the ranking are held by cities in the United States, Europe and Asia. New York ranked first with 100 points, followed by London with 98.8 points. Both cities scored highly in economics and human capital. Paris ranked third with 93.4 points. The top 10 also includes Seattle, San Francisco, Dublin, Boston, San Jose, Tokyo and Zurich. Among Central Asian cities, Almaty ranked 265th, while Astana ranked 281st. Bishkek ranked 461st, Ashgabat 668th and Dushanbe 672nd. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 7 314 # global cities index # tashkent

https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/28/uzbe.body: Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE Uzbekistan wins Chess Olympiad in Samarkand Uzbekistan’s first men’s team won the World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. Its main rival, India, drew with Hungary in the final round, securing first place for Uzbekistan. This is the team’s second Olympic gold after its triumph in Chennai in 2022. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 28 September 2026, 00:08 Sport Uzbekistan’s first men’s team became the champion of the 46th World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. The team secured the gold medal after its main rival, India, drew 2−2 with Hungary in the final round. Uzbekistan then defeated Ukraine 2.5−1.5 in its own final match. Before the final round, Uzbekistan led with 18 match points, one point ahead of India. For Uzbekistan, this is its second Olympic gold in the last three Olympiads. In 2022, the team won the title for the first time in Chennai, while two years later it took bronze in Budapest. India finished second, while Germany took third place. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/10/06/safa.body: Sodiq Safoyev. “Central Asia is becoming more predictable” — senator Sodiq Safoyev Central Asia is becoming more predictable amid global instability, senator Sodiq Safoyev said. He called for Consultative Meetings to be elevated to a new institutional level. According to him, further rapprochement between the countries of the region requires strengthening trust and shared values. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 6 October 2026, 10:35 Politics First deputy chairman of the Senate of the Oliy Majlis of Uzbekistan Sodiq Safoyev spoke on 1 October in Baku at a regional forum of the CAMCA (Central Asia, Mongolia, Caucasus, Afghanistan) network, which brings together the countries of Central Asia and the Caucasus, as well as Mongolia and Afghanistan. He said that amid the international crisis, Central Asia is becoming a more predictable and attractive region, but that further development requires stronger cooperation, regional identity and trust. Gazeta presents the main quotes from his speech. “Being a crossroads is the destiny of Central Asia” Speaking about the role of Central Asia and the region, Safoyev noted that the perception of Central Asia as a crossroads is not new. “For Central Asia, perhaps it’s a destiny to be in a crossroads. From time immemorial, it has been a region connecting different macro-regions, a region which has changed so many times its borders, composition, predominant faith, languages,” he said. Advertising on Gazeta However, according to him, the world itself is now at a crossroads: “What we’re observing today is something unusual worldwide. And of course, Central Asia and the CAMCA region are centrally located and under the effect of the main trends worldwide. And if we are trying to make an analysis of current ongoing or unfolding events in the CAMCA region and its future, we might consider it within the framework of the general context.” According to Safoyev, the world is in a state of polycrisis, which he described as the simultaneous occurrence of several catastrophic events. He said he had never witnessed a situation like this in his lifetime. “Crisis follows another crisis: bloody wars, sanctions, disruption of the chain of supply, etc. And mistrust among the leading actors. And acceptance of using the force, which is, to my mind, very insane. Last year, the world’s spending on the armaments was $2.7 trillion, while 1 billion people worldwide were living in miserable conditions,” Safoyev stressed. In his assessment, this indicates a transformation of the global order. “Which doesn’t mean the ignorance of international law, fragmentation, and I define it as a main crisis is that the world is not getting less connected. Globalization is not abolished. There is no process of deglobalization. But at the same time, trust and mutual understanding among the nations and major actors are going away. It’s very dangerous combination.” “It is manifested in the disregard for international law and fragmentation. At the same time, the main crisis is that the world is not becoming less interconnected: globalization has not been cancelled, and there is no process of deglobalization. However, trust and mutual understanding between states and key players are disappearing. This is a dangerous combination: interconnectedness is growing while trust is disappearing.” The senator stressed the need for collective action and joint efforts to address global challenges. “But at the same time, the ability of major international agencies and institutions like the United Nations and others to address these challenges is at a critically minimal level. The unfortunate point is that this crisis will not be over tomorrow or in the coming years. We are just entering a long period of world transformation. And for us, the CAMCA region, we should know about that. And there must be a joint response of the countries of this region,” he said. Central Asia as a more predictable region Safoyev noted that despite the bleak picture of global developments, opposite trends can be observed in Central Asia and the broader CAMCA region. “Astonishingly, the CAMCA area and Central Asia have some reverse tendencies. I talk about the decline of multilateral diplomacy, but in the CAMCA area, multilateral diplomacy is enhancing year by year. It’s very interesting that before, Central Asia was defined in many definitions, mainly due to its proximity to major regional or global powers. Today, more and more, Central Asia is not just a post-Soviet area, not ‘another stans,' not something in between, but the region linking major markets, major powers.” The senator also addressed the concept of landlocked and stressed that Central Asia is gradually transforming from a landlocked region into a land-linked region, meaning a region connected to other spaces. “Look to the family of the transatlantic community, the Islamic world, the Arab world, etc. Everywhere, we are observing fragmentation. But in the CAMCA region, there are going to be some gravitating forces bringing us together.” Safoyev linked these processes, in particular, to the transformation of Uzbekistan’s foreign policy under president Shavkat Mirziyoyev. “In Central Asia, we’re today seeing a very strong tendency to consolidate cooperation. I’m not talking about integration. Maybe today we should restrain from using the word ‘integration'; it’s too strong. But stronger and deeper cooperation is going on,” he said. In his assessment, this makes the region more predictable. “One point which the world is missing today is predictability. And if we’re talking about geopolitical uncertainty in the world, today we might be more optimistic about the CAMCA region and Central Asia. This means Central Asia is becoming more attractive worldwide,” Safoyev explained. He also recalled the decision to admit Azerbaijan as a full participant in the Consultative Meetings. “I think that it’s a time to transform the Consultative Meetings of Central Asian head of states to kind of maybe council or another institution, which will not just be a consultative meeting, but something beyond that,” he said. The senator also mentioned that two years ago, the leaders of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan held a summit in Baku that created a “solid geostrategic triangle”. Voluntary cooperation and regional identity Speaking about integration, Safoyev stressed that it should first and foremost be voluntary. “Forced integration, when someone forces you to join some kind of formation, is never durable and never sustainable. You must gain politically and economically from joining some kind of formation. Secondly, and first of all, coming back, it must have a well-defined goal of integration,” he said. The senator noted that benefits are important, but that the main elements of any integration are shared values and common principles: “Any economic gain or political or security matters cannot replace this most important ingredient. Creating these shared values is perhaps the most important challenge for CAMCA and the Central Asian region.” He suggested calling this “regional identity”. At the same time, he said, this identity does not need to be created, as it already exists thanks to the region’s rich history; rather, it needs to be strengthened and reinforced. Speaking about values, Safoyev gave a personal example: “Here in Baku, I feel myself like at home. Being in the streets, talking to the people on the streets. It’s the same way of thinking, the same mentality. Likewise, being in Almaty or Dushanbe or Bishkek, or in Ashgabat and Georgia. I always feel myself among those who are close to me by their way of life, hospitality, cherishing the same values, like respect for the elders, respect for your neighbors, respecting your neighborhood.” Middle Corridor and infrastructure of trust Speaking about closer ties between Central Asia and the South Caucasus, Safoyev highlighted the importance of the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspi

https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/24/audi.body: Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Tashkent apartment buildings to undergo energy audits with World Bank participation Apartment buildings in Tashkent will undergo energy audits involving World Bank specialists. Experts will assess the technical and energy condition of the buildings, identify sources of heat loss and develop solutions to address them. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 24 September 2026, 13:12 Society From 21 September , apartment buildings in Tashkent are undergoing comprehensive energy audits involving World Bank specialists, the city hokimiyat (administration) said . The buildings selected for the audit are those that were heated in violation of regulatory requirements during the previous heating season. The audit will examine the technical and energy condition of the buildings, including exterior walls, roofs and basements, doors and windows, internal heating systems and the efficiency of heat use. Advertising on Gazeta Foreign specialists will also conduct instrumental measurements, identify the main factors causing heat loss in each building and develop technical solutions to address them, the city hokimiyat said. Based on the results of the energy audits, a methodology for efficient heating of apartment buildings in Tashkent is planned to be developed. It will take into account the technical condition and energy efficiency of buildings, the level of heat loss and other indicators. According to the city hokimiyat, the methodology will serve as a basis for assessing the energy efficiency of buildings, identifying those that require modernization and developing measures to reduce heat loss and ensure the efficient use of electricity and natural gas. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/25/tenn.body: Photo: Muhammad Amin, UzA Uzbekistan plans to resume ATP and WTA tennis tournaments Uzbekistan plans to resume hosting international ATP and WTA tournaments and ITF competitions. The authorities also plan to develop school tennis and aim to place the country among Asia’s top five in tennis by 2030. Some tennis courts will move to self-financing or be transferred to investors. На русском языке Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida 25 September 2026, 10:27 Sport Uzbekistan plans to once again host international tennis tournaments under the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) and Women’s Tennis Association (WTA). The regular hosting of such competitions is provided for in a presidential decree dated 21 September. According to the document, starting from 1 October 2026, Uzbekistan will regularly host international ATP and WTA tournaments, as well as competitions of the International Tennis Federation (ITF). The costs of organizing these tournaments and prize money will be financed through charitable donations. In addition, the Uzbekistan Cup for juniors and adults, national championships for juniors, teenagers and adults, the international Uzbekistan Open tournament and a men’s ATP Challenger tournament will be held regularly. Uzbekistan has previously hosted top-level professional tournaments. The men’s ATP President’s Cup was held in Tashkent from 1997 to 2002. No ATP Tour tournaments have been held in the capital since 2002. Advertising on Gazeta The WTA Tashkent Open was held from 1999 to 2019. The last tournament took place on 23−28 September 2019. Starting in 2020, a tournament in Lyon took its place on the WTA calendar. Uzbekistan has also hosted ITF competitions over the years. In particular, a W15 tournament was scheduled to take place in Tashkent in March 2026, but it was cancelled. Tennis in schools From 1 January 2027, the Juniors Tennis Initiative program will be launched in schools. Basic tennis lessons aimed at increasing students' interest in the sport will be held during physical education classes for pupils in grades 1−4. Schools will be selected based on students' interest and the availability of the necessary infrastructure. Tennis sections will be established, facilities will be upgraded and equipment, including tennis practice walls, will be installed. The costs will be covered by the Uzbekistan Tennis Federation. The classes will be taught by trainers from sports schools located near the selected schools. The Tennis Federation will also take over management of the Republican Tennis School of Olympic Reserve. Within two months, the federation must attract foreign specialists and coaches. Starting in 2027, international ITF competitions are planned to be held at the school. Goal: enter Asia’s top five By 2030, the authorities plan to increase the number of regular tennis players to 3,000 and the number of coaches to 200. Another goal is for Uzbekistan to enter the top five Asian countries in tennis and include tennis among the country’s promising sports. Some tennis courts to move to self-financing From 1 January 2027, tennis courts at sports and educational institutions that can provide paid services will switch to self-financing. The institutions themselves will be able to set service fees. The funds raised must first be used to cover utility costs, while sports organizations will be able to dispose of the remaining funds at their discretion. Courts whose revenues do not cover operating costs and which require renovation may be transferred to private investors through public-private partnerships. However, training sessions for existing groups must remain free of charge. By 1 January 2027, the authorities must conduct an inventory of state-owned tennis courts and prepare a list of facilities eligible for transfer to investors. Budget funds saved through the transition to self-financing will be used to provide tennis players with vitamins, sportswear and other necessary supplies. The decree also establishes cash rewards for winners and medalists of the Asian Games and Asian Para Games: athletes will receive $25,000 for gold, $12,500 for silver and $6,250 for bronze. Coaches will receive $10,000, $5,000 and $2,500, respectively. Subscribe to our Telegram channel Gazeta 6 482 # tennis

https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/28/cong.body: Photo: Saida Mirziyoyeva / Telegram Uzbekistan to host UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in 2031 Uzbekistan will host the 16th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in 2031. The decision was approved at the 15th Congress in the UAE. “I see this as an important sign of international trust in Uzbekistan,” Saida Mirziyoyeva, head of Presidential Administration, said. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 28 September 2026, 18:51 Politics Uzbekistan will host the 16th UN Congress on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice in 2031, head of the Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva said. She participated in the 15th Congress, currently underway in Abu Dhabi, UAE. The decision is also enshrined in the Abu Dhabi Declaration adopted by the congress. “I see this as an important sign of international trust in Uzbekistan. Trust in our openness, our willingness to engage in dialogue and join forces for a common goal. Five years of preparation lie ahead,” Saida Mirziyoyeva wrote on her Telegram channel. The focus of this year’s congress is the relationship between crime prevention, criminal justice, the rule of law and digital transformation. Advertising on Gazeta Issues under consideration include fighting transnational crime, terrorism, drug trafficking, corruption and environmental violations, as well as protection of children and strengthening the rule of law. Speaking at the event, Saida Mirziyoyeva noted: “We live at a difficult moment in human history. Crises are affecting one region after another. Crime is taking on new forms. It crosses borders easily, moves through technology, and adapts faster than the system designed to contain it.” She stressed that crime prevention and justice “cannot remain abstract ideas discussed from a distance; they must reach people or they will mean nothing”. The congress runs from 26 September to 1 October. The event has been held every five years since 1955 in different parts of the world. As a global forum, the congress facilitates the exchange of information and best practices among states and experts working in this field, including from international organizations, civil society, and academia. During the congress, Saida Mirziyoyeva met with Monica Juma, UN under-secretary-general and executive director of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. “We actively collaborate with the UNODC and implement joint projects,” she noted. The head of the Presidential Administration also met with UAE president Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. They discussed expanding trade and economic cooperation between the countries and touched on the development of artificial intelligence. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/23/ches.body: Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE “Cautious optimism” justified: Uzbekistan’s performance halfway through Chess Olympiad Uzbekistan’s men’s national team has won all six matches at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand and leads the standings outright. In the sixth round, the hosts defeated defending champions India. China awaits next. Gazeta reviews the performances of the country’s three men’s and three women’s teams. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 23 September 2026, 19:11 Sport Halfway through the international Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, both Uzbekistan’s men’s and women’s teams are living up to their supporters' expectations and challenging for the top places. Gazeta columnist Georgy Shvanov takes a closer look at their performances. After the sixth round, Uzbekistan’s men’s national team moved into sole possession of first place in the tournament. The team consists of Nodirbek Abdusattorov (2762), Javokhir Sindarov (2778), Nodirbek Yakubboev (2685), Shamsiddin Vokhidov (2654) and Mukhiddin Madaminov (2611), all five of whom are grandmasters. Particular attention at this Olympiad is focused on Sindarov, who is set to play a match for the world chess title later this year. After six rounds, having missed one, he has scored 4 points out of a possible 5, with three wins and two draws. Sindarov’s preparation and participation in international tournaments, including the Chess Olympiad, as well as his work with coaches, are supported by the National Bank of Uzbekistan . Javokhir Sindarov. Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE Advertising on Gazeta Before the competition began, coach of Uzbekistan’s first men’s team Rustam Kasimdzhanov said he had “cautious optimism”. Serious tests for his players began in the third round, when Uzbekistan faced Austria, led by experienced grandmaster Kirill Alekseenko, who competed in the 2020−2021 Candidates Tournament. The classic team strategy worked in that match: players with the black pieces aimed to hold their opponents, while those playing White sought to win. The result was two wins and two draws, giving Uzbekistan a 3−1 victory. They were followed by Türkiye, which many experts considered a highly underrated team. In the fourth round, 15-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, playing on the first board, scored 4.5 points out of 5 and had already entered the online top 20. He had the initiative against Abdusattorov as well, but in a better position opted to repeat the position. Sindarov and Vokhidov drew their games with the black pieces, while Yakubboev, playing on the third board, found a refutation to Vahap Sanal’s adventurous idea. His opponent had played inaccurately in the opening, which resulted in the loss of a pawn. Yakubboev went on to win comfortably, securing a 2.5−1.5 victory for Uzbekistan. In the fifth round, Uzbekistan faced Hungary. On the first board, the Europeans fielded Richard Rapport, a top grandmaster known for his unconventional style, while on the second board was his complete chess opposite, the extremely resilient Peter Leko, who once played Vladimir Kramnik in a World Championship match. But neither their status nor their experience helped the Hungarian players. When Abdusattorov and Yakubboev confidently and quickly reached winning positions, Sindarov and Vokhidov could have offered draws to secure the team victory. Instead, they continued playing and eventually overcame their opponents, finishing the match with a clean 4−0 score. Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Gukesh Dommaraju. Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE India, another Olympiad favorite, was also moving at a strong pace. In the first round, Arjun Erigaisi unexpectedly lost to young international master Prin Laohawirapap from Thailand, but after that India went on a long winning run, taking victory in all five of its remaining matches. The sixth-round match between Uzbekistan and India carried additional symbolism: it brought together the winners of the previous two Olympiads. Uzbekistan won the tournament in Chennai in 2022, while India won in Budapest in 2024. The opening stages confirmed that the match would be difficult. Abdusattorov failed to gain an advantage against Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa, while Sindarov was holding a strategically questionable position against Erigaisi. Vokhidov equalized against reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju. All three games ended in draws, leaving Yakubboev’s game against Nihal Sarin as the decider. Nodirbek Yakubboev. Photo: Michal Walusza Yakubboev’s position was no better, but in a sense it was safer. Apparently, this prompted him to reject a simple continuation that would have been sufficient for a draw and instead choose a line that was objectively losing but allowed him to create attacking chances. By move 31, the situation looked particularly unpleasant: Yakubboev had less than 10 minutes remaining, while Sarin, known for his fast play, had 38 minutes. However, Sarin was the first to lose his composure. Sarin played overly optimistically, exposing his king to attacks. He first missed a winning opportunity and then allowed a tactical blow following a knight fork, which led to Yakubboev’s victory. Yakubboev later admitted that this moment of the game was very emotional for him. https://twitter.com/ChessbaseIndia/status/2102055391454757319 Thus, Uzbekistan won all six of its matches without losing a single individual game. The main rivals, defending champions India, have already been defeated, but there is no room for complacency. In the seventh round, Uzbekistan will face China — another dangerous opponent and a two-time Olympic champion. Over the first six rounds, China has missed out on a team victory only once, drawing with Armenia. Former world champion Ding Liren appears to be returning his form and defeated German grandmaster Vincent Keymer, who is in the world top 10. China won the match 3−1. Ding Liren. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta Wei Yi, who competed in the latest Candidates Tournament, is also performing excellently. He began with three wins over grandmasters before holding two games with the black pieces against strong opponents. Although Sindarov is unlikely to fear a meeting with the Chinese grandmaster, whom he has defeated both at the World Cup and in the Candidates Tournament — Sindarov won the Candidates Tournament in April this year and is now awaiting his World Championship match against Dommaraju — the balance of power in this matchup is far from clear. Javokhir Sindarov and Wei Yi at the Candidates Tournament. Photo: Michal Walusza Besides China, Armenia could also pose a challenge for Uzbekistan. Their team spirit has repeatedly compensated for differences in ratings. The United States could also become a threat if they manage to find their rhythm and reach the pace expected of a team of their status. Uzbekistan’s second team is also producing excellent results. Its lineup consists of Jakhongir Vakhidov (2527), Abdimalik Abdisalimov (2548), Mukhammadzokhid Suyarov (2540), Khumoyun Begmuratov (2514) and Ortik Nigmatov (2484). Pavel Eljanov is the captain. Photo: Evgeniy Sorochin / Gazeta After six rounds, the team is in 13th place. Having lost only to the strong German team, Uzbekistan’s second team has defeated all its other opponents, including a strong Spanish side. On the first board, Vakhidov has held his own against some of the strongest players from other countries, while Abdisalimov and Suyarov, playing on the second and third boards, can be described as the team’s “hitters”. https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/24/said.body: Photo: UN Photo/Laura Jarriel “Uzbekistan's choice is human dignity”. What Saida Mirziyoyeva said at UN GA session Head of Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva spoke on behalf of Uzbekistan at the general debate of the UN General Assembly. She touched upon issues like Uzbekistan’s position on modern challenges, including AI, expectations from the UN, changes in the country and Central Asia. Full text. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 24 September 2026, 10:24 Politics Head of Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva spoke on behalf of Uzbekistan at the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on 23 September. In her speech in Uzbek language, she touched upon such issues as Uzbekistan’s position on modern challenges, including AI, expectations from the UN, reforms in the country and changes in the region of Central Asia, and underscored the importance of human dignity and justice. Gazeta presents the speech in full with minor editing. Uzbekistan chooses human dignity Today, humanity does not live in an easy time. Wars continue around the world. Geopolitical tensions are escalating. Trust is fading. Inequality is increasing. The times like these countries are faced with a choice. Uzbekistan, under the leadership of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, has made its choice. That is openness. Good relations with neighbors. The dialogue with the world. Advertising on Gazeta Openness does not translate into weakness On the contrary, striving for peace means taking responsibility for the future. We see: counties are posed with the question: “Which side do you choose?” Uzbekistan’s response is clear. Our choice is human dignity. We choose young people who are determined to pursue education, acquire a profession and define their own future. Because we do not measure the true strength of a statehood by its military or economic capacity. The country’s might is determined, first and foremost, by the extent to which it can protect human dignity, rights, and interests. Therefore, we view peace, development, and human dignity not as three separate goals, but as a single, unified task. Need for UN capable of implementing decisions Today, no nation, however powerful can address all global problems alone. None of the threats stop at national borders. That is why we need the United Nations more than ever. We do not need the UN that discusses the conflict after it occurred. But the organization capable of preventing one. We need the UN, capable of implementing decisions, not just making them. We need the UN where voices of every country are heard. Uzbekistan supports the UN Secretary-General's efforts within the framework of the UN-80 Initiative, aimed at adapting the organization to modern requirements. We support expanding the composition of the UN Security Council based on modern realities. Next year, Uzbekistan will take up the chairmanship of the Non-Aligned Movement. At a time of escalating tensions, we take this as a responsibility to create new platforms for dialogue. In that spirit, Uzbekistan has offered its candidacy for the nonpermanent membership in the Security Council for 2035 and 2036. We count on your support. For us, the international law is not an instrument that changes based on the interests. It is a common rule for all countries. There cannot be universal justice without universal law. Photo: Saida Mirziyoyeva / Telegram. Central Asia and Afghanistan Until recently, Central Asia was often mentioned against the backdrop of unresolved border disputes, water resource management issues, and many other conflicts. Thanks to the initiative of the President of Uzbekistan and the political will of the Central Asian heads of state, the situation and atmosphere in the region have completely changed. We began to view each other as partners not as source of threat. The same is true of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s approach to the Afghan issue. Viewing Afghanistan solely as a source of danger will not solve the problem. Nor it is a way out to leave multi-ethnic Afghan people alone with their problems. They must be given hope and confidence to achieve a peaceful life. Reforms for people The reforms being implemented by the head of Uzbekistan are primarily based on the criterion of whether people’s lives are improving. We measure the results by this very criterion. Over the past 10 years, the purchasing power of our population has doubled. Our economy grew from $50 billion to $147 billion. More than $150 billion in foreign investment has been attracted. Exports have almost tripled. The poverty rate dropped to 4 percent, and nearly 10 million people were lifted out of poverty. Preschool education coverage increased from 27 percent to 78 percent. Higher education coverage grew from 9 percent to nearly 50 percent. Average life expectancy rose from 66 to over 75 years. Maternal and infant mortality decreased fourfold. The true value of the reform is reflected in the lives of these people. A child is the state’s greatest responsibility. If a child is not born healthy and does not receive a quality education, we put the future of not just one person, but the entire society at risk. In the coming days, we will hold a high-level dialogue with the United Nations Population Fund on issues of demographic stability and human capital. And in October, we will bring together the international community in Samarkand around the issue of children’s well-being. Aral Sea lessons to the world Central Asia has another lesson that it can offer the whole world. That is the Aral Sea. It did not dry up due to a natural disaster. This is a consequence of decades of wrong decision and unjust treatment of nature. New Uzbekistan is creating green areas on the dried seabed to reduce the scale of this problem. We are introducing modern water-saving technologies. We aim to increase the share of renewable energy to 54 percent by 2030. We do not want the Aral Sea to remain merely a symbol of environmental tragedy. It should become a testing ground for environmental solutions. At the initiative of Uzbekistan, the UN General Assembly declared 2027−2036 the “Decade of Action for Afforestation and Reforestation.” The time has come to back this resolution with practical results. Humanity must be at heart of technological progress Today, humanity stands on the brink of another massive transformation. I speak of artificial intelligence. But one question remains unanswered: Does technology serve humankind, or are we forced to adapt to technology? However, the principle must be clear. Humanity and its destiny must be at the heart of technological progress. Artificial intelligence must be inseparable from human rights, security, equal opportunity, and accountability. Technological progress should not force people to change, but rather serve to improve human life. Uzbekistan advocates strengthening international dialogue in this regard. Power is not above law The power is not above the law. Every person who turns to the court, regardless of who they are, must have faith that justice will prevail. A separate international commercial court based on the principles of English law is being established at the Tashkent International Financial Centre. We have eradicated child labor and systemic forced labor. We have tightened the responsibility for domestic violence. We also rely on this criterion when it comes to women’s rights and opportunities. Therefore, we have created a separate system to support women’s entrepreneurship. Today, women make 39 percent of our parliament. In Tashkent, the Islamic Civilization Center was built at the initiative of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. We see it not only as a place that showcases the past, but as a house of knowledge, thought, and enlightenment. Today, in an era when social networks and artificial intelligence are spreading hatred and stereotypes at a rapid pace, it is important to remind this truth once again. Uzbekistan

https://www.gazeta.uz/en/2026/09/29/op-e.body: Photo: Husniddin Ato / UNDP Uzbekistan’s future will increasingly be shaped in its cities. Op-ed Cities are not just places where people live and work. They are where many of today’s most complex challenges converge. By adopting integrated approaches to urban development, it is possible to strengthen institutions and enhance their resilience to future changes. Op-ed by Anas Fayyad Qarman. Ўзбек тилида O‘zbek tilida На русском языке 29 September 2026, 10:21 Columns Economy Author: Anas Fayyad Qarman, UNDP Deputy Resident Representative in Uzbekistan. According to recent census data, Uzbekistan is now a majority-urban country, with 54.5% of its population living in urban areas. Yet urbanization is uneven — from 100% in Tashkent City to under 40% in Khorezm. At the same time, a young population, including 21.7 million people of working age, and more than 2 million people already moving for work are reshaping where opportunities are created and where pressures are felt. These trends put cities increasingly at the center of Uzbekistan’s transformation. Cities are no longer simply places where people live and work; they are where many of today’s most complex challenges converge from economic uncertainty and demographic change to climate pressures and social inequalities. But they are also where many of the solutions can emerge. Advertising on Gazeta Photo: Husniddin Ato / UNDP. For many years, governments and UNDP have supported cities in addressing development challenges through targeted, locally focused projects. As urban challenges become increasingly interconnected and complex, there is an opportunity to build on these efforts by moving toward more integrated approaches that strengthen coordination, connect local priorities with national ambitions, and give cities a greater role in shaping their own development pathways. This also means ensuring that ambitious national goals are matched with the guidance, capacities and financing needed for implementation at the local level, while enabling cities to mobilize diverse resources and make decisions that translate growth and investment into tangible benefits for their communities. Adding to this, new technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital platforms are rapidly changing how economies work. This creates a huge opportunity but also a risk. Without smart planning, cities might see value and jobs go elsewhere, rather than being created and kept locally. This isn’t a problem for tomorrow; it’s happening right now. Solution: integrated, systemic approach So, how can cities truly get ahead and turn these challenges into opportunities? If you look carefully, transport is not only a transport issue, it also affects access to jobs, air quality, productivity and inclusion. Also, housing is not only about buildings, it connects to land use, infrastructure, mobility, energy and affordability. Photo: Husniddin Ato / UNDP. Hence, the answer lies in moving beyond scattered projects to integrated systemic approaches. This means looking at all these problems as connected parts of a bigger system, working together, learning, and adapting. To this day, UNDP globally has a lot of experience helping cities do just that. Here is a breakdown of how cities can use this approach: Understand the System : Start by listening to communities, identifying how challenges are interconnected, and anticipating future trends. Build Integrated Portfolios : Move beyond isolated projects by developing portfolios of connected actions that allow cities to test solutions, learn what works, and consider financing from the outset. Mobilize Partnerships and Investment : Bring together government, communities, investors, the private sector and development partners to turn promising solutions into scalable and investable opportunities. Build Capacity, Learn and Adapt : Strengthen local skills and institutions, continuously learn from implementation, and establish ways of working that sustain collaboration and innovation over time. UNDP can support cities throughout this process, drawing on its experience in systems thinking, portfolio approaches and capacity development. Real-world success stories This is not inventing a wheel — this is bringing global experience to Uzbekistan. Various initiatives are already putting these ideas into action. These programmes have involved over 450 cities and helped train over 1000 city officials. For example, in Kapan, Armenia, the city used this approach to reimagine tourism as a way to boost community wellbeing and local identity. Kutaisi, Georgia, developed a vision as an eco-smart city, focusing on green innovation and involving its citizens. Ceadîr-Lunga, Moldova, tackled rising energy costs not just with new tech, but by involving citizens and building local skills for an energy transition. Not starting from zero Building on the findings of UNDP’s City Experiment Fund (CEF) and Mayors for Economic Growth (M4EG ) initiatives, in July 2026, the City of Namangan and UNDP convened a three-day Portfolio Design work to explore how digital technologies, artificial intelligence and systems thinking can support the city’s long-term urban economic transformation. Bringing together representatives of municipal and national government, universities, the private sector, development partners and the wider innovation ecosystem, this portfolio design marked the first major milestone in the development of Namangan’s Urban Digital Economy Portfolio. Photo: Husniddin Ato / UNDP. A key conclusion of the workshop was that Namangan is not starting from zero . The city already possesses many of the institutional, technological and human capabilities needed to support digital transformation, including advanced digital public services, universities, innovation programmes and strong national policy support. Participants consistently concluded that the city’s greatest opportunity lies not in creating entirely new systems, but in strengthening collaboration, connecting existing capabilities and unlocking greater value from the assets already in place. Looking to the future By adopting these integrated approaches, cities gain a lot. They get a clear, shared goal for their future, ensure everyone works together, and continuously test new solutions. Most importantly, their institutions become better prepared for future changes and uncertainty. This creates a pipeline of opportunities that attract investment and builds a strong foundation for lasting economic transformation. Ultimately, this empowers cities to stop simply reacting to change and instead become active shapers of their own economic and social futures. It’s about building cities that are not just resilient, but thriving, innovative, and future-ready. Photo: Kun.uz No temperature records were broken, but the month ranked among the warmest Septembers in the country’s meteorological records, according to a review published by Uzhydromet. Temperatures above average September brought typically warm early-autumn weather, without sharp temperature swings. Daytime temperatures across most of Uzbekistan generally ranged from 29°C to 34°C, rising to 35–37°C in some areas on the hottest days and reaching 38°C in the south and desert regions. These readings remained below the September temperature records, which stand at 38–40°C across most of the country and 41–42°C in the north, south and desert areas. Temperatures gradually declined during the final week of the month. Daytime highs generally stayed between 24°C and 27°C, reaching 28–30°C in the far south. The average monthly temperature was 1.2–2.5°C above normal across most of Uzbekistan. In the north and parts of the Fergana Valley, temperatures were close to the seasonal average. In Tashkent, September ranked fourth among the warmest months of its kind on record. Dry conditions across most of the country Rainfall was particularly scarce in September. Most of Uzbekistan, apart from the northern and eastern areas, received little or no rain, with only one to three episodes of brief, light showers in some locations. In most parts of Karakalpakstan and the Fergana Valley, however, rainfall exceeded the monthly norm by 1.5–3 times. In some areas, it was four to six times higher than average. Total precipitation in these areas reached 5–14 millimeters, compared with a typical September norm of 2–4 millimeters. Dust haze and strong winds Strong winds of 13–18 meters per second were recorded on some days in the north, south and desert areas, and less frequently in central Uzbekistan. Wind gusts reached 20–21 meters per second over the Ustyurt Plateau on September 2–3 and in the high-altitude areas of Tashkent region on September 20. In some locations, stronger winds stirred up dust close to the ground, while dust haze was frequently observed.

https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/10/08/world-.body: Photo: AP The bank also upgraded its 2027 growth forecast for Uzbekistan from 6.7% to 7.5%. The economy is expected to expand by 7.1% in 2028. The revised forecasts were published on October 6 in the World Bank’s latest Europe and Central Asia Economic Update, titled “Making AI Work: Jobs, Firms, and Productivity.” At 7.9%, Uzbekistan is expected to record the second-highest growth rate among developing economies in Europe and Central Asia in 2026, behind Kyrgyzstan at 9.6%. In 2027, Uzbekistan is projected to lead the group with 7.5% growth. The World Bank attributed Uzbekistan’s continued growth to resilient domestic demand, supported by higher real wages and employment, remittances and investment in infrastructure, energy and housing. It also pointed to ongoing structural reforms. Remittances to Uzbekistan rose 13% in the first half of 2026 to a record $9.2 billion for the period, with nearly 70% coming from Russia. Excluding gold, Uzbekistan’s exports increased by almost 30%, driven by stronger shipments to China and neighboring Central Asian countries. Overall exports declined, however, because of lower gold exports. The country also continues to attract substantial foreign direct investment, including into major energy, digital infrastructure and industrial projects. The World Bank said investments financed through foreign sources, including direct investment and loans, accounted for more than 70% of total investment in Uzbekistan. The bank expects Uzbekistan’s budget deficit to remain broadly unchanged in 2026 at 2.2% of GDP. Higher social and investment spending is expected to be offset by reduced energy subsidies and targeted lending to state-owned enterprises, along with stronger budget revenues. More than 60% of private-sector jobs in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan remain informal, with little change in the share over the past five years. The World Bank said current economic growth was not generating enough productive formal jobs as the working-age population continues to expand. Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion Central Asia remains the fastest-growing subregion of Europe and Central Asia, with economic growth projected at 5.8% in 2026. Domestic demand and government investment in transport and energy are expected to continue supporting activity.
